docs.title: Calvin Documentation
docs.text: Welcome to the Calvin documentation! Calvin is a lightweight, self-hosted home dashboard system for Raspberry Pi that displays calendars, photos, and external web services with keyboard navigation support.

docs.title: What is Calvin?
docs.text:
Calvin is a DAKBoard alternative designed to run on Raspberry Pi hardware. It provides:

  • 📅 Calendar Integration - Connect to Google Calendar and other calendar services
  • 🖼️ Photo Slideshow - Automatic image rotation and display
  • 🌐 Web Services - Embed external web services and content
  • ⌨️ Keyboard Navigation - Support for compact 7-button keyboards and full keyboards
  • 🔌 Plugin System - Extensible plugin architecture for custom functionality
  • 🔄 Hot Reload - Development mode with automatic reloading
  • 📱 Responsive Design - Works on various display sizes and orientations
  • 🐧 Cross-Platform - Develop on Windows/Linux, deploy on Raspberry Pi

docs.title: Documentation Setup
docs.text: This document describes the documentation structure and how to build it.

docs.title: Documentation System
docs.text: Calvin uses MkDocs with the Material theme for documentation. The documentation is automatically built and hosted on GitHub Pages.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Install documentation dependencies:

cd backend
uv sync --extra docs

Or using pip:

pip install -e backend[docs]

docs.title: Build Documentation
docs.text:
# From project root
mkdocs build

docs.title: Serve Documentation Locally
docs.text:
# From project root
mkdocs serve

This will start a local server (usually at http://127.0.0.1:8000) where you can view the documentation.

Auto-rebuild: mkdocs serve automatically watches for changes in the docs/ directory and mkdocs.yml file. When you save changes to any documentation file, MkDocs will automatically rebuild and refresh the browser. No need to manually restart the server!

Note: If you see a warning about README.md being excluded, this is expected. MkDocs automatically excludes README.md files when they conflict with index.md files. This is normal behavior.

docs.title: Documentation Structure
docs.text:
Documentation files are in the docs/ directory:

  • index.md - Home page
  • setup/ - Installation and setup guides
  • plugins/ - Plugin documentation
  • configuration/ - Configuration guides
  • testing/ - Testing documentation
  • archive/ - Archived/legacy documentation

docs.title: GitHub Pages Deployment
docs.text:
The documentation is automatically built and deployed to GitHub Pages via the .github/workflows/docs.yml workflow. The documentation is automatically built from the main branch when changes are pushed to the docs/ directory or mkdocs.yml file, and is available at:

https://osterbergsimon.github.io/calvin/

docs.title: Contributing Documentation
docs.text:

  1. Edit files in the docs/ directory
  2. Update mkdocs.yml navigation if adding new pages
  3. Test locally with mkdocs serve
  4. Commit and push - GitHub Actions will automatically build and deploy to GitHub Pages

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Calvin event system enables plugin-to-plugin communication and system-level event notifications. It uses an asyncio-based, in-memory event system that is lightweight, non-blocking, and requires no external dependencies.

docs.title: Design Principles
docs.text:
1. System-Emitted Events: Core system emits events for system-level operations
  2. Plugin-Emitted Events: Plugins can emit custom events for plugin-specific operations
  3. Centralized Detection: System automatically detects changes (e.g., new images) and emits events
  4. No Duplication: Plugins don't need to emit system events - the system handles it

docs.title: Event Delivery Patterns
docs.text:
• Fire-and-Forget (default): Events emitted asynchronously, handlers run in background, don't wait for results
  • Fire-and-Wait (optional): For critical events, wait for all handlers to complete

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Non-blocking: Event emission never blocks the main application
  • Error Isolation: One bad handler cannot crash the system or block other handlers
  • Rate Limiting: 10 events/second per plugin per event type (configurable)
  • No External Dependencies: Pure asyncio implementation

docs.title: Event Naming Convention
docs.text:
Calvin distinguishes two namespaces:

  • System-emitted events use bare snake_case names that describe a noun + past-tense verb: image_uploaded, plugin_enabled, plugin_instance_started. These are stable contracts — the host owns them and won't rename them silently.
  • Plugin-emitted events must be prefixed with the emitting plugin's type_id: <plugin_id>.<event_name>, e.g. image_processor.image_processed, mealie.recipe_imported. The prefix prevents collisions between independently developed plugins and makes log/trace output unambiguous.

Subscribers may listen to either namespace. When you emit an event from a plugin, always include the prefix; when you subscribe, match the exact name.

Legacy: Some early plugins (notably image-processor) emit unprefixed events like image_processed and image_processing_failed. New plugins should use the prefixed form. Existing emitters will be migrated incrementally; subscribers should tolerate both during the transition.

docs.title: Event Registry
docs.text: Quick lookup of every event name a plugin author may want to emit or subscribe to. The detailed schema for each event lives in the section below.

docs.title: System-emitted (stable contract)
docs.text: Event Emitted from Trigger image_uploaded LocalImagePlugin.scan_images() New image detected. image_deleted PluginImageService.delete_image() Image removed. plugin_enabled routes/plugins/management.update_plugin Plugin type enabled. plugin_disabled routes/plugins/management.update_plugin Plugin type disabled. plugin_installed routes/plugins/management.install_plugin Plugin installed. plugin_uninstalled routes/plugins/management.uninstall_plugin Plugin uninstalled. plugin_instance_created routes/plugins/instances.update_plugin_instance Instance row created. plugin_instance_updated routes/plugins/instances.update_plugin_instance Instance edited. plugin_instance_started routes/plugins/instances.start_plugin_instance Instance started. plugin_instance_stopped routes/plugins/instances.stop_plugin_instance Instance stopped.

docs.title: Plugin-emitted (example, not exhaustive)
docs.text:
Event Emitter Notes image_processed image-processor Legacy unprefixed name; will become image_processor.image_processed. image_processing_failed image-processor Same — will become image_processor.image_processing_failed.

If you add a new event in your plugin, add a row here in the same PR so other plugin authors can find it.

docs.title: System-Emitted Events
docs.text: These events are emitted by the core system automatically:

docs.title: image_uploaded
docs.text:
Emitted by: LocalImagePlugin.scan_images() when a new image is detected

When: - New image file appears in the local images directory - Works for ANY source: IMAP downloads, manual uploads, file system additions, etc.

Event Data: 

{
    "image_id": str,      # Unique image identifier
    "filename": str,      # Image filename
    "path": str,          # Full path to image file
    "plugin_id": str      # Plugin ID that detected the image (usually "local-images")
}

Important: Plugins that download images (like IMAP) don't need to emit this event. The system automatically detects new images during scan and emits the event.

docs.title: image_deleted
docs.text:
Emitted by: PluginImageService.delete_image() when an image is deleted

When: Image is deleted via the image service

Event Data: 

{
    "image_id": str,      # Unique image identifier
    "filename": str,      # Image filename
    "plugin_id": str      # Plugin ID that deleted the image
}

docs.title: plugin_enabled
docs.text:
Emitted by: app/api/routes/plugins/management.py::update_plugin() when a plugin type is enabled

When: Plugin type enabled status is set to true (via PUT /plugins/{plugin_id} with enabled: true)

Event Data: 

{
    "plugin_id": str,        # Plugin type ID
    "plugin_type": str,      # Plugin type (calendar, image, service, theme, etc.)
    "enabled_at": str        # ISO timestamp
}

docs.title: plugin_disabled
docs.text:
Emitted by: app/api/routes/plugins/management.py::update_plugin() when a plugin type is disabled

When: Plugin type enabled status is set to false (via PUT /plugins/{plugin_id} with enabled: false)

Event Data: 

{
    "plugin_id": str,        # Plugin type ID
    "plugin_type": str,      # Plugin type
    "disabled_at": str       # ISO timestamp
}

docs.title: plugin_installed
docs.text:
Emitted by: app/api/routes/plugins/management.py::install_plugin() when a plugin is successfully installed

When: Plugin is installed via POST /plugins/install

Event Data: 

{
    "plugin_id": str,        # Plugin ID
    "plugin_type": str,      # Plugin type
    "version": str,          # Plugin version
    "installed_at": str      # ISO timestamp
}

docs.title: plugin_uninstalled
docs.text:
Emitted by: app/api/routes/plugins/management.py::uninstall_plugin() when a plugin is uninstalled

When: Plugin is uninstalled via DELETE /plugins/installed/{plugin_id}

Event Data: 

{
    "plugin_id": str,        # Plugin ID
    "plugin_type": str,      # Plugin type
    "uninstalled_at": str    # ISO timestamp
}

docs.title: plugin_instance_created
docs.text:
Emitted by: app/api/routes/plugins/instances.py::update_plugin_instance() when a plugin instance is created

When: Plugin instance is created (when instance doesn't exist and is enabled)

Event Data: 

{
    "instance_id": str,      # Plugin instance ID
    "plugin_id": str,        # Plugin type ID
    "name": str,             # Instance name
    "created_at": str        # ISO timestamp
}

docs.title: plugin_instance_updated
docs.text:
Emitted by: app/api/routes/plugins/instances.py::update_plugin_instance() when a plugin instance is updated

When: Plugin instance is updated (config, enabled status, or name) via PUT /plugins/instances/{instance_id}

Event Data: 

{
    "instance_id": str,      # Plugin instance ID
    "plugin_id": str,        # Plugin type ID
    "changes": {             # What changed
        "enabled": bool | None,
        "config": dict | None,
        "name": str | None
    },
    "updated_at": str        # ISO timestamp
}

docs.title: plugin_instance_started
docs.text:
Emitted by: app/api/routes/plugins/instances.py::start_plugin_instance() when a plugin instance starts

When: Plugin instance is started via POST /plugins/instances/{instance_id}/start or auto-started

Event Data: 

{
    "instance_id": str,      # Plugin instance ID
    "plugin_id": str,        # Plugin type ID
    "started_at": str        # ISO timestamp
}

docs.title: plugin_instance_stopped
docs.text:
Emitted by: app/api/routes/plugins/instances.py::stop_plugin_instance() when a plugin instance stops

When: Plugin instance is stopped via POST /plugins/instances/{instance_id}/stop or auto-stopped

Event Data: 

{
    "instance_id": str,      # Plugin instance ID
    "plugin_id": str,        # Plugin type ID
    "stopped_at": str        # ISO timestamp
}

docs.title: Future System Events
docs.text:
• config_changed: When system configuration changes
  • scheduled_task_started: When a scheduled task starts
  • scheduled_task_completed: When a scheduled task completes
  • scheduled_task_failed: When a scheduled task fails
  • calendar_events_refreshed: When calendar events are fetched
  • system_started: When the system starts up
  • system_shutting_down: When the system is shutting down

docs.title: Plugin-Emitted Events
docs.text: Plugins can emit custom events for plugin-to-plugin communication:

docs.title: Example: image_processed
docs.text:
Emitted by: ImageProcessorPlugin after processing an image

Event Data: 

{
    "image_id": str,
    "filename": str,
    "original_path": str,
    "processor_id": str,
    "processing_results": {
        "resized": bool,
        "thumbnail_generated": bool,
        # ... other processing results
    }
}

docs.title: Example: sync_completed
docs.text:
Emitted by: A sync plugin after completing a sync operation

Event Data: 

{
    "sync_type": str,
    "items_synced": int,
    "success": bool
}

docs.title: Subscribing to System Events
docs.text:
Plugins can subscribe to system events to react to changes in the application state:

class MyBackendPlugin(BackendPlugin):
    async def get_subscribed_events(self) -> list[str]:
        """Subscribe to multiple system events."""
        return [
            "image_uploaded",
            "plugin_enabled",
            "plugin_installed",
            "plugin_instance_created",
        ]

    async def handle_event(
        self, event_type: str, event_data: dict[str, Any]
    ) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
        """Handle various system events."""
        if event_type == "image_uploaded":
            image_id = event_data["image_id"]
            filename = event_data["filename"]
            # Process the image...
            return {"success": True}

        elif event_type == "plugin_enabled":
            plugin_id = event_data["plugin_id"]
            plugin_type = event_data["plugin_type"]
            # React to plugin being enabled...
            logger.info(f"Plugin {plugin_id} ({plugin_type}) was enabled")
            return {"success": True}

        elif event_type == "plugin_installed":
            plugin_id = event_data["plugin_id"]
            version = event_data["version"]
            # Auto-configure newly installed plugin...
            logger.info(f"Plugin {plugin_id} v{version} was installed")
            return {"success": True}

        elif event_type == "plugin_instance_created":
            instance_id = event_data["instance_id"]
            plugin_id = event_data["plugin_id"]
            # React to new instance creation...
            logger.info(f"Instance {instance_id} of plugin {plugin_id} was created")
            return {"success": True}

        return None

docs.title: Emitting Events
docs.text:
class MyBackendPlugin(BackendPlugin):
    async def run_scheduled_task(self):
        # Do some work
        result = process_data()

        # Emit custom event (fire-and-forget)
        await self.emit_event(
            "data_processed",
            {"result": result, "timestamp": time.time()},
            wait_for_handlers=False
        )

        # Emit critical event (fire-and-wait)
        results = await self.emit_event(
            "critical_data_changed",
            {"key": "config", "value": "new_value"},
            wait_for_handlers=True  # Wait for all handlers
        )

        return {"success": True}

docs.title: Example 1: IMAP → Image Processor
docs.text:
1. IMAP Plugin downloads image from email
  2. Saves image to ./data/images/photo.jpg

  3. Does NOT emit any events

  4. LocalImagePlugin scans directory (periodically or on demand)

  5. Detects new image photo.jpg

  6. Emits image_uploaded event (fire-and-forget)

  7. ImageProcessorPlugin receives event

  8. Processes image (resize, optimize, etc.)

  9. Emits image_processed event (fire-and-forget)

  10. Other Plugins can subscribe to image_processed if needed

docs.title: Example 2: Plugin Installation → Auto-Configuration
docs.text:
1. User installs a new plugin via POST /plugins/install

  2. System installs plugin and reloads plugin list

  3. System emits plugin_installed event

  4. Event includes plugin_id, plugin_type, version, and timestamp

  5. AutoConfigPlugin subscribes to plugin_installed events

  6. Receives the event
  7. Automatically configures the new plugin with default settings

  8. May emit plugin_instance_created if it creates an instance

  9. MonitoringPlugin also subscribes to plugin_installed

  10. Logs the installation event for audit purposes

docs.title: Example 3: Plugin Instance Lifecycle
docs.text:
1. User creates a new plugin instance via PUT /plugins/instances/{instance_id}

  2. System creates the instance and enables it

  3. System emits plugin_instance_created event

  4. Event includes instance_id, plugin_id, name, and timestamp

  5. System automatically starts the instance

  6. Emits plugin_instance_started event

  7. CoordinatorPlugin subscribes to both events

  8. When instance is created: Sets up dependencies
  9. When instance is started: Starts related services

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Use System Events: Subscribe to system-emitted events rather than requiring plugins to emit them
  2. Fire-and-Forget Default: Use fire-and-forget for most events (non-blocking)
  3. Fire-and-Wait for Critical: Use fire-and-wait only for critical events that need confirmation
  4. Error Handling: Always handle errors gracefully in event handlers
  5. Rate Limiting: Be aware of rate limiting (10 events/second per plugin per event type)

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
The event system automatically rate-limits events to prevent event storms:

  • Default: 10 events/second per plugin per event type
  • Purpose: Prevents a single plugin from overwhelming the system
  • Behavior: If rate limit exceeded, event is silently dropped (logged at debug level)

docs.title: Migration from External Queue Frameworks
docs.text:
The current asyncio-based implementation is sufficient for: - Low-to-medium event volume (< 1000 events/second) - Single-process applications - Fire-and-forget event delivery - In-memory event delivery (no persistence)

Consider Redis/Celery/RQ if you need: - High event volume (> 1000 events/second) - Multi-process/multi-instance deployment - Event persistence - Guaranteed delivery with ACK/retry - Event replay capabilities

docs.title: IMAP Plugin and Local Images Relationship
Overview
docs.text: The IMAP plugin and Local Images plugin are separate, independent image plugins that can work together or independently.

docs.title: Local Images Plugin
docs.text:
• Type: local
  • Purpose: Manages images uploaded directly to the server
  • Default Directory: ./data/images
  • Behavior:
  • Users upload images via the web UI
  • Images are stored in the configured directory
  • Plugin scans the directory and serves images

docs.title: IMAP Plugin (Backend Plugin)
docs.text:
• Type: backend (converted from image plugin)
  • Purpose: Downloads images from email attachments to local directory
  • Default Directory: ./data/images (same as local images)
  • Behavior:
  • Connects to IMAP email server (Gmail, Outlook, etc.)
  • Checks for emails with image attachments (via scheduled tasks)
  • Downloads images to configured directory
  • Does NOT serve images directly - relies on LocalImagePlugin for display

docs.title: Default Behavior (Shared Directory)
docs.text: By default, both plugins use the same directory (./data/images): - Local Images stores uploaded images there - IMAP downloads email images there - Both plugins scan the same directory - Images from both sources appear together in the slideshow

docs.title: Custom Directories (Separate)
docs.text: Each plugin can be configured with a different directory: - Local Images: Can use ./data/images/local - IMAP: Can use ./data/images/imap or any custom path - Each plugin only sees images in its own directory - Images are kept separate

docs.title: IMAP Plugin Configuration
docs.text:
{
  "image_dir": "./data/images/imap"  // Optional: defaults to ./data/images
}

docs.title: Local Images Plugin Configuration
docs.text:
{
  "image_dir": "./data/images/local"  // Optional: defaults to ./data/images
}

docs.title: Shared Directory (Default)
docs.text:
• Use case: Simple setup where all images appear together
  • Pros:
  • Single source of truth
  • Easy to manage
  • Images from email and uploads appear together
  • Cons:
  • Can't distinguish source of images
  • Potential filename conflicts

docs.title: Separate Directories
docs.text:
• Use case: Want to keep email images separate from uploaded images
  • Pros:
  • Clear separation of image sources
  • No filename conflicts
  • Can disable one plugin without affecting the other
  • Cons:
  • More complex configuration
  • Images appear in separate rotations (unless both plugins enabled)

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text: Both plugins respect the image ordering system: - Plugin-level ordering: Controls which plugin's images appear first - Instance-level ordering: Controls order of multiple IMAP instances (if configured) - Images are combined in order: Plugin 1 images → Plugin 2 images → etc.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. For most users: Use default shared directory - simple and works well
  2. For organization: Use separate directories if you want to keep sources distinct
  3. For multiple IMAP accounts: Each instance can use its own directory or share one
  4. Ordering: Set display_order to control which plugin's images appear first

docs.title: Releasing Calvin
docs.text:
Calvin is released from main, published as a version tag (vX.Y.Z), and installed by pinning that tag. develop is the integration branch where work lands first; testers can run it, but it is not a release.

This page is the whole process. Nothing here is manual except merging two pull requests — the changelog, the tag and the container images are automated.

docs.title: Branches at a glance
docs.text: Branch What it is Who should install it develop Integration branch. Every push publishes :develop and :sha-<commit>. Testers, contributors, the next release main Release branch. Only receives merges from develop and release-please commits. Nobody directly — releases are installed by tag vX.Y.Z (tag) An immutable release on main. Publishes :X.Y.Z, :X.Y, :latest and :sha-<commit>. Everyone else

docs.title: The flow
docs.text:
feature PR ──▶ develop ──(CI passes)──▶ promote PR ──▶ main ──▶ release PR ──▶ vX.Y.Z tag
                  │                      (automatic)            (automatic)      │
                  └─ :develop image                              CHANGELOG.md     └─ :X.Y.Z, :X.Y, :latest images
                                                                  GitHub Release
  1. Work lands on develop. PRs target develop. Use conventional commit messages (feat:, fix:, docs:, chore:, …) — release-please reads them to build the changelog and pick the version.
  2. CI succeeds on develop. promote-develop-to-main.yml opens (or updates) the Promote develop to main PR. Merging it is a release-candidate step: main now builds exactly what passed CI on develop. Merge it as a merge commit, not a squash — main must stay a descendant of develop or the next promotion conflicts.
  3. release-please opens the release PR. Every push to main runs release-please.yml (googleapis/release-please-action). It maintains a single PR titled chore(main): release X.Y.Z containing:
  4. the new CHANGELOG.md section, grouped by commit type,
  5. the bumped version in .release-please-manifest.json.

Review it. If a commit should not appear, fix the wording on develop and promote again rather than editing the generated changelog by hand. 4. Merge the release PR. Keep the generated title. Merging it makes release-please create: - the tag vX.Y.Z on the merge commit (the PR already carries the CHANGELOG.md and .release-please-manifest.json update), - the GitHub Release with the changelog as its body. 5. Images publish. A tag created with GITHUB_TOKEN does not trigger another workflow's push: tags event, so the release workflow dispatches docker-build.yml at the new tag. That build publishes the release images (below). Watch it under Actions → Build and Push Docker Image.

Never create or push a v* tag by hand. release-please is the only tag source; a hand-made tag has no release PR, no changelog, and the next release cannot find it as its predecessor.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
• Pre-1.0: feat bumps the minor (0.1.x → 0.2.0), fix/perf bump the patch, a breaking change bumps the minor (never to 1.0.0 on its own — bump-minor-pre-major is on).
  • 0.1.0 is the starting version in .release-please-manifest.json. The first release PR proposes the next 0.x version from the commits since the repository began, so its changelog covers the project history up to that point.
  • The version shown in Settings → System comes from backend/app/__init__.py (__version__). release-please bumps it through the extra-files entry in release-please-config.json in the same release PR as the manifest, so do not edit it by hand. The Docker build stamps the same release version (CALVIN_VERSION) and the commit (CALVIN_GIT_SHA) into the image; a git checkout reads the revision from git instead.
  • Release candidates. release-please-config.json has prerelease: true, versioning: prerelease and prerelease-type: rc, so a release is marked as a GitHub prerelease and the next one normally bumps the rc number (0.1.0-rc.1 → 0.1.0-rc.2). An rc image is tagged :0.1.0-rc.N and :sha-… only; it never becomes :latest or :0.1. The first candidate is pinned with release-as: 0.1.0-rc.1. Remove release-as in a PR to develop right after the rc.1 release PR merges, or the next release PR proposes 0.1.0-rc.1 again. For the final 0.1.0, set release-as: 0.1.0 and remove the three prerelease keys, then remove release-as once more after that release.
  • After 1.0.0, normal semver applies: breaking → major, feat → minor.

docs.title: Images a release publishes
docs.text:
ghcr.io/osterbergsimon/calvin (public, multi-arch: linux/amd64, linux/arm64, linux/arm/v7) gets, for tag vX.Y.Z:

Tag Use :X.Y.Z Reproducible pin for a release. Use this in production. :X.Y Latest patch of a minor line; moves within X.Y. :latest Most recent release. Convenient, not reproducible. :sha-<commit> That exact build; useful for rollback/debugging.

develop continues to publish :develop (and :sha-<commit>) on every push, unchanged.

docs.title: One-time repository setup
docs.text:
These are repository settings, not code. Check them once:

  • Settings → Actions → General → Workflow permissions: Read and write permissions. The release workflow needs contents: write (tag + changelog commit) and pull-requests: write (release PR).
  • Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests: on. Both the promotion PR and the release PR are opened with GITHUB_TOKEN; with this off, the release workflow fails at "create pull request".
  • main protection: allow PRs from develop (the promotion PR) and the autorelease: pending release PR to be merged by a maintainer. Do not let anyone push tags directly.

docs.title: Installing a release
docs.text:
See SETUP_SCRIPTS.md for the exact commands. In short:

# Stable release: pin the tag in both the script URL and the checkout.
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/v0.1.0/scripts/setup.sh \
  | sudo GIT_BRANCH=v0.1.0 bash

setup.sh derives the image tag from the ref, so a tag install runs :v0.1.0 (no separate CALVIN_IMAGE_TAG needed). Re-running setup with a newer tag moves both the checkout and the image. update-calvin.sh on such a host refreshes host files from the pinned tag and keeps that image — to upgrade, re-run setup with the new tag.

Before the first release exists, use the develop one-liner; it is also the right choice for testing the next release.

docs.title: Hotfixes
docs.text: Calvin has no separate hotfix branch. Fix on develop, let CI pass, merge the promotion PR, then merge the release PR release-please opens (it will be a patch bump). Emergency changes that cannot wait for develop can be merged into main through a PR, but the same commit must also land on develop — otherwise the next promotion conflicts.

docs.title: If a release goes wrong
docs.text: Symptom What to do Release PR has the wrong version Close it, fix the commit messages on develop, promote again, re-run the workflow (Actions → Release Please → Run workflow). No release PR after merging the promotion Check the workflow run. A commit that is not conventional (e.g. a reworded merge) is ignored; chore(main): release … hidden commits do not bump. Tag exists, images missing Run Actions → Build and Push Docker Image → Run workflow with push_image ticked on the tag ref, or re-run the failed job. Bad release already tagged Do not delete/reuse the tag. Fix forward: land the fix on develop, promote, and cut the next patch release.

docs.title: Admin authentication
docs.text: Calvin asks for one admin password before anything that changes the server or reveals a secret. Viewing the dashboard, and the touch interactions people use on a kiosk (next photo, switch screen, calendar view, theme), stay open.

docs.title: First run
docs.text:
On a fresh install — or after upgrading from a version without admin auth — open Settings. Calvin shows one card: a setup code and an admin password to choose. The password can be any characters, at least 8. Whoever does this first claims the install, and is signed in immediately; the browser keeps that session for up to 400 days.

The setup code is what stops someone else on the network from claiming the install before you do. Calvin generates an 8-character code (shown as XXXX-XXXX) the first time it starts without an admin password and:

  • logs it at startup as Calvin setup code: XXXX-XXXX, and
  • writes it to setup-code.txt (mode 0600) next to admin-auth.json in the data directory.

Enter that code with the new password. The code is single-use: once a password exists Calvin deletes the file and the code stops working. A restart keeps the same code until it is used. A wrong code is rate limited like a wrong password (5 within 60 seconds → 429, then a cooldown).

Where to read it:

How Calvin runs Read the code Docker / Compose docker logs calvin — look for Calvin setup code: Unraid Docker tab → Calvin → Logs, or docker logs calvin Pi all-in-one sudo journalctl -u calvin-app -n 100 Native / development the server's terminal output, or <data dir>/setup-code.txt Kiosk on the same server the kiosk's setup screen shows it when the browser reaches Calvin over loopback (http://localhost:8000). Through Docker's port mapping the request no longer looks like loopback, so use docker logs calvin.

Kiosks do not open Settings, so the card appears on the server's own screen or a phone/laptop. The setup code is never returned to a public request.

If you want no window in which another LAN device could claim the install, set CALVIN_ADMIN_PASSWORD before the first start.

docs.title: CALVIN_ADMIN_PASSWORD
docs.text:
Set this environment variable (Unraid field, Docker Compose, systemd Environment=, or .env) to the password you want. On every start Calvin compares it with the stored password:

  • different → it replaces the stored password and signs every other session out;
  • same → nothing changes, so a restart does not log anyone out.

An empty or unset value leaves the stored password alone. The value must be at least 8 characters.

docs.title: CALVIN_SETUP_CODE
docs.text: Set this to pre-seed the one-time setup code instead of letting Calvin generate one — useful for headless installs where you would rather hand the owner a known code. Case does not matter and -/spaces are ignored, so abcd-efgh matches ABCD-EFGH. It is ignored once an admin password exists. Leave it unset to use the generated code in the log and setup-code.txt.

docs.title: Forgot the password
docs.text:
Either:

  • delete <data dir>/admin-auth.json (override the path with ADMIN_AUTH_PATH) and restart, then choose a new password in Settings with the new setup code from the log; or
  • set CALVIN_ADMIN_PASSWORD to a new value and restart.

Deleting the file also discards the session-signing secret, so every old cookie becomes invalid. The file is never in the database, a backup, or GET /api/config; see Data directory.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
• Cookie calvin_admin: HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Path=/, Max-Age=34560000 (400 days, the browser cap).
  • Stateless value issued_at.generation.HMAC, signed with a server secret kept in admin-auth.json (mode 0600, next to the kiosk signing key).
  • Changing the password bumps the generation, so every other browser is signed out. Sign out just clears the cookie.
  • Login failures are limited per peer IP: 5 within 60 seconds → 429, then a 60-second cooldown that doubles on each further lockout, capped at 15 minutes. The counter is in memory and resets on restart. X-Forwarded-* is not trusted; behind a proxy everyone shares one bucket.

docs.title: Host and Origin checks
docs.text:
Host (DNS rebinding). Calvin accepts the normal LAN ways of reaching it:

  • IP literals (IPv4 and IPv6), localhost, *.localhost
  • single-label names such as calvin or raspberrypi
  • .local, .lan, .home, .home.arpa, .internal, .localdomain
  • the host in PUBLIC_URL
  • anything listed in CALVIN_ALLOWED_HOSTS (comma-separated, case-insensitive; * turns the check off)

Anything else — evil.example, or a name that merely ends in an allowed suffix like calvin.local.evil.example — gets 400 with a plain-text message naming CALVIN_ALLOWED_HOSTS and PUBLIC_URL. Set PUBLIC_URL when you reach Calvin through a real domain, or list the name in CALVIN_ALLOWED_HOSTS.

Origin (cross-site writes). Every unsafe request (POST/PUT/PATCH/ DELETE) under /api must come from the same host and port as the request's Host header, or from an origin listed in CORS_ORIGINS. The scheme is ignored, so a TLS proxy in front still matches. Requests with no Origin (curl, the kiosk agent) pass; Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site without an Origin is rejected. A refusal is 403 {"detail":{"code":"cross_origin"}}. CORS_ALLOW_ALL (development only) skips this check.

docs.title: What needs the admin password
docs.text:
Tier Routes Public read dashboard data and kiosk delivery — GET /api/config, /api/calendar/*, /api/images/*, /api/plugins* (except the two admin reads below), /api/kiosks/*, /api/keyboard/*, /api/security/*, /api/system/* (except update/stream) Viewer write (same-origin, no login) POST /api/images/next, POST /api/images/previous, POST /api/calendar/refresh, POST /api/plugins/{id}/fetch, POST /api/system/display/power/on, POST /api/system/display/power/off, POST /api/config (display keys only) Admin every other write, plus GET /api/backup/*, GET /api/config/git/branches, GET /api/plugins/{id}/scan, GET /api/plugins/local/suggest, GET /api/system/update/stream

The write policy is default-deny: every POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE needs admin unless its route is on the short viewer-write list above, so new routes are protected without anyone remembering to add them. Plugins cannot add routes.

POST /api/config accepts these keys without admin, because the dashboard itself writes them: dashboardScreens, regionsLocked, showUI, themeMode, selectedTheme, darkModeStart, darkModeEnd, lastSideViewMode. A request that mixes one of them with anything else (for example gitBranch) is rejected as a whole.

An unauthenticated admin request answers 401 {"detail":{"code":"admin_required"}}. Before a password exists it answers 401 {"detail":{"code":"setup_required"}}. Kiosk dashboards should never see either.

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
Apps and scripts (Home Assistant, a cron job) can use Calvin without the admin password by sending a key. Create, list and revoke keys in Settings › Security › API keys, or through the API below.

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer clv_YOUR_KEY_HERE" http://calvin.local:8000/api/backup/files
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer clv_YOUR_KEY_HERE" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"showUI": true}' \
     http://calvin.local:8000/api/config

Scopes form a ladder, host ⊇ admin ⊇ read:

Scope May do read Every public GET, but not the admin-only reads (backup export and files, scans, git branches, update stream): those need admin. The viewer writes anonymous callers have (next/previous photo, calendar refresh, display power, display settings in POST /api/config) work too. Every other unsafe method (POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE) is refused. admin Everything a signed-in admin may do, except the host-acting routes below. host admin, plus the host-acting routes that anonymous viewers can't call: POST /api/system/update, /reboot, /restart-backend, /restart-frontend, /reload-ui, /display/timeout/configure.

A host key does not bypass CALVIN_HOST_CONTROL: with it off, host routes answer 409 host_control_disabled for everyone, keys included, and creating a host key is refused with 403 host_control_disabled. A key never gets less than an anonymous caller (display power on/off stay open to every key, subject to CALVIN_HOST_CONTROL). A key of too low a scope gets 403 insufficient_scope.

Rules:

  • The key goes in the Authorization: Bearer header only, never in the URL. A bearer request ignores any cookie. A malformed, unknown or revoked key answers 401 invalid_api_key, even on public routes: it never falls back to anonymous.
  • Keys cannot manage keys. GET/POST /api/auth/keys and DELETE /api/auth/keys/{id} need an admin session (the cookie); a key of any scope gets 403 session_required. Changing the admin password needs the session too.
  • POST /api/auth/keys {"name", "scope"} returns 201 {"key": {...}, "secret"}. The secret (clv_ + 43 URL-safe characters) is shown only in that response. 409 for a duplicate name (case-insensitive), 422 for an unknown scope or a name that is empty or over 40 characters. GET returns {"keys": [{id, name, scope, prefix, createdAt, lastUsedAt}]}, never the secret.
  • Revoking (DELETE, 204) takes effect on the very next request.
  • Changing the admin password does not revoke keys. Revoke them one by one.
  • Bearer requests skip the cookie Origin/CSRF check (a header can't be forged cross-site) but still get the Host check. Failed bearer attempts are rate limited per IP like logins (5 in a minute, then 429 with Retry-After), in their own counter, so a stale script can't lock you out of the password form.
  • Only a SHA-256 of each secret is stored, in api-keys.json next to admin-auth.json (mode 0600). last_used_at is updated at most once a minute per key. Key-shaped strings are redacted from the logs.
  • Deleting api-keys.json revokes every key.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Calvin is normally served over plain HTTP on the LAN; TLS remains a reverse proxy job.
  • Anyone on the LAN can still rearrange the dashboard, switch screens and change the theme. That is deliberate: display state is writable without a password, but code, secrets and backups are not.
  • One password, no usernames or multiple admins. API keys are the only other credential.
  • Installed plugins run in the server process, as before. An upload is first imported once in a short-lived child interpreter (python -I -m app.plugins.check_plugin), so a plugin that crashes, calls sys.exit() or hangs at import is rejected without the server importing it. The child runs as the same user: that is a "don't load rejected code into the server" guard, not a sandbox.

docs.title: Backup and restore
docs.text: A backup is one file that brings a fresh Calvin back to a configured state: calendars, photo sources, web services, layout and screens, keyboard map, plugins, themes and kiosks. Use it to move to a new server, to rebuild a container, or to seed a dev setup instead of entering everything again.

docs.title: What is in a backup
docs.text:
Included Notes All app settings Layout, screens and regions, clock bar, display schedule, theme choice, appearance, security allowlist and sealed mode, update branch, plugin type settings Keyboard map Plugins and their instances Calendar sources, image sources, web services and backend plugins, with their ids, names, on/off state, settings and order Installed plugin and theme packages Optional, on by default. Restore installs them (and their Python dependencies) on the new server Kiosks Each kiosk's id, hostname and per-kiosk settings Passwords and API keys Optional, on by default. See Secrets Kiosk signing key Optional, off by default. See Kiosk signing key Not included Why Photos and other image files They are your content, not settings; copy the image folder separately if you need it Caches (images, calendars, weather) Rebuilt automatically Kiosk status (last seen, agent version) Reported again by each kiosk Logs, the Python environment, the frontend build Part of the install, not the setup The automatic-backup schedule Belongs to each server (see below)

Instance ids are kept exactly, because screens and regions point at sources by id.

One thing in a backup can depend on the machine: a source whose settings contain a local path (for example the Local Images folder). It is restored as it was; adjust it in Settings if the new server keeps images elsewhere.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
Plugin settings can hold passwords, API keys and tokens. By default they are included, so a restore needs no retyping. The file then contains them in plain text: store it like a password. Backups that Calvin writes to its own backup folder are readable only by the Calvin user (0600).

Turn off Include passwords and API keys (or pass --no-secrets / include_secrets=false) to blank them. On restore, a blanked value is taken from the server's current settings when it has one, so a blank never overwrites a password the server already has (sources and plugin-level settings alike). A source still missing one is restored switched off, with its other settings intact, and listed under "needs credentials"; enter the password in Settings and switch it on.

A setting counts as secret when its name contains password, api_key, api_token, token, secret, access_token or refresh_token, or when the plugin declares it as a password field.

docs.title: Kiosk signing key
docs.text:
Calvin signs the kiosk agent's update manifest with a key in KIOSK_SIGNING_KEY_PATH. A new server makes a new key, so kiosks set up against the old server stop accepting updates until they are set up again.

To move a whole installation, include the key in the backup and, when restoring, choose Also restore the kiosk signing key (or --restore-signing-key, restore_signing_key=true, CALVIN_RESTORE_SIGNING_KEY=1). It is opt-in on both sides because anyone with the key can sign kiosk updates, and a dev machine restoring a production backup should not take over production's key by accident.

docs.title: Making a backup
docs.text:
• Settings: System → Backup → Download backup.
  • API: GET /api/backup/export (query include_packages, include_secrets, include_signing_key) returns the zip.
  • Command line (works while Calvin runs), from backend/:
uv run python -m app.services.backup export --out calvin.zip
uv run python -m app.services.backup export --no-secrets --no-packages
uv run python -m app.services.backup export --include-signing-key

In Docker: docker exec calvin python -m app.services.backup export --out /var/lib/calvin/backups/manual.zip.

docs.title: Automatic backups
docs.text:
System → Automatic backups saves a backup to the backup folder every N hours and keeps the newest N (default: every 24 hours, keep 7). They include packages and secrets but not the signing key. Backups saved there before a restore (pre-restore-*) and by Save a backup now are never deleted automatically. The schedule is also available at GET/PUT /api/backup/schedule.

The backup folder is BACKUP_DIR if set, else backups/ in the data directory (Docker/Unraid: /var/lib/calvin/backups; source checkout: backend/data/backups).

docs.title: Restoring
docs.text: Restore is the same everywhere: the file is checked, you see what will change, the current setup is saved to the backup folder as pre-restore-<time>.zip, then the backup is applied.

docs.title: Replace or merge
docs.text:
• Replace (default): this Calvin ends up like the backup. Settings, key bindings and sources that are not in the backup are removed. Installed plugin packages are not uninstalled; their sources are removed.
  • Merge: everything in the backup is added or updated; everything else is kept.

Kiosks are always merged: they re-register on their own, so a restore never deletes one.

docs.title: What happens, in order
docs.text:
1. Check. The file must be a Calvin backup (format: calvin-backup). A backup from a newer Calvin is refused with "made by a newer Calvin" and nothing is changed; upgrade first. Older backup formats are upgraded automatically.
  2. Preview. Counts of settings, sources, key bindings and kiosks; plugins to install; sources that will be created, updated, removed or skipped; warnings (for example a plugin installed here at a different version than in the backup: the installed one is kept).
  3. Safety backup of the current setup.
  4. Apply. Plugin and theme packages from the backup that are not installed are installed (with their Python dependencies). Then settings, key bindings, plugin on/off state, sources (through the normal plugin instance manager, so they start straight away) and kiosks.
  5. Result. What was done, sources that need credentials, warnings and errors. Reload the UI to see everything.

A source whose plugin is neither installed nor in the backup (or whose plugin failed to install) is kept switched off with its settings, with a warning; install the plugin and switch the source on again. Its screen region stays. Restore is not one database transaction: if something goes wrong part-way, restore the pre-restore-* file to go back.

docs.title: From Settings
docs.text: System → Restore → choose the file → check the preview → pick Replace or Merge → Restore this backup → Reload Calvin.

docs.title: From the API
docs.text:
# preview only
curl -F file=@calvin.zip -F mode=replace http://calvin:8000/api/backup/preview
# restore
curl -F file=@calvin.zip -F mode=replace http://calvin:8000/api/backup/restore
# a backup already in the backup folder
curl -F mode=merge -F dry_run=true http://calvin:8000/api/backup/files/auto-pi-20261029-030000-000000.zip/restore

Responses: 200 with the plan or result; 400 when the file is rejected (with the reason in detail); 409 when another restore is running.

docs.title: From the command line
docs.text:
Stop Calvin first (the command changes the database and plugin folders directly), then from backend/:

uv run python -m app.services.backup restore calvin.zip --dry-run
uv run python -m app.services.backup restore calvin.zip --mode merge
uv run python -m app.services.backup restore calvin.zip --restore-signing-key

Exit code 0 = restored, 1 = restored with errors (listed in the output), 2 = the file was rejected.

docs.title: On first start (fresh deploys and dev setups)
docs.text:
Point Calvin at a backup and it restores it during startup, after plugins are loaded and before defaults are filled in:

  • CALVIN_RESTORE_FROM=/path/to/backup.zip (or .json), or
  • drop the file into the backup folder as restore-on-start.zip or restore-on-start.json.

CALVIN_RESTORE_MODE picks replace (default) or merge; CALVIN_RESTORE_SIGNING_KEY=1 also restores the signing key.

Each file is applied once: Calvin remembers its checksum, so the variable can stay set and the file can live on a read-only mount; restarts do not undo your later changes. Put a different file there to seed again. A file that is rejected is logged and Calvin starts with its current setup. If the restore ran but reported errors (for example a plugin whose dependencies could not be downloaded), it is not marked as applied and is tried again on the next start.

Docker/Unraid example:

services:
  calvin:
    environment:
      CALVIN_RESTORE_FROM: /var/lib/calvin/backups/seed.zip

Dev setup: keep a backup of your usual configuration and start the backend with CALVIN_RESTORE_FROM=~/calvin-dev-seed.zip.

A seed can also be a hand-written backup.json (no packages). The smallest valid one:

{
  "format": "calvin-backup",
  "format_version": 1,
  "data": {
    "config": [{"key": "time_format", "value": "24h", "value_type": "string"}],
    "plugin_instances": [
      {"id": "ical-family", "type_id": "ical", "name": "Family", "enabled": true,
       "config": {"ical_url": "https://example.com/family.ics"}}
    ]
  }
}

docs.title: File format
docs.text:
A zip:

backup.json                 # header + all settings
packages/plugins/<id>/...   # installed plugin files (if included)
packages/themes/<id>/...    # installed theme files (if included)
signing-key                 # only if the key was included

backup.json carries format (calvin-backup), format_version (currently 1), created_at, calvin_version, schema_revision (the database migration the source was on, for information), source (hostname, deploy kind), the export options, stripped_secrets, the packages list and data (config, keyboard_mappings, plugin_types, plugin_instances, kiosks).

format_version is the backup's own version, separate from the database schema. When it changes, a migration step in backend/app/services/backup/format.py (MIGRATIONS) upgrades older files, so old backups keep restoring. Unknown fields are ignored, so database columns added later do not break older backups.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Calvin's API has no login; anyone who can reach it can download a backup (including secrets) or restore one, the same as they can already install a plugin that runs code on the server. Keep Calvin on a trusted network.

docs.title: Data directory
docs.text:
Everything the Calvin backend writes lives under one directory, set with CALVIN_DATA_DIR. Where the server is started from (its working directory) makes no difference.

Install CALVIN_DATA_DIR Source checkout (dev, bare-metal Pi) unset: backend/data of the checkout Docker image, compose, Pi server /var/lib/calvin (set in the image; the volume is mounted there) Unraid /var/lib/calvin in the container = /mnt/user/appdata/calvin on the host

docs.title: What goes where
docs.text:
Path under the data dir Contents Override db/calvin.db SQLite database (Alembic migrates it at startup) DATABASE_URL images/ Local Images uploads and their thumbnails/ IMAGE_DIR plugins/ Installed plugins, plus per-instance scan_cache.json PLUGIN_DIR (or PLUGINS_DIR) themes/ Installed themes THEMES_DIR python/<major>.<minor>/site-packages/ Plugin pip dependencies, one target per interpreter version (survives image updates) — image_cache/ Cached remote image bytes IMAGE_CACHE_DIR logs/ Backend log directory LOG_DIR backups/ Saved and automatic backups BACKUP_DIR kiosk-signing.key Kiosk manifest signing key KIOSK_SIGNING_KEY_PATH admin-auth.json Admin password hash and session-signing secret (mode 0600) ADMIN_AUTH_PATH setup-code.txt One-time first-run setup code while no admin password exists (mode 0600); deleted once one is set follows ADMIN_AUTH_PATH

python/ holds one directory per interpreter version (3.11, 3.12, …). After a base-image Python upgrade Calvin builds the new one; the old one is no longer imported and is safe to delete by hand.

An override wins over the data dir for that one path; everything else stays under the data dir. A relative value (for CALVIN_DATA_DIR or an override) is taken relative to the backend/ directory, not the working directory, so older .env files with ./data/... paths keep pointing where they used to. An empty value (CALVIN_DATA_DIR=, BACKUP_DIR=, ...) counts as unset.

image_cache/ is bounded so it can't slowly fill an SD card. Past IMAGE_CACHE_MAX_MB (default 500) the least recently viewed images are evicted, and a single remote image larger than IMAGE_CACHE_MAX_ITEM_MB (default 25) is refused instead of being read into memory.

docs.title: Upgrading when the data dir moves
docs.text:
Before CALVIN_DATA_DIR was read, everything without its own variable was written to backend/data of the checkout. The dev compose stack (setup.sh --mode dev) is the common case: its database was on the volume, but uploads, installed themes and the kiosk signing key were in the bind-mounted checkout.

On the first start with a data dir other than backend/data, the backend copies what it finds there (database, uploads, plugins, installed themes, caches, backups, kiosk signing key) to where the settings now put it. It never overwrites a file that already exists, skips the old database when one is already in place, and leaves the originals where they were. It then writes .legacy-data-migrated in the data dir and does not look again, so files you delete later are not brought back. The log says how many files were copied.

docs.title: Not in the data dir
docs.text:
• the built-in themes (backend/data/themes/builtin.json), which ship with the code;
  • alembic.ini and the migrations, found next to the app package; the backend refuses to start if alembic.ini is missing rather than run on an un-migrated database;
  • the host updater's log and state (/var/lib/calvin-update-status/), which scripts/update-calvin.sh writes as root and only native installs use. Older installs kept them in <repo>/backend/logs/, which the backend still reads as a fallback.

docs.title: Local Images
docs.text: The Local Images plugin always stores images in IMAGE_DIR (by default <data dir>/images). Older installs saved image_dir: ./data/images in the plugin instance's settings; that value is now ignored, so it can no longer send uploads to a directory that depends on where the server was started.

docs.title: Host control (CALVIN_HOST_CONTROL)
docs.text:
Some Calvin actions act on the machine the backend runs on, not just on the web UI: rebooting, restarting the calvin-backend/calvin-frontend systemd units, running the update script, and driving the local display with vcgencmd, xset and xrandr.

CALVIN_HOST_CONTROL decides whether Calvin may do that. It defaults to on only when Calvin owns the machine; everywhere else the routes answer 409 and never run the command.

docs.title: Default rule
docs.text:
Deployment Default Native install on a Raspberry Pi, not a dev checkout (backend/.dev absent) on Native backend on a desktop/laptop, or any dev checkout off Docker container (compose, the Pi image, Unraid) off

The backend evaluates this once at startup from CALVIN_DEPLOYMENT, is_dev_mode and a Raspberry Pi check, and reports the result as host_control in GET /api/system/environment.

Containers never control the host. In a container these routes are refused with the container instructions (use the Docker/Unraid update flow), even if CALVIN_HOST_CONTROL=1 is set.

docs.title: Overrides
docs.text:
CALVIN_HOST_CONTROL=1   # Calvin owns this machine: allow host actions
CALVIN_HOST_CONTROL=0   # never act on the host, on any deployment

An explicit value always wins. Set 1 on a Pi install that is not detected as one (unusual kernel/device-tree), or on another single-purpose kiosk machine you are happy to let Calvin reboot.

docs.title: What is disabled when it is off
docs.text:
• POST /api/system/reboot
  • POST /api/system/restart-backend
  • POST /api/system/restart-frontend
  • POST /api/system/update
  • POST /api/system/reload-ui
  • POST /api/system/display/power/on and /off
  • POST /api/system/display/timeout/configure
  • Applying a saved display rotation / orientation to the physical display

The startup display-orientation sync and the display power scheduler are skipped entirely, with one log line, so a dev backend never runs xrandr or xset against the developer's desktop.

The routes answer:

{
  "detail": {
    "code": "host_control_disabled",
    "message": "Rebooting is disabled on this deployment. Set CALVIN_HOST_CONTROL=1 if Calvin owns this machine."
  }
}

The UI shows that message instead of a generic error. Reads such as GET /api/system/display/power/state still work; they only query the display.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: By default the frontend calls /api on the same origin that served it. When you run npm run dev on your laptop, that means the local backend, so settings you edit are written to the laptop's database instead of the remote dashboard's.

docs.title: Solution
docs.text: Point the frontend at the remote backend, either with the Vite dev proxy or with an absolute API URL.

docs.title: Option 1: Dev proxy (VITE_API_PROXY_TARGET)
docs.text:
The Vite dev server proxies /api/* to http://127.0.0.1:8000 by default. Point it at the remote dashboard instead:

cd frontend
VITE_API_PROXY_TARGET=http://192.0.2.100:8000 npm run dev

To keep the setting, create frontend/.env.local (Vite loads it automatically; there is no checked-in frontend/.env.example):

# frontend/.env.local
VITE_API_PROXY_TARGET=http://192.0.2.100:8000

The browser keeps calling same-origin /api, so no CORS configuration is needed.

docs.title: Option 2: Absolute API URL (VITE_API_URL)
docs.text:
Set VITE_API_URL when the browser should call the remote backend directly. It must include the /api suffix:

# frontend/.env.local
VITE_API_URL=http://192.0.2.100:8000/api

This applies to npm run dev, npm run build, and the packaged frontend. Restart the dev server (or rebuild) after changing it.

docs.title: Option 3: Build with a remote API
docs.text:
cd frontend
VITE_API_URL=http://192.0.2.100:8000/api npm run build

The production Docker image serves the frontend from the backend, so the relative default (/api) is the usual choice there.

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
Cross-origin browser calls (VITE_API_URL) need the backend to allow the frontend origin. CORS is not hard-coded in main.py; it comes from two settings read from the environment (backend/app/config.py):

  • CORS_ORIGINS — comma-separated list of allowed origins. Default: http://localhost:5173,http://localhost:8000.
  • CORS_ALLOW_ALL — set to true to allow every origin (development only; never on a network you don't control).

Example for a dev machine at 192.0.2.50:5173:

# backend/.env or docker/.env
CORS_ORIGINS=http://localhost:5173,http://localhost:8000,http://192.0.2.50:5173

Restart the backend after changing it. If you point the frontend at the backend's own origin (or use the dev proxy), leave CORS alone.

docs.title: Finding Your Remote Dashboard's IP Address
docs.text:
On the remote dashboard (Raspberry Pi):

hostname -I
# or
ip addr show | grep "inet " | grep -v 127.0.0.1

From your development machine, check your router's client list or scan the LAN (nmap -sn 192.0.2.0/24).

docs.title: Verifying the Connection
docs.text:
1. Start the frontend with the remote target configured.
  2. Open the browser console (F12) → Network.
  3. Confirm /api/... requests go to the remote host (via the proxy or the absolute URL).
  4. Change a setting and confirm it appears on the remote dashboard.

docs.title: CORS errors
docs.text:
• Set CORS_ORIGINS on the backend to include the exact frontend origin (scheme, host, and port), then restart it.
  • For a quick local check only, CORS_ALLOW_ALL=true.
  • Prefer the dev proxy (VITE_API_PROXY_TARGET) to avoid CORS entirely.

docs.title: Connection refused
docs.text:
• Check the backend: curl http://192.0.2.100:8000/api/health.
  • Check firewall rules and that the backend binds an interface reachable from your machine.
  • Verify the IP and port.

docs.title: Settings still not syncing
docs.text:
• Confirm the URL in frontend/.env.local and restart npm run dev.
  • Check the browser console for API errors.
  • Make sure you are editing the frontend instance pointed at the remote backend.

docs.title: Switching Back to Local Development
docs.text: Remove VITE_API_URL / VITE_API_PROXY_TARGET from frontend/.env.local (or delete the file) and restart the dev server. The frontend then uses the same-origin /api path and the local backend.

docs.title: How Settings Are Saved
docs.text: Calvin saves settings per field. There is no "Save All Settings" button; changing a control writes the changed keys immediately.

docs.title: Per-field saves
docs.text:
The settings form (useConfigForm.js) exposes updateConfigValue(key, value), which sends the changed key to POST /api/config as soon as the control changes. updateConfig(updates) does the same for a group of keys (for example a segmented control that edits several related values together).

What this means in practice:

  • Orientation, theme, display schedule, clock-bar options, calendar view, time format, refresh intervals, and similar settings are persisted as you change them.
  • A short "saved" indicator appears, and errors are shown in the settings header if the request fails.
  • Navigating away without pressing anything cannot lose a change that was already sent.

docs.title: Keyboard mappings
docs.text: Keyboard bindings are saved through their own endpoint when you apply them in Settings → Keyboard; they are independent of the general config form.

docs.title: Plugin settings
docs.text: Plugin type settings and plugin instance settings each have their own save action in their respective settings panels. They are not part of the general config POST.

docs.title: Plugin instances
docs.text: Creating or editing an instance in the instance modal saves that instance when you press Save. Instance data is stored separately from the global config.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• ✅ Settings save automatically, per field, when changed
  • ✅ There is no "Save All Settings" button
  • ✅ Keyboard mappings, plugin settings, and instances have their own save actions
  • ✅ Errors surface in the settings UI; a failed save does not silently succeed

docs.title: User Experience
docs.text: Users can change a setting and see it applied immediately. The repository's config store is updated alongside the backend so a reload shows the same values. If a save fails, the settings header reports the error instead of pretending the change was stored.

docs.title: Share links: let guests add photos
docs.text: A share link lets someone add photos to Calvin from their phone without the admin password. Each link only adds photos to one folder in Local photos. It can't open Settings, see your other photos or touch the machine Calvin runs on, and you can turn it off at any time.

docs.title: Create a link
docs.text:
1. Open Settings › Content › Photos and find Share links.
  2. Tap Create link.
  3. Fill in:
  4. Name: who it is for ("Grandma"), so you know which link to revoke.
  5. Folder in Local photos: where the photos land. Calvin creates the folder if it doesn't exist (default Guests).
  6. Link works for: until you revoke it, or 1 day, 1 week or 30 days.
  7. Photo limit: how many photos the link takes in total (default 500). Each link also stops at 2 GB of photos; the API takes max_mb to change that.
  8. Guests see all photos (on by default): everyone using the link sees every photo added with it and can remove any of them. Turn it off so each guest sees and removes only the photos sent from their own phone.
  9. Tap Create. A QR code and the link's address appear.

Scan the QR code with the guest's phone, or send them the address. You can show the QR code again at any time with Show QR, and Rename a link without changing its address.

The list shows each link's folder, when it was created and last used, whether guests see all photos, and how many photos came in through it. The switch on each link changes Guests see all photos at any time.

Only folders made for share links are part of Local photos: Calvin marks them with a hidden .calvin-share file. Other subfolders you keep in the photos folder (an archive, backups) stay out of the slideshow, as before. Pick a folder of your own as a link's folder only if you want its photos on show.

docs.title: What the guest sees
docs.text:
A page with one big Add photos button. It opens the phone's photo picker (several photos at once is fine), shows progress while sending, and then thumbnails of the photos added with the link. With Guests see all photos on, that is every photo anyone added with the link, and the guest can remove any of them. With it off, it is only the photos sent from that phone, and another phone using the same link can't see or remove them.

A phone is recognised by a cookie in its browser, so two browsers on one phone (Firefox and Chrome) count as two phones, and clearing the browser's site data or opening the link at another address (calvin.local instead of the IP address) starts afresh. The installed app shares the cookie of the browser it was installed from. Photos shared from the gallery stay with the phone even when Android sends the share without the cookie: the page that opens after the share claims them.

Calvin scales each photo down for display (longest side 2560 px), turns it upright and removes the GPS location from its EXIF data. Only JPEG, PNG, WebP and GIF images are accepted, up to 25 MB each. Animated GIFs are written again too, at most 200 frames and 1280 px on the longest side.

There is no moderation. A guest's photo goes on the display as soon as it arrives; nobody approves it first. Give links only to people you trust with your screen, and remove a photo you don't want from Settings › Content › Photos › Local photos › Manage photos (or revoke the link with its photos).

docs.title: Install it on Android (share from the gallery)
docs.text:
1. Open the link in Chrome on the phone.
  2. Tap Install on this phone on the page, or Chrome's ⋮ › Add to Home screen › Install.
  3. From now on, in Google Photos or the gallery: pick photos › Share › Calvin photos. The photos are sent and the page confirms how many were added.

Firefox for Android can't install the page or add it to the Share menu; the page says so and asks the guest to open the link in Chrome.

docs.title: iPhone and iPad
docs.text: Open the link in Safari and tap Share › Add to Home Screen. The icon opens the page with its Add photos button. iOS doesn't let web apps appear in the Share menu, so sharing from the Photos app isn't available there.

docs.title: Revoke a link
docs.text: Tap Revoke next to the link. It stops working immediately: the guest page says the link no longer works, and uploads are refused. Photos already sent stay in Local photos unless you turn on Also remove the photos sent with this link (only that link's photos go; anything else in the folder stays).

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• The link's address is the key. Anyone who has it can add photos to that folder (nothing else) until it is revoked or runs out. Give each person their own link, and revoke a link you no longer need.
  • With Guests see all photos on (the default), anyone holding the link can see and remove every photo added with it, from any phone. It still reaches only that link's photos: not other photos in the folder, nor another link's. Turn it off for a link given to people who shouldn't remove each other's photos.
  • Calvin stores only a hash of each link's secret in share-links.json next to admin-auth.json in the data directory. share-links.key sits in the same directory and lets Calvin show the address again, so anyone who can read the data directory can work out every link's address: the hash protects the links file on its own, not a copy of the whole directory. Keep the data directory private (both files are mode 0600) and revoke every link if a copy leaks. Deleting both files revokes every link. Links are not part of a backup.
  • The secret part of the address is removed from Calvin's logs. A reverse proxy in front of Calvin keeps its own access log, which does record the full address: turn that log off for these paths, or treat the log file as secret.
  • Wrong addresses are slowed down: a few wrong tries lock that device out of further wrong tries for a while. A working link is never locked out. Behind a reverse proxy every guest seems to come from the proxy, so set CALVIN_TRUSTED_PROXIES to the proxy's address; Calvin then counts each guest by the X-Forwarded-For address the proxy sends.
  • Each link accepts at most 100 photos per 10 minutes from one device, its photo limit and 2 GB in total. Calvin refuses guest photos when less than 512 MB of disk space is left.
  • An upload from the guest page (one photo per request) may be at most 26 MB, and one Android share (all the shared photos at once) at most 256 MB; larger requests are refused before Calvin reads them. A request from another website to the share target is refused.

docs.title: On your home network
docs.text: This is the expected setup: the guest's phone must be on the same Wi-Fi as Calvin. Nothing else is needed.

docs.title: From the internet (only if you expose Calvin)
docs.text:
A guest away from home can only reach the link if you make Calvin reachable from the internet (a reverse proxy, a tunnel or port forwarding) and set PUBLIC_URL so the QR code uses that address. Know the risk before you do:

  • Calvin's dashboard and its read-only API need no login on your home network. Exposed as a whole, anyone on the internet could see your calendars and photos. Expose only the paths a guest needs: /share/, /api/guest/, /assets/, /sw.js, /favicon.svg, /icon-192.png, /icon-512.png and /apple-touch-icon.png. For example, with Caddy:
photos.example.com {
  @guest path /share/* /api/guest/* /assets/* /sw.js /favicon.svg /icon-*.png /apple-touch-icon.png
  handle @guest {
    # Refuse oversized uploads at the proxy (Calvin's own cap is 256 MB).
    request_body {
      max_size 256MB
    }
    reverse_proxy calvin.local:8000
  }
  respond 404
}

and start Calvin with CALVIN_TRUSTED_PROXIES set to the proxy's address (for Caddy on the same machine: 127.0.0.1).

  • Use HTTPS (the share target and home-screen install need it off the home network anyway).
  • Give exposed links an expiry, and revoke them when the event is over.

docs.title: For developers
docs.text:
• Store: backend/app/security/share_links.py
  • Routes: backend/app/api/routes/share.py; the guest routes are listed in GUEST_ROUTES in backend/app/security/route_policy.py. backend/app/security/guest_gate.py (pure ASGI middleware) resolves the token, caps the body and refuses a cross-site share target before any body is read; the route policy repeats the token check for an app without it.
  • The service worker (frontend/public/sw.js) leaves /share/* and /api/guest/* alone, so no share-link page or token URL is cached.
  • Photo checks: backend/app/services/guest_image.py
  • Guest page: frontend/src/views/GuestShare.vue; admin list: ShareLinksSection.vue in Settings › Content.

docs.title: Calvin — Cycle B: Dashboard
docs.text: Status: Design approved (direction). Awaiting implementation planning. Date: 2026-06-28 Part of: Touch + Visual Redesign (umbrella spec §6, §8 "B — Dashboard"). Builds on: Cycle A foundation — tokens (theme.css), type themes (useTypeTheme), and ui/ primitives (FocusPanel, SegmentedControl, ToggleSwitch, SelectPill). Reference mock: mocks/mock-nobar.png (final dashboard direction).

docs.title: 1. Goal
docs.text: Apply the focus-light design language to the live dashboard and add a parallel touch layer, without changing the keyboard action vocabulary. Touch and keyboard converge on the same shared state and the same handlers; touch is a second way to drive what already exists, not a second system.

docs.title: 2. Core architectural insight
docs.text:
Region focus is already clean shared state: activeScreen.activeRegionId (on the active dashboard screen, persisted via the config store). The keyboard moves it (region_next/prev → cycleActiveDashboardRegion). The visual highlight renders off it.

Therefore: - Touch sets the same activeRegionId (tap a region) and calls the same generic_* handlers (tap a control). - The focus-light is a richer render of that same state. - The keyboard path is untouched — same actions, same functions, same persistence.

This is the whole design: one state, one set of handlers, two input grammars, one light.

docs.title: 3. Scope
docs.text:
In scope (Cycle B): - Promote the active-region highlight to the focus-light (lit active region; configurable dimming of others). - Tap-to-focus and tap-item-to-act direct manipulation. - Contextual region controls (‹ › ↻ ⤢) on the focused region, mapped to existing handlers by region kind. - Dialog scrim with backdrop-dismiss and dim-behind (blur optional). - Horizontal clock-bar full restyle: wordmark, optional room label, screen dots, restyled clock/date, weather + connection, admin overflow menu, settings gear. - Inactivity fade/bloom of touch chrome (and of the focus-light in interaction mode), reusing the existing inactivity machinery. - Three new config keys with sensible defaults.

Out of scope (deferred): - Swipe gestures (within-region next/prev, on-stage screen change) — a later cycle. Every action remains reachable via the contextual controls and dots, so nothing is stranded. - Vertical clock-bar structural restyle — vertical bars inherit the new tokens (color/type) but keep their current structure this cycle. - Settings UI — Cycle C. The new config keys ship in Cycle B with sensible defaults; their Settings rows are added in Cycle C. - Keyboard vocabulary changes — explicitly forbidden (umbrella spec §2 non-goal).

docs.title: 4. Interaction states
docs.text:
The dashboard has three interaction states, layered over the existing inactivity machinery (usePhotoFrameMode.resetInactivityTimer, configStore.shouldShowUI, configStore.photoFrameTimeout):

State Trigger Appearance Ambient (idle) no recent interaction Calm content. No lit region, no dimming, no touch chrome. Just the calendar/photo split (or whatever the screen shows). Closest to today's resting state. Active a keypress moved focus, or a finger touched the screen Focus-light blooms on the active region; contextual controls + dots + admin-overflow visible; (others dim if configured). Photo-frame inactivity beyond photoFrameTimeout (existing) Existing photo-frame slideshow takes over (unchanged by this cycle).

The focus-light and touch chrome bloom and recede together, both gated on the interaction window — defined as configStore.shouldShowUI, the same signal the clock bar already uses (useClockBar's shouldShow). In kiosk this is exactly the bloom/recede behavior wanted: any touch or keypress calls resetInactivityTimer() → showUITemporarily(...) opens the window, and inactivity closes it. In non-kiosk/dev shouldShowUI may stay true, so the light stays visible — acceptable. This replaces the old hardcoded 2.5s ACTIVE_HIGHLIGHT_MS timer entirely. (resetInactivityTimer is already wired for touchstart, keydown, etc.)

Exception — always focus-light mode (see §5): the light stays on the active region permanently, independent of the interaction window. Touch chrome still fades.

docs.title: 5. Configuration (new keys)
docs.text:
All defaults preserve a sensible resting experience and are documented for migration. Settings rows land in Cycle C; Cycle B ships the keys + behavior.

Key Type Default Meaning focusLightMode 'interaction' \| 'always' \| 'off' 'interaction' interaction: light blooms on interaction, recedes when idle. always: active region stays lit. off: never highlight (pure ambient). focusLightDimOthers boolean true When the light is active, do unfocused regions recede (opacity + slight desaturation)? true = the spec's "lit control panel" signature; false = glow on active only, others stay full-brightness. displayName string '' (empty → hidden) Optional room/display label shown next to the wordmark in the clock bar.

docs.title: New
docs.text:
composables/useTouchCapability.js - Returns a reactive isTouch derived from matchMedia('(pointer: coarse)'), updated on change. - Single source of truth for "show touch chrome." On the 24" non-touch unit isTouch is false.

components/dashboard/RegionControls.vue - Props: regionKind ('calendar' | 'photos' | 'service'). - Renders the contextual control cluster for the focused region. Each button calls the existing handler for that kind (see §7). Buttons that don't apply to a kind are not rendered (e.g. refresh for photos). - The expand/fullscreen verb (⤢) is --focus-filled (primary, per mock); prev/next/refresh are quiet cbtn-style 46px buttons. - Emits no new domain logic — it is a touch surface over existing actions.

components/ui/ScreenDots.vue - Props: screens (array), activeScreenId. - Renders one dot per dashboard screen; active dot uses --focus. Tap a dot emits select-screen(id) → caller sets active screen via the existing screen path (setActiveDashboardScreen / the same mutation screen_next uses). - Hidden when there is only one screen.

components/ui/DialogScrim.vue - Reusable backdrop for dialog-style overlays. Props: blur (boolean, default false). - Renders a dim scrim (cheap opacity layer) over the content behind; blur adds backdrop-filter: blur() as a progressive enhancement. - Emits dismiss on backdrop tap. Reduced-motion safe (instant under prefers-reduced-motion).

components/dashboard/AdminOverflow.vue (or an overflow affordance integrated into BarActionCluster) - A ⋯ button that toggles a small popover containing the admin buttons (mode toggle, orientation, side-view, UI-hide). The settings gear stays visible outside the overflow. - The overflow trigger is part of the touch chrome and fades with the interaction window. - Closes on outside tap / action / Escape (reuse the SelectPill outside-click + Escape pattern from Cycle A).

docs.title: Modified
docs.text:
components/DashboardRegion.vue - Wrap region content in the Cycle-A FocusPanel, driven by activeRegionId (focused vs dimmed). Respect focusLightMode (off → never focused-styled) and focusLightDimOthers (controls the dim treatment). - Emit focus-region(id) on tap of region chrome/background. - Host RegionControls in the region header when the region is focused and isTouch and the interaction window is open.

views/Dashboard.vue - Replace the 2px-outline + 2.5s-fade highlight (ACTIVE_HIGHLIGHT_MS, activeRegionHighlightVisible, the watch + timer) with the focus-light driven by interaction state + focusLightMode. - Handle focus-region taps → set activeRegionId (same mutation region_next uses). - Provide isTouch and interaction-window state down to regions and the clock bar. - Keep the existing MinimalUIOverlay path.

components/ClockBarHorizontal.vue (+ BarLogo, BarActionCluster) - Full restyle to the mock: left = wordmark + optional room label + ScreenDots; center = tabular clock (--font-display) + date (--font-data); right = weather + connection (PluginStatusbarItems) + AdminOverflow + settings gear. - Keep all existing admin functions (now behind the overflow); retokenize. - Vertical bars (ClockBarVertical.vue): inherit new tokens only, no structural rework.

composables/useClockBar.js / stores/config.js - Add displayName, focusLightMode, focusLightDimOthers config keys with defaults and persistence, following the existing config-key pattern.

docs.title: Reused as-is (no rewrite)
docs.text:
• useKeyboardActions.js — frozen vocabulary; RegionControls/dots/taps call its existing handlers/resolvers.
  • The generic_next/prev/refresh/expand resolvers and the per-mode handlers.
  • usePhotoFrameMode.resetInactivityTimer + configStore.shouldShowUI — drive the fade/bloom.
  • Cycle-A FocusPanel — the focus-light primitive.

docs.title: 7. Per-region control mapping
docs.text:
RegionControls maps each button to the existing handler for the region kind (the same functions the keyboard generic_* resolvers dispatch to). No new navigation logic.

Region ‹ prev › next ↻ refresh ⤢ expand / fullscreen calendar calendar_prev calendar_next calendar_refresh calendar_expand photos images_prev images_next — (not rendered) photos_enter_fullscreen service web_service_prev web_service_next service_refresh web_service_enter_fullscreen

docs.title: 8. Tap & direct-manipulation rules
docs.text:
• Tap a region (background/header/chrome) → that region becomes active (activeRegionId); the light follows. Identical end-state to keyboard region_next.
  • Tap an actionable item → focuses the region and performs the item action:
