docs.title: Deployment Topologies
docs.text: Calvin's backend serves both the API (/api/*) and the built frontend (/) from a single FastAPI process. That gives you flexibility in how you split the work across hosts. Two shapes are officially supported.

docs.title: Mode A — All-in-one Pi (default)
docs.text:
The Pi runs everything: backend, frontend, and the kiosk browser.

┌─────────────────────────── Raspberry Pi ───────────────────────────┐
│                                                                    │
│   cog (kiosk)      ──> http://localhost:8000  ──> Calvin backend   │
│                                                  │                 │
│                                                  └── SQLite, data  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Use when: - One Pi, simple setup. - You want the SD card / SSD to be the single source of truth.

Setup:

sudo bash scripts/setup.sh --mode prod

See SETUP_LINUX.md for the full walkthrough.

The kiosk browser follows the same display-stack rule as a kiosk Pi (see Display stack):

  • A fresh install uses cog (WPE WebKit on DRM/KMS, calvin-cog.service), on every board. It waits for the local backend before it opens the dashboard.
  • --display-stack x11|wayland|cog picks one explicitly: sudo bash scripts/setup.sh --mode prod --display-stack x11 gives the previous X11 + Chromium kiosk (calvin-x.service + calvin-kiosk.service).
  • A re-run (or update-calvin.sh) keeps the stack recorded in /etc/default/calvin-kiosk as CALVIN_DISPLAY_STACK. An all-in-one Pi installed before this setting existed is X11 and stays X11; it is never migrated silently. Re-run setup with --display-stack cog to move it.
  • X11 + Chromium stay installed on every stack, so switching back is one re-run of setup with --display-stack x11, not a reimage.
  • setup.sh --refresh skips apt, except when the stack it applies needs a package that is missing (cog, or labwc on Wayland): it installs that first, and stops before changing any display unit if the install fails.

The screen on/off schedule needs vcgencmd/xset (or, on cog, the panel helper) on the host, which the container does not have, so setup also installs the same calvin-display-agent.service the kiosk Pis use, pointed at http://localhost:$CALVIN_PORT (it reads the global config; it does not show up under Settings → Screens). Rotation and output settings go in /etc/default/calvin-kiosk exactly as on a kiosk Pi.

docs.title: Mode B — Remote backend + kiosk Pi
docs.text:
The backend (and its data) live on a home server. One or more Pis run only Chromium, pointed at the server's URL.

┌─────── Home server ───────┐         ┌──── Raspberry Pi ────┐
│                           │         │                      │
│   Calvin backend          │ <─────  │   Chromium (kiosk)   │
│   ├── SQLite, photos      │   LAN   │                      │
│   └── plugin data         │         │                      │
└───────────────────────────┘         └──────────────────────┘

Use when: - You already run a 24/7 server and don't want SQLite / photos / plugin data on the Pi's SD card. - You want multiple kiosk Pis sharing one backend (each just runs Chromium against the same URL). - Plugin syncs are heavy and you want them on a beefier host.

docs.title: Why no proxy on the Pi?
docs.text: The kiosk Pi opens the server's URL directly in Chromium. From the browser's view it's same-origin: the server hosts both / and /api/*. No CORS, no reverse proxy on the Pi, no env vars baked into the frontend. The Pi is genuinely "dumb."

docs.title: What stays on the Pi
docs.text:
• X server, openbox, Chromium — installed by setup-kiosk.sh.
  • Display / cursor / screensaver tweaks.
  • Anything OS-level you've added (e.g. a hardware reboot button script driven by evdev). Calvin's app code does not handle hardware input in the browser path; physical buttons are wired up at the OS level.

docs.title: What moves to the server
docs.text:
• The backend Docker container (or whatever you use to run it).
  • /var/lib/calvin/ — SQLite database, photos, plugin install dirs, kiosk signing key.
  • Plugin installs, including their pip dependencies (live, no rebuild).

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Server. Run the standard backend deployment, but bind the port to a LAN-reachable interface. On Unraid, use the Docker template in UNRAID.md. On a regular Linux server, the simplest path is the same Docker compose used in Mode A:

# On the server (any Linux box with Docker):
# v0.1.0 = the release you want; use develop only to test the next one.
git clone -b v0.1.0 https://github.com/osterbergsimon/calvin.git
cd calvin
cp deploy/calvin.env.example docker/.env
# Edit docker/.env — set CALVIN_IMAGE_TAG=v0.1.0, CALVIN_PORT, DATABASE_URL, etc.
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up -d

Verify it answers from another host on the LAN:

curl http://<server-host>:8000/api/health

Pin the server to a stable hostname (mDNS homeserver.local, a static DHCP lease, or a DNS entry) so the kiosk URL doesn't drift.

2. Pi. On a fresh Raspberry Pi OS Lite, run the installer the server serves:

curl -fsSL http://homeserver.local:8000/api/kiosks/install.sh | sudo bash

Step-by-step guide, including the signed (SSH) variant, the signing key, and supported Pi models: KIOSK_INSTALL.md. The installer downloads setup-kiosk.sh from the server and runs it. From a checkout, sudo bash scripts/setup-kiosk.sh --backend-url http://homeserver.local:8000 does the same. setup-kiosk.sh installs xserver-xorg, openbox, chromium, and friends; writes /etc/default/calvin-kiosk with the backend URL; and installs the kiosk bundle:

  • calvin-x.service — starts the X server on tty1.
  • calvin-kiosk-remote.service — waits for the backend to answer, then launches Chromium in kiosk mode against CALVIN_BACKEND_URL.
  • calvin-display-agent.service — applies rotation/resolution and the screen on/off schedule (see below).
  • calvin-kiosk-update.service — a root oneshot used by the remote display-agent update flow.

The update bundle installed by update-kiosk.sh --bootstrap also includes the first-boot helper where the image uses it.

The installer reboots when it finishes, and Chromium opens to the dashboard.

Zero-touch alternative: instead of SSHing in, you can bake the backend URL + wifi into the card before first boot so the Pi self-provisions. See KIOSK_INSTALL.md.

docs.title: Screen scheduling on a Mode-B kiosk
docs.text: Calvin's screen on/off schedule is authored in the dashboard UI, but the backend cannot reach a remote kiosk's display. setup-kiosk.sh therefore installs calvin-display-agent.service, a small local agent that reads the schedule from ${CALVIN_BACKEND_URL}/api/config and powers the panel with vcgencmd/xset. It computes on/off boundaries locally and wakes exactly at the next one, and re-reads the config every CALVIN_DISPLAY_REFRESH_SECONDS (default 60, set in /etc/default/calvin-kiosk to override), so a schedule edit reaches the panel within about a minute. Set the schedule in the UI as usual; the kiosk follows it. Logs: journalctl -u calvin-display-agent.service.

docs.title: Screen rotation on a Mode-B kiosk
docs.text:
Screen rotation, output selection, and resolution are physical to each Pi, so they live in the device-local /etc/default/calvin-kiosk, not in the (global) server config. The display-agent applies them via xrandr at startup and whenever the per-kiosk device-config version changes:

  • CALVIN_DISPLAY_ROTATION — rotation mode: normal, left, right, or inverted.
  • CALVIN_DISPLAY_OUTPUT — the xrandr output name (e.g. HDMI-1) to select as primary and target for resolution/rotation. Optional; when unset the agent auto-detects the first connected output.
  • CALVIN_DISPLAY_RESOLUTION — the mode to apply, as WIDTHxHEIGHT or WIDTHxHEIGHT@RATE (e.g. 1920x1080 or 1920x1080@60). Optional; when unset the current mode is left unchanged.

Example:

CALVIN_DISPLAY_ROTATION=left
CALVIN_DISPLAY_OUTPUT=HDMI-1
CALVIN_DISPLAY_RESOLUTION=1920x1080@60

These device-local env vars win over the equivalent server config (displayOutput / displayResolution / displayRotation); the display-agent applies them via xrandr at startup and whenever the per-kiosk device-config version changes. Then sudo systemctl restart calvin-display-agent.service. This replaces the old backend-side display_orientation_service, which cannot reach a remote kiosk's display. (Per-device settings are tracked under epic calvin-dd9.)

docs.title: Kiosk agent self-update
docs.text:
The small Python display-agent and its systemd units that setup-kiosk.sh installs can be updated remotely without re-running setup or SSHing into the Pi.

Flow: Settings → Screens → Kiosk software → Update all (or Update in one screen's Software section) → the backend sets a per-kiosk agentUpdateRequested flag → the kiosk picks it up on its next config poll → it fires the root oneshot calvin-kiosk-update.service → update-kiosk.sh fetches the bundle from ${CALVIN_BACKEND_URL}/api/kiosks/agent/*, verifies sha256 (+ py_compile for Python files), backs up the current files, atomic-swaps only changed files, restarts only the affected units, and auto-rolls-back if the agent doesn't come up healthy within 30 seconds.

The bundle source is the local Calvin server — the kiosk needs no internet access and carries no full repo checkout. Six files make up the bundle: the display-agent script, three systemd units, the updater script, and the oneshot update service unit.

The Screens list summarises the fleet in a Kiosk software row: how many kiosks can be updated to the available bundle, with Update all in one click. Each kiosk card shows its running version and the outcome of its last update; a kiosk whose OS/Python is too old is marked "update needs a newer OS" and is never included in Update all. While at least one kiosk is behind, System › Updates shows a pointer to that row.

min_python floor: the manifest carries "min_python": "3.9". If the kiosk's Python is below 3.9 the update is aborted (status: "device python < 3.9; keeping current agent") — the kiosk needs an OS upgrade before it can accept a newer bundle. The same floor is enforced at startup: the agent exits immediately on Python < 3.9.

For full details — health-check readiness marker, sudoers fragment, auto-clear of the flag, initial bundle install, and the zipapp future option — see the Kiosk agent self-update section in KIOSK_PROVISIONING.md.

docs.title: Kiosk identity
docs.text:
Each kiosk Pi has a stable CALVIN_KIOSK_ID in /etc/default/calvin-kiosk, generated by setup-kiosk.sh as <hostname>-<machine-id suffix> (a stock Pi image defaults its hostname to raspberrypi, so the machine-id suffix keeps multiple Pis unique). Rename it to something friendly (kitchen, hallway) and sudo systemctl restart calvin-kiosk-remote.service.

The kiosk's Chromium opens ${CALVIN_BACKEND_URL}/?kiosk=<id>, so the server learns which kiosk is talking to it: every /api/config?kiosk=<id> request registers the kiosk (id, hostname, last-seen). List known kiosks with curl http://<server>:8000/api/kiosks. A request with no id behaves exactly as before — this is the foundation the per-kiosk config model builds on.

docs.title: Per-kiosk configuration
docs.text:
Each kiosk reads its effective config from GET /api/kiosks/<id>/config — the global config with that kiosk's overrides applied (device-physical values like rotation included; the browser ignores what it can't act on, the display-agent applies them). The response carries an ETag/deviceConfigVersion so a client can cheaply detect device-physical changes (If-None-Match → 304).

Per-kiosk overrides are edited via GET/PUT /api/kiosks/<id>/overrides (a sparse layer that replaces on PUT). GET /api/config is now global-only (Mode-A Pis and the template new kiosks inherit). List known kiosks with curl http://<server>:8000/api/kiosks.

Assigning content to a kiosk. Two override keys control which screens a kiosk shows: availableScreens (a list of screen ids the kiosk may switch between — omit for all) and defaultScreenId (the screen it boots into). Set them via PUT /api/kiosks/<id>/overrides. In this mode the active screen is local to each kiosk — switching screens on one kiosk (keyboard or on-screen dots) no longer changes the others, and a kiosk boots to its defaultScreenId. The screen catalog itself is authored once, globally.

Per-kiosk orientation from the server. When CALVIN_KIOSK_ID is set, the display-agent fetches the kiosk's effective config (/api/kiosks/<id>/config) and applies the server-configured orientation via xrandr — re-applying only when it changes (tracked by deviceConfigVersion). Set a kiosk's orientation with PUT /api/kiosks/<id>/overrides. The device-local CALVIN_DISPLAY_ROTATION env still wins as a break-glass override; the schedule is likewise now per-kiosk (each kiosk reads its own effective config).

Managing screens from the UI. Settings → Screens lists every screen that has connected (name, id, last-seen, Online/Offline). Select one to open its page: Name and Pages (which pages it shows and which one it starts on), Display (orientation, upside down, rotation), Power, Touch & keyboard and Software. Every row says Same as all screens or Only this screen, and Use the shared setting clears that one override so the screen inherits again. The shared defaults live under the All screens card on the same page. Changes save immediately and the screen applies them at its next check-in (~30s).

docs.title: Changing the backend URL later
docs.text:
sudo nano /etc/default/calvin-kiosk
sudo systemctl restart calvin-kiosk-remote.service
# The display agent reads the same file for rotation/schedule:
sudo systemctl restart calvin-display-agent.service

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
Mode B does not require any CORS configuration: the browser hits the server's URL directly, so requests to /api/* are same-origin.

CORS only matters if you run npm run dev on a different host than the backend (e.g. hacking on the frontend from a laptop while pointing at the home server). For that case the backend already exposes CORS_ORIGINS and CORS_ALLOW_ALL env vars — see backend/app/config.py.

docs.title: Public URL (phone setup and Add kiosk)
docs.text:
Settings shows the server's address as a QR code ("set up from your phone"), and Screens › + Add a screen prints curl -fsSL <server>/api/kiosks/install.sh | sudo bash. The address comes from PUBLIC_URL when set, otherwise from the browser's own address, falling back to the LAN IP the backend detects for itself. That last guess is wrong in Docker (it sees the container IP), so on Docker/Unraid set PUBLIC_URL=http://<server-lan-ip>:8000 in .env (passed through by docker/docker-compose.yml) or the template's Public URL field.

The served installer (GET /api/kiosks/install.sh) bakes the same address in, so behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy set PUBLIC_URL=https://<your-domain>. Without it the app only sees the proxy's plain-HTTP request: it can use X-Forwarded-Proto/X-Forwarded-Host instead, but only from a peer listed in CALVIN_TRUSTED_PROXIES (comma-separated IPs/CIDRs, * for any; empty by default). Forwarded headers from any other client are ignored, so a kiosk cannot be pointed at an attacker-chosen URL.

docs.title: Security note
docs.text:
Calvin's backend has no built-in authentication. Mode B exposes it on your LAN, so:

  • Bind to the LAN interface, not 0.0.0.0 on a host that's reachable from the internet.
  • Don't port-forward it. If you need remote access, put it behind a VPN or reverse proxy with auth.

docs.title: Picking a mode
docs.text:
Question Mode A Mode B Single Pi, no other hardware ✅ Already run a 24/7 home server ✅ Multiple displays sharing one dashboard ✅ Want SQLite + photos off the SD card ✅ Want everything reachable on first boot, no LAN ✅ Plugin installs are heavy (image processing) ✅

You can switch later — both modes use the same backend image and the same /var/lib/calvin/ data layout. Migrating is mostly: stop the backend on the Pi, copy /var/lib/calvin/ to the server, start it there, and reflash the Pi with setup-kiosk.sh.

docs.title: Getting Started with Calvin
docs.text: Calvin is a self-hosted Raspberry Pi dashboard — calendars, photos, web services — with a Vue 3 frontend and a FastAPI backend. This page gets you running in development and points you at the right deployment doc for production.

docs.title: Two things you might want to do
docs.text:
• Run Calvin in development to hack on it. → Development
  • Deploy Calvin to a Raspberry Pi to actually use it. → Deployment

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Docker (with Compose v2) — required for the dev workflow.
  • Git.
  • uv and Node.js 20+ — only needed if you want to run native tests, linters, or formatters in your editor. Not needed to run the app.

The backend targets Python 3.12+, but you don't install Python locally unless you're running native tooling — the dev container ships with the right interpreter.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
The dev workflow is Docker Compose. One stack runs the backend with hot-reload (uvicorn --reload) and the frontend with the Vite dev server, both bind-mounting your checkout.

git clone https://github.com/osterbergsimon/calvin.git
cd calvin

make install   # creates docker/.env from the example, one-time
make dev       # starts the dev stack, streams logs

Windows uses the same targets through a PowerShell wrapper:

.\make.ps1 install
.\make.ps1 dev

Access points: - Backend + API: http://localhost:8000 - Frontend dev server (with HMR): http://localhost:5173 - API docs: http://localhost:8000/docs

make dev-down stops the stack. make doctor checks your Docker install and shows what ports are in use. make clean tears the stack down and removes dev data.

docs.title: VS Code Dev Containers
docs.text: The repo ships a .devcontainer/ config. Open the folder in VS Code, run Dev Containers: Reopen in Container, and you get the same dev stack with extensions pre-installed.

docs.title: Running tests, lint, format, type-check natively
docs.text:
These targets shell out to uv and npm directly (faster than round-tripping through Docker, and they integrate with editors):

make test          # backend pytest + frontend vitest
make lint          # ruff + eslint
make format        # ruff format + prettier
make type-check    # mypy + vue-tsc

make type-check type-checks the backend with mypy and the frontend with vue-tsc, but the frontend scope is deliberately narrow: only src/api/ (including the generated types.ts) is checked. The rest of the frontend is JavaScript, so .vue and .js files are not type-checked yet.

If you don't have uv/node installed, the Windows setup script (.\setup-windows.ps1) and the Linux dev script (scripts/setup-dev.sh) install them for you. They are otherwise unnecessary.

docs.title: Sample data
docs.text:
Calvin can fill itself with realistic sample content — a calendar, photos and two dashboard pages — so you can try it, take screenshots, or run a demo before connecting any accounts. No accounts or internet access are needed, and nothing you created is touched:

# Dev stack: the compose stack keeps its data in docker/.calvin-dev-data.
make demo-seed DATA_DIR=$PWD/docker/.calvin-dev-data

# Native install: the same data dir the service uses (CALVIN_DATA_DIR, or
# backend/data when unset).
cd backend && uv run python -m app.demo seed

# Remove exactly the seeded items again.
make demo-clear DATA_DIR=$PWD/docker/.calvin-dev-data

For a Docker install, point --data-dir at the directory bind-mounted as /var/lib/calvin, or run the command inside the container.

seed adds:

  • a sample calendar with events anchored to today (served by the backend at /api/demo/calendar.ics, so it also works in Docker),
  • twelve small CC0 sample photos in the local photos source,
  • two pages — “calendar + photos” and “photo frame” — but only when you have no pages of your own (Calvin's untouched default “Home” page is replaced),
  • a manifest at <data-dir>/demo/manifest.json marking every seeded item.

clear reads that manifest and removes only those items, so your own calendars, photos, pages and screen names survive both commands. The demo sets no room name: that is each screen's own Name in Settings › Screens. Plugin instances load at startup, so restart Calvin after seeding or clearing to see the change.

The two sample pages are only added when you have no pages of your own. Calvin's untouched default “Home” page is replaced; as soon as you rename, edit or add a page, seeding leaves your pages alone. The calendar and photos are added either way.

The equivalent commands are uv run python -m app.demo seed|clear from backend/; add --data-dir DIR to point at another data directory and --calendar-url URL if the backend is not reachable at http://127.0.0.1:<API_PORT>.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
Production runs in one of two shapes — see Deployment Topologies for the full comparison and the security caveats.

Mode A — All-in-one Pi. One Pi runs backend, frontend, and the kiosk browser. Easiest to set up. From the Pi:

# Stable release (replace v0.1.0 with the latest tag from
# https://github.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/releases)
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/v0.1.0/scripts/setup.sh \
  | sudo GIT_BRANCH=v0.1.0 bash
sudo reboot

The script installs Docker, the kiosk dependencies, the published runtime image for that release, and the systemd units. The dashboard comes up at http://localhost:8000 after reboot.

The kiosk browser is cog (WPE WebKit) by default, the same as on a kiosk Pi. Add --display-stack x11 for X11 + Chromium instead (... | sudo GIT_BRANCH=v0.1.0 bash -s -- --display-stack x11). A re-run keeps the stack the Pi already has; an older all-in-one Pi stays on X11 until you re-run setup with --display-stack cog. See Display stack.

When the kiosk runs Chromium (X11 or Wayland), on Pi 3-class boards (Pi 3/3B+, Zero 2 W, CM3) the kiosk runs Chromium without its GPU path, because that path crashes the dashboard renderer on their VC4 graphics; Pi 4/5 keep it. The flags live in /etc/default/calvin-kiosk-display; see Pi 3 and GPU for the override.

Testers can track the integration branch instead. It runs the :develop image and moves with every push:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/develop/scripts/setup.sh | sudo bash

main is release-only and is never installed directly — releases are installed by tag. Pass GIT_BRANCH=<branch-or-tag> after sudo (... | sudo GIT_BRANCH=v0.1.0 bash) to pin another ref, or --mode dev for a hot-reload Pi. Details in SETUP_LINUX.md and SETUP_SCRIPTS.md. Before the first release exists, use the develop command.

Mode B — Remote backend + kiosk Pi. A home server runs the backend; one or more Pis run only Chromium pointed at the server's URL. Move SQLite and photos off the SD card, share one backend across multiple displays.

For Unraid, use the Docker template in UNRAID.md.

# Server: same Docker compose as Mode A.
docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up -d

# Pi (kiosk only):
sudo bash scripts/setup-kiosk.sh --backend-url http://homeserver.local:8000
sudo reboot

Details and the picker table live in DEPLOYMENT_TOPOLOGIES.md.

The Pi's display-agent (rotation, resolution, on/off schedule) can be updated later without SSH or re-flashing: click Update on the kiosk in Settings → Screens, and it pulls a verified bundle from the server on its next poll. See Kiosk agent self-update.

docs.title: First sign-in
docs.text:
A fresh install has no admin password. Open Settings and Calvin asks for a one-time setup code together with the password you want. The code is in the server log, and in setup-code.txt in the data directory:

# Docker / Compose
docker logs calvin | grep "Calvin setup code"

# Unraid (Docker tab → Calvin → Logs works too)
docker logs calvin | grep "Calvin setup code"

# Pi all-in-one
sudo journalctl -u calvin-app -n 100 | grep "Calvin setup code"

A kiosk that reaches Calvin over loopback (http://localhost:8000) shows the code on its own setup screen. Once a password exists the code stops working. For a headless install you can choose the code up front with CALVIN_SETUP_CODE; see Admin authentication.

docs.title: Verifying it works
docs.text:
After make dev (or after a Pi reboot), check:

  • http://localhost:8000/api/health returns {"status":"healthy"}.
  • http://localhost:8000/ shows the dashboard.
  • http://localhost:8000/docs shows the API.

In dev, http://localhost:5173/ is the Vite-served frontend with HMR; it proxies API calls to the backend on :8000.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Port already in use (8000 or 5173):

make dev-down       # stop the dev stack first
lsof -i :8000       # Linux/macOS — find the holdout
# Windows: netstat -ano | findstr :8000  ;  taskkill /PID <pid> /F

Docker permission denied (Linux): add yourself to the docker group, then re-login.

sudo usermod -aG docker $USER
newgrp docker

Pi services not starting:

sudo systemctl status calvin-app
sudo journalctl -u calvin-app -n 50
sudo systemctl status calvin-cog          # Mode A, cog (default)
sudo systemctl status calvin-kiosk        # Mode A, X11/Wayland (Chromium)
sudo systemctl status calvin-kiosk-remote # Mode B

Native tooling missing (only matters if you run make test / lint / etc.): re-run .\setup-windows.ps1 or scripts/setup-dev.sh, or install uv and Node 20+ manually.

docs.title: Install a kiosk Pi: fresh SD card to Calvin on screen
docs.text:
This is the short path for Mode B: the Calvin server runs elsewhere (Unraid, or any Docker host), and the Raspberry Pi is only a display. See DEPLOYMENT_TOPOLOGIES.md for the background.

Your Calvin server hands out everything the Pi needs. You don't need a repo checkout on the Pi, and nothing comes from GitHub, so the kiosk always matches the server's version.

docs.title: Supported hardware and OS
docs.text:
Supported Notes Pi model Raspberry Pi 5, Pi 4 (2 GB+), Pi 400 Recommended. cog (WPE WebKit) by default. Pi 3B / 3B+ Supported. cog by default; verified end to end on a 3B+ (2026-10-31). Pi Zero 2 W Uses cog (WPE WebKit) by default; still unmeasured on 512 MB, so not recommended yet. Older Pis (Pi 1/2, Zero) Not supported (too little RAM for the dashboard). OS Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit), Trixie (Debian 13) Verified with cog on a Pi 3B+ and a Pi 400 (boot/reboot, rotation, screen off/on, real sites, 60 min soak; 2026-10-31). Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit), Bookworm (Debian 12) Should work; 64-bit is preferred. Raspberry Pi OS Lite 32-bit, Bookworm Should work; 64-bit is preferred. Raspberry Pi OS Desktop Not supported: Calvin starts its own X session on tty1, which conflicts with the desktop.

You need a reachable Calvin server. Check from any machine on the LAN with curl http://<server>:8000/api/health. Use a stable hostname or IP for the server, such as a DHCP reservation or tower.local.

docs.title: Step 0: get the signing key from the server (recommended)
docs.text:
The server signs the kiosk software it serves. When you give the Pi the server's key, the Pi rejects anything another device on your network might try to slip in. That covers the setup scripts, the kiosk agent, and every later update. Copy the key over a trusted channel (your own SSH/terminal access to the server), never over plain HTTP. The server creates it on first start:

Server Where the key is Unraid (template) /mnt/user/appdata/calvin/kiosk-signing.key (Unraid web terminal or SSH as root) Docker compose ${CALVIN_DATA_DIR:-/var/lib/calvin}/kiosk-signing.key on the host, or docker exec calvin cat /var/lib/calvin/kiosk-signing.key Source checkout the path logged at startup: Kiosk manifest signing key: …

The file is one line of 64 hex characters. It sits in the server's data volume, so it survives container updates.

You can skip the key. The kiosk still works, but then it trusts whatever answers at the server's address on your LAN.

docs.title: Option A: install over SSH on a running Pi
docs.text:
1. Flash. In Raspberry Pi Imager, pick Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit). Using Imager's OS customisation is fine here: set a hostname (e.g. kitchen), a user, Wi-Fi, and enable SSH. Boot the Pi.
  2. Install, using one of these two ways:

Signed (recommended). Run this from your workstation. It copies the key and the installer from the server to the Pi over SSH, so nothing that touches the key comes over plain HTTP:

SERVER=tower PI=<user>@kitchen.local
ssh root@$SERVER cat /mnt/user/appdata/calvin/kiosk-signing.key \
  | ssh $PI 'umask 077; cat > calvin.key'
ssh root@$SERVER docker exec Calvin cat /app/kiosk-bundle/deploy/kiosk-agent/install-kiosk.sh \
  | ssh $PI 'cat > install-kiosk.sh'
ssh -t $PI "sudo bash install-kiosk.sh --backend-url http://$SERVER:8000 \
  --signing-key-file calvin.key --no-reboot && rm calvin.key && sudo reboot"

Calvin is the Unraid template's container name; with Docker compose it is calvin, and the key path is the one from Step 0. You can also copy deploy/kiosk-agent/install-kiosk.sh from a Calvin checkout. The installer stores the key root-only in /etc/default/calvin-kiosk-signing, but only after the server's signature has proved the key is correct.

Quick (trusts your LAN). On the Pi, run:

curl -fsSL http://tower:8000/api/kiosks/install.sh | sudo bash

Do not add the signing key to this form. The script arrives over plain HTTP, and a tampered copy could steal the key.

Either way, the install takes a few minutes, mostly package installs, and the Pi then reboots. 3. Done. After the reboot the Pi starts the kiosk browser (cog by default) on the dashboard. Within a minute it appears in Settings → Screens on the server.

The quick form bakes in the URL the server saw the request on. Behind a reverse proxy that can be an internal or http:// address. If the Pi should use a different URL, add -s -- --backend-url http://<server>:8000.

docs.title: Option B: bake the SD card (no SSH, no typing on the Pi)
docs.text:
Use this for several Pis, or for a Pi you hand to someone else. You need a Calvin checkout on your workstation (Linux/macOS) at the release you run on the server (a vX.Y.Z tag; develop is fine for testing).

  1. Flash Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit) with Imager and do not use Imager's OS customisation (it writes a competing first-boot hook).
  2. Re-insert the card, then copy the key to the workstation as above (ssh root@tower cat … > calvin.key; chmod 600 calvin.key). Then bake:
sudo bash scripts/bake-kiosk-firstrun.sh \
  --backend-url http://tower:8000 \
  --boot-dir /media/$USER/bootfs \
  --hostname kitchen \
  --wifi-ssid HomeNet --wifi-psk 's3cret' --wifi-country SE \
  --ssh-pubkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub \
  --signing-key-file calvin.key

Omit --wifi-* on Ethernet. --ssh-pubkey is optional and gives you recovery access as calvin-admin (key-only, passwordless sudo; --admin-user renames it). 3. Put the card in the Pi and power on. It reboots twice by itself and comes up on the dashboard. Boot 1 applies the hostname, Wi-Fi and SSH. Boot 2 waits for the server, then installs, showing its progress on the screen. Boot 3 is the kiosk.

Details and troubleshooting: KIOSK_PROVISIONING.md.

docs.title: Pin a release
docs.text:
A kiosk installs the software its server serves, so the way to pin a kiosk to a release is to run the server on that release (see SETUP_SCRIPTS.md). The Pi then matches the backend exactly, and Settings → Screens → Update moves with the server.

The install scripts themselves also accept a release tag, which is what you want when the card is baked from a checkout or setup-kiosk.sh is fetched directly:

# Kiosk-only install from a release tag (the fallback common script is
# fetched from the same tag)
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/osterbergsimon/calvin/v0.1.0/scripts/setup-kiosk.sh \
  | sudo GIT_BRANCH=v0.1.0 bash -s -- --backend-url http://tower:8000

# Bake a card from a release checkout
git clone --branch v0.1.0 https://github.com/osterbergsimon/calvin.git
cd calvin
sudo bash scripts/bake-kiosk-firstrun.sh --backend-url http://tower:8000 ...

GIT_BRANCH=v0.1.0 pins the scripts and the checkout the server side uses; it never selects an image for the Pi (a kiosk runs a browser, not Calvin). The server container's image tag (CALVIN_IMAGE_TAG) is the version that matters, and setup.sh sets it from the same tag.

docs.title: What the install does
docs.text:
Pi                                         Calvin server
──                                         ─────────────
install-kiosk.sh (over SSH, piped  ◀──── GET /api/kiosks/install.sh  (server URL baked in)
  from the server, or on the card)
  ├─ store key → /etc/default/calvin-kiosk-signing (0600)
  ├─ fetch manifest, verify HMAC     ◀──── GET /api/kiosks/agent/manifest (signed)
  ├─ fetch setup scripts, check sha  ◀──── GET /api/kiosks/installer/setup-{kiosk,common}.sh
  └─ setup-kiosk.sh
       ├─ apt: cog (WPE WebKit) + the X11/Chromium fallback packages, sudo
       │       (+ labwc, wlr-randr, wlopm on the opt-in Wayland stack)
       ├─ /etc/default/calvin-kiosk (server URL, kiosk id, hostname,
       │                            display stack; other keys kept)
       └─ update-kiosk.sh --bootstrap ◀─── GET /api/kiosks/agent/files/*  (verified)
            └─ display agent + calvin-cog (or calvin-x / calvin-wayland) + calvin-display-agent units
reboot → cog shows Calvin; the agent polls /api/kiosks/<id>/config → listed in Settings → Screens

Trust boundary: with a key, every file after the installer is verified against the server's signature: the setup scripts, the kiosk agent, and every later update. The installer itself must come over a trusted channel: SSH from the server (Option A, signed), or your own checkout (Option B). The quick curl | bash form trusts whatever answers on your LAN, so use it without a key.

docs.title: Pi 3 and GPU
docs.text:
Pi 3-class boards (Broadcom VC4, OpenGL ES 2.0 through Mesa) cannot run Chromium's GPU path: the dashboard's renderer crashes within seconds with "Aw, Snap! error 11" and the tab reloads forever. --disable-gpu makes the same page load and stay up, so the installers add that flag on those boards — and only there. Pi 4/5 have a working GPU path and keep it. This covers both deployment shapes: the remote kiosk installer (setup-kiosk.sh) and the all-in-one install (setup.sh). It only matters when a kiosk runs Chromium (the X11/Wayland fallback); the cog default does not run Chromium at all.

Board (/proc/device-tree/model) CALVIN_CHROMIUM_GPU=auto (the default) Raspberry Pi 3 / 3B / 3B+, Zero 2 W, Compute Module 3 --disable-gpu Raspberry Pi 4, Pi 5, Compute Module 4/5 GPU path on, no extra flag anything else (unknown board, no device tree) GPU path on, no extra flag

The flag lands in CALVIN_CHROMIUM_DISPLAY_FLAGS in /etc/default/calvin-kiosk-display, which both kiosk units pass to Chromium (calvin-kiosk-remote.service on a kiosk, calvin-kiosk.service on an all-in-one install), so it applies to both stacks (Wayland keeps --ozone-platform=wayland and the GPU flag follows it). The installer and an update (a kiosk Update on a remote kiosk, update-calvin.sh on an all-in-one install) recompute that line from the board instead of appending to it, so re-running never duplicates it.

docs.title: Override it
docs.text:
Set CALVIN_CHROMIUM_GPU in the file the other kiosk settings live in:

sudo nano /etc/default/calvin-kiosk
# CALVIN_CHROMIUM_GPU=auto   # default: decide from the board
# CALVIN_CHROMIUM_GPU=on     # never add --disable-gpu
# CALVIN_CHROMIUM_GPU=off    # always add --disable-gpu
sudo systemctl restart calvin-kiosk-remote   # or calvin-kiosk on an all-in-one install

The installer and the updater read it on their next run; an exported CALVIN_CHROMIUM_GPU at install time wins over the file. Use off on a board that is not detected and still crashes, and on only to test a newer Chromium/Mesa that may have fixed it. Narrower flags that keep compositing (for example --disable-gpu-rasterization) are being measured on hardware in bead calvin-8by7.

docs.title: Crash-page recovery
docs.text:
The GPU flag removes the common cause, but a renderer can still die (memory pressure, an OOM kill). When only the renderer dies, Chromium's browser process stays up, so the kiosk unit's Restart=always never fires and the screen keeps showing "Aw, Snap!". Nothing inside that page can reload itself.

calvin-display-agent.service (already installed on every kiosk) therefore acts as a watchdog: every 30 s it asks Chromium, over the Chrome DevTools Protocol on 127.0.0.1:9222, whether the dashboard page answers a trivial script. After three consecutive failures it restarts the kiosk unit — the browser start-up path the kiosk already has: a fresh browser, a fresh page, the same backend. This covers the X11 and Wayland stacks (it talks to Chromium, not to X11 or Wayland); on cog, recovery is cog's own --webprocess-failure=restart.

Chromium runs with its own profile, not the account's default one: --user-data-dir=/home/calvin/.config/calvin-kiosk-chromium. That is required — Chromium 136 and later (Raspberry Pi OS Trixie ships 156) ignore the debugging port when it runs on the default profile, which would silently disable recovery. The profile holds only Chromium state and its cache (the unit clears Cache and Code Cache there at start-up); Calvin's own data comes from the server. FULL (all-in-one) installs are covered too: calvin-kiosk.service passes the same flags, and the same agent watches it.

It fails safe. If nothing that is Chromium answers on the port — recovery disabled, an older unit file without the flag, or a Chromium that ignores it — the agent logs crash recovery is idle once and restarts nothing: an unreachable probe never triggers a restart. Once the endpoint answers as Chromium, however, a page that probes dead counts as crashed even if it was never seen alive (the renderer can die during the first load, leaving an empty target list), and a probe or two of endpoint flapping does not discard that evidence. Repeated restarts back off (300 s, 600 s, 900 s …) up to CALVIN_KIOSK_WATCHDOG_BACKOFF_MAX (15 min by default), each restart after the first is logged as a crash loop, and a healthy page resets that.

journalctl -u calvin-display-agent -f            # watchdog lines
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9222/json/list          # what the agent probes

The debugging port is loopback-only (--remote-debugging-address=127.0.0.1) and exists only for this probe. Settings live in /etc/default/calvin-kiosk:

Setting Default Meaning CALVIN_KIOSK_WATCHDOG 1 0/off turns recovery off (the browser is then left alone) CALVIN_KIOSK_CDP_PORT 9222 loopback DevTools port; the unit and the agent must agree CALVIN_KIOSK_WATCHDOG_SECONDS 30 seconds between probes (minimum 5) CALVIN_KIOSK_WATCHDOG_FAILURES 3 consecutive failed probes before a restart CALVIN_KIOSK_WATCHDOG_COOLDOWN 300 seconds before the first, and after a recovered, restart CALVIN_KIOSK_WATCHDOG_BACKOFF_MAX 900 cap for the doubling wait between repeated restarts (15 min)

sudo systemctl restart calvin-display-agent applies a change. Two guards keep the watchdog out of the way: it never touches a unit that is not running (systemd owns that case) or one that started less than two minutes ago.

docs.title: Display stack (cog default everywhere, Wayland opt-in)
docs.text:
A kiosk installs cog (WPE WebKit directly on DRM/KMS) by default on every board — no X server, no compositor, no Chromium. This is the owner decision of 2026-10-31 after cog passed boot/reboot, rotation, screen off/on, real sites and a 60 minute soak on both a Pi 3B+ and a Pi 400 (cog ~67 MB + WPE ~273 MB, CPU ~94 % idle). See ../research/2026-10-29-kiosk-cog.md.

X11 + Chromium stays available as the fallback for a site WPE cannot show (native <select> dropdowns are the known one, see the limitations below); Wayland + labwc is opt-in and still experimental. Both alternate stacks stay installed, so switching is an installer re-run — not a re-flash. Your server URL, kiosk id, hostname, signing key and display settings are kept.

Every board follows the same rule: a fresh install selects cog. An existing kiosk keeps the stack recorded in /etc/default/calvin-kiosk — the default does not silently migrate an X11 kiosk — and you switch it with an explicit --display-stack (see Switch an existing kiosk). FULL (all-in-one) installs (scripts/setup.sh, which also runs the server) follow the same rule: a fresh install selects cog, --display-stack wins, and a re-run keeps the recorded stack (an all-in-one Pi from before the setting existed stays X11). Switch one with sudo bash setup.sh --display-stack <stack>.

docs.title: Choose Wayland on a fresh install (opt-in, experimental)
docs.text:
Wayland is a phase-1 pilot tracked in bead calvin-8by7; see the design notes in ../research/2026-10-29-kiosk-wayland.md. It is not the default on any board.

Add --display-stack wayland to the installer:

curl -fsSL http://tower:8000/api/kiosks/install.sh \
  | sudo bash -s -- --display-stack wayland

For a signed install, add the flag to the SSH form from Option A:

ssh -t $PI "sudo bash install-kiosk.sh --backend-url http://$SERVER:8000 \
  --signing-key-file calvin.key --display-stack wayland --no-reboot \
  && rm calvin.key && sudo reboot"

Wayland installs labwc, wlr-randr, wlopm and wtype in addition to the X11 packages, writes ~/.config/labwc/autostart and rc.xml, and enables calvin-wayland.service instead of calvin-x.service. Chromium runs with the same kiosk flags plus --ozone-platform=wayland.

docs.title: cog (the default on every board)
docs.text:
A fresh install reads /proc/device-tree/model only for the Chromium GPU flags; the stack itself is cog on every board — no flag needed. To be explicit, or to move an existing kiosk, add --display-stack cog:

curl -fsSL http://tower:8000/api/kiosks/install.sh \
  | sudo bash -s -- --display-stack cog

It installs the cog package (WPE WebKit; Debian's libwpewebkit-2.0-1 on Trixie) in addition to the X11 packages, writes /etc/default/calvin-kiosk-display and /etc/default/calvin-kiosk-cog, and enables calvin-cog.service instead of calvin-x.service / calvin-wayland.service. Chromium (calvin-kiosk-remote.service) is disabled on this stack: there is no X or Wayland session for it, and it would fight cog for the panel.

cog runs as the calvin user with video, render and input groups, on tty1 like calvin-x.service but without a PAM/logind session (PAMName=login makes cog trap with SIGTRAP on the Pi 3B+). As the first DRM client it becomes DRM master by opening /dev/dri/card0, and systemd gives the unit its own XDG_RUNTIME_DIR (/run/calvin-cog). It is launched as:

cog --platform=drm \
    --platform-params=renderer=gles,rotation=N \
    --webprocess-failure=restart \
    "http://tower:8000/?kiosk=..."
  • Rotation comes from the Screens display setting. The display agent maps Calvin's xrandr names to cog's counter-clockwise quarter turns: normal → 0, left (90° CCW) → 1, inverted → 2, right → 3. It persists the value in /etc/default/calvin-kiosk-cog and restarts calvin-cog.service when it changes (rotation is a cog startup property). The renderer=gles part is required: cog's default modeset renderer cannot rotate.
  • Screen power (display schedule) works: cog is the only DRM client, so the agent's root helper stops calvin-cog.service, waits up to 5 s for its MainPID to disappear (the kernel restores the console mode when the last DRM client closes, which would otherwise turn DPMS back on), clears tty1, then writes 0 and 4 to /sys/class/graphics/fb0/blank (DPMS off), verifies the connected connectors report dpms=Off and retries the 0/4 pair once before failing, so the agent retries on its next poll. On wake it clears tty1, writes 0 and starts the unit again (the dashboard is back in ~5 s). Starting is idempotent, and a kiosk that boots inside its off window recovers at the next on boundary: the agent retries a panel command that failed (for example while the unit was still transitioning) on its next poll instead of waiting for the next schedule change. The agent polls its config every CALVIN_DISPLAY_REFRESH_SECONDS (default 60, override in /etc/default/calvin-kiosk) and also wakes at each schedule boundary, so a schedule edit made in Settings reaches the panel within about a minute. cog aborts on SIGTERM (SIGSEGV as root, SIGABRT as calvin), so the unit lists both in SuccessExitStatus and a scheduled screen-off does not leave it failed. The helper (/usr/local/bin/calvin-cog-panel.sh) is the only thing calvin may run through a sudoers drop-in.
  • Crash recovery is cog's own --webprocess-failure=restart; the Chromium DevTools watchdog does not run on this stack. A hung page still recovers through Restart=always when cog exits.

docs.title: Switch an existing kiosk
docs.text:
Re-run the installer on the Pi with the other stack. Everything else is preserved. An existing kiosk is not migrated by the new default: it keeps the stack in /etc/default/calvin-kiosk until you pass a flag.

# X11 -> cog (what the default does on a fresh install)
curl -fsSL http://tower:8000/api/kiosks/install.sh -o /tmp/install-kiosk.sh
sudo bash /tmp/install-kiosk.sh --display-stack cog

# cog -> X11/Chromium, or -> Wayland
sudo bash /tmp/install-kiosk.sh --display-stack x11
sudo bash /tmp/install-kiosk.sh --display-stack wayland

# From a server checkout over SSH (signed installs use the stored key)
ssh -t $PI "sudo bash /tmp/install-kiosk.sh --display-stack cog"

The installer disables the other display units, enables the chosen one (and disables Chromium on cog), rewrites /etc/default/calvin-kiosk-display for the new session, and reboots. Re-running it twice is harmless.

docs.title: Roll back to X11
docs.text:
The same command with x11 — every package set is still on the Pi:

sudo bash /tmp/install-kiosk.sh --display-stack x11

This re-enables calvin-x.service and Chromium and disables calvin-cog.service (and the Wayland compositor). Chromium and cog were both left installed, so it is a service switch, not a re-image; sudo apt remove cog only frees space.

docs.title: Choosing without a flag
docs.text:
The stack comes from, in order: the --display-stack flag, an exported CALVIN_DISPLAY_STACK, the value already in /etc/default/calvin-kiosk (auto, x11, wayland, cog), then auto. auto means cog on every board; only an explicit x11 selects Chromium and only an explicit wayland selects labwc.

The installer records the resolved stack in /etc/default/calvin-kiosk, so a re-run with no flag keeps the stack an existing kiosk already has — an existing X11 kiosk does not jump to cog. Kiosks installed before the setting existed have no stored stack; they also stay on X11 and only move with an explicit flag. To switch, pass it (--display-stack x11 to go back to Chromium, cog or wayland to move).

docs.title: Known limitations in phase 1
docs.text:
• OS: validated on Raspberry Pi OS Trixie (Lite, 64-bit) only. Bookworm ships an older labwc and no wlopm, so the installer warns and panel power will not work there.
  • Hardware: cog is the default on every board. It was verified end to end on the owner's Pi 3B+ and Pi 400 (install, rotation via the agent, screen off/on, reboot, real sites, 60 min soak). If anything misbehaves, --display-stack x11 switches back to Chromium in place.
  • Cursor: labwc has no idle-hide. rc.xml binds HideCursor + WarpCursor and the autostart fires it once; the pointer reappears on pointer/touch input.
  • Rotation: on Wayland the agent uses wlr-randr --transform, which counts counter-clockwise (left -> 90, inverted -> 180, right -> 270). Verify it on the panel.
  • Panel power: on Wayland, wlopm --off/--on, with wlr-randr --on as the wake fallback. A monitor that fakes a hotplug can still wake; autoEnableOutputs is off in rc.xml. On cog, the framebuffer-blank path below is used.
  • Fullscreen/mode: output names differ (HDMI-1 -> HDMI-A-1); the agent accepts both and auto-detects the first connected output.
  • Remote update: a bundle update installs the Wayland unit and labwc config but never switches the stack or enables the other compositor. Switching is always an explicit installer run.
  • FULL installs (scripts/setup.sh) take the same --display-stack values and the same default (cog); the backend display services are unchanged.

docs.title: Known limitations of cog
docs.text:
• OS/hardware: validated on Raspberry Pi OS Trixie (Lite, 64-bit) with a Pi 3B+ and a Pi 400 (boot/reboot, rotation, screen off/on, real sites, 60 min soak). Debian's cog/WPE packaging is older than Trixie's on Bookworm, so the installer warns there.
  • Native <select> dropdowns do not open under cog's DRM backend (upstream issues #793/#503). Configure such settings from a phone/desktop; the rest of the dashboard and Settings work.
  • Rotation needs a restart (cog has no runtime rotation API) — the agent restarts the unit, so the screen blanks for a few seconds.
  • Screen power is the framebuffer-blank path; HDMI-CEC (cec-ctl) is not used by the agent. A monitor that ignores DPMS stays lit.
  • Touch capability may not reach the page under cog; set touchControls and onScreenKeyboard to on for the kiosk if the on-screen keyboard does not appear automatically.
  • Security horizon: Debian's wpewebkit on Trixie lags Chromium's patches (see the research doc §1.3). Keep Pi 3-class kiosks on trusted networks; an explicit --display-stack x11 returns that board to Chromium.

docs.title: Updating a kiosk later
docs.text: Use Settings → Screens → Update for that kiosk. The Pi pulls the new agent from the server, verifies it, swaps it in, and rolls back if it doesn't come up healthy. See Kiosk agent self-update. To pick up a new Calvin version, update the server container; the kiosk follows when you press Update.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• The installer can't reach the server: check the URL from the Pi with curl http://<server>:8000/api/health.
  • "manifest signature invalid": the key doesn't match this server. Re-copy kiosk-signing.key. A server that lost its data volume generates a new key, and then every kiosk needs the new one.
  • "server manifest lists no installer files": the server is older than this installer. Update the server container.
  • Install log: /var/log/calvin-setup.log. For a baked card, run journalctl -u calvin-kiosk-firstboot (ssh calvin-admin@<kiosk> with the baked key).
  • Kiosk missing from Settings → Screens: systemctl status calvin-display-agent on the Pi.
  • Wrong server later: edit CALVIN_BACKEND_URL in /etc/default/calvin-kiosk, then sudo systemctl restart calvin-kiosk-remote calvin-display-agent.

docs.title: Zero-touch kiosk provisioning
docs.text:
Prepare a Raspberry Pi card once so a non-technical person can plug in power and reach a running Calvin kiosk — no SSH, no typing on the Pi.

This is for Mode B (remote backend + kiosk Pi). See DEPLOYMENT_TOPOLOGIES.md. For the short version (including the one-command install over SSH), start with KIOSK_INSTALL.md.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Raspberry Pi and an SD card / SSD.
  • Raspberry Pi Imager.
  • The Calvin repo checked out on your workstation (Linux/macOS) at the release your server runs — a vX.Y.Z tag; develop is fine to test the next one. Only the bake script and the installer it embeds come from this checkout. The Pi gets everything else from your Calvin server, never from GitHub.
  • Your backend URL, e.g. http://homeserver.local:8000.
  • Recommended: the server's signing key (see KIOSK_INSTALL.md).

docs.title: Step 1 — Flash a CLEAN image
docs.text:
In Raspberry Pi Imager, choose Raspberry Pi OS Lite (64-bit) and flash.

Important: Do not use Imager's OS-customization (the gear / "Edit settings"). Calvin's bake step writes its own first-boot hook, and Imager's customization writes a competing one. Flash a clean image.

docs.title: Step 2 — Bake the first-boot bundle
docs.text:
Re-insert the flashed card; the boot partition auto-mounts (often /media/$USER/bootfs). From the repo root:

sudo bash scripts/bake-kiosk-firstrun.sh \
  --backend-url http://homeserver.local:8000 \
  --hostname kitchen \
  --wifi-ssid HomeNet --wifi-psk 's3cret' --wifi-country SE \
  --ssh-pubkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub \
  --signing-key-file calvin.key \
  --boot-dir /media/$USER/bootfs

Only --backend-url and --boot-dir are required. Omit --wifi-* if the Pi is on Ethernet. --ssh-pubkey creates a recovery admin user, calvin-admin (rename with --admin-user), with key-only SSH login and passwordless sudo; without it the kiosk has no admin login. calvin, which runs Chromium, gets no SSH key and no sudo. The old --git-repo/--git-branch flags are gone because nothing is fetched from GitHub any more.

Eject the card.

docs.title: Step 3 — Boot
docs.text:
Put the card in the Pi and power on. It self-provisions unattended:

  1. Boot 1 sets hostname, wifi and SSH, creates the admin user (if a key was baked), turns off the interactive first-user wizard (userconfig.service), seeds config and the signing key, installs the kiosk installer (/usr/local/bin/calvin-kiosk-install.sh), deletes firstrun.sh from the boot partition (it held the wifi PSK and key), and reboots.
  2. Boot 2 waits up to 15 minutes for the server's /api/health, then runs the installer. The installer fetches setup-kiosk.sh from the server (verified against the signed manifest when a key is baked), installs X, openbox, Chromium and the Calvin services, and reboots.
  3. Boot 3 — Chromium opens the dashboard.

First provisioning takes several minutes (package installs). Boot 2 prints its progress on the screen (tty1): waiting for the server, installing, or the error and that it will retry. Over SSH: ssh calvin-admin@<kiosk> then journalctl -u calvin-kiosk-firstboot -f.

docs.title: After provisioning
docs.text: The kiosk behaves exactly like one set up by hand with setup-kiosk.sh: stable CALVIN_KIOSK_ID, display-power agent, rotation via /etc/default/calvin-kiosk. See the kiosk identity section to rename it.

docs.title: Kiosk agent self-update
docs.text: The kiosk's Python display-agent and its systemd units can be updated remotely from the Calvin admin UI — no SSH, no re-flash.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Admin triggers the update. In Settings → Screens, click Update next to a kiosk. This sets a per-kiosk agentUpdateRequested flag in the backend registry (POST /api/kiosks/{id}/update).

  2. Agent sees the flag on its next config poll. On every successful GET /api/kiosks/{id}/config (roughly once per minute), the display-agent checks for agentUpdateRequested: true and a new agentAvailableVersion. If the available version differs from its own running version (/var/lib/calvin/agent-version.json) and hasn't already been tried this session, the agent fires the root oneshot updater:

sudo -n systemctl start --no-block calvin-kiosk-update.service

The sudoers fragment installed at /etc/sudoers.d/calvin-kiosk-update (mode 0440) allows exactly this call for the calvin user — nothing else.

  1. Updater fetches the bundle from the local backend. update-kiosk.sh (installed to /usr/local/bin/) pulls the bundle manifest from GET /api/kiosks/agent/manifest and downloads only changed files from GET /api/kiosks/agent/files/{name}. The bundle source is the local Calvin server, not GitHub — no internet access required on the kiosk.

The bundle is 6 files: the display-agent script, three systemd units, the updater itself, and the oneshot service unit. The updater only installs these six, each at its fixed path and mode (0755 scripts, 0644 units), and only restarts or enables their units; anything else in a manifest is refused. A new bundle file therefore needs the updater that knows it: when a manifest brings both, the old updater installs the known files and re-runs the new updater for the rest. Units that should be enabled are re-enabled on every run. This pinning is defence in depth only: the updater is itself a bundle file and runs as root, so without a signing key a hostile server can still ship its own updater. Only the manifest signature protects against that. No full repo checkout lives on the kiosk.

  1. Verify, backup, atomic swap, restart. For each changed file the updater:
  2. verifies the sha256 against the manifest value,
  3. runs py_compile on Python files,
  4. backs up the current file to /var/lib/calvin/agent-backup/,
  5. atomic-replaces via install -m <mode>,

  6. restarts only the systemd units that own the changed files (uses daemon-reload when a unit file changed).

  7. Auto-rollback on unhealthy agent. If the display-agent was among the restarted units, the updater waits up to 30 seconds for it to become both active and to have written the ready-marker (/run/calvin/agent-ready, a tmpfs file created on the first successful backend contact). If the agent doesn't come up healthy in time, all changed files are restored from backup and the affected units are restarted again.

  8. Update flag auto-clears. On the next config poll after a successful update the agent reports its new version via the kagent query parameter. The backend auto-clears agentUpdateRequested once it sees kagent == agentAvailableVersion.

docs.title: Bundle source: local Calvin server only
docs.text: setup-kiosk.sh and update-kiosk.sh both pull the bundle from ${CALVIN_BACKEND_URL}/api/kiosks/agent/*. The kiosk needs no internet access and no copy of the Calvin git repo; everything comes from the server it is already talking to.

docs.title: Updating the updater itself
docs.text: update-kiosk.sh is part of the bundle, so it updates itself like any other file. Before a new copy is adopted it is verified up front — bash -n for syntax and a read-only --self-check run (which fetches and parses the manifest but changes nothing). If either fails, the whole update aborts before anything is swapped and the current, known-good updater stays installed. This is what makes it safe to evolve the updater remotely: a dead-on-arrival updater is never installed. --self-check validates the new code against the current manifest and environment, so it proves the updater starts and can parse today's manifest — a new updater that misbehaves only mid-apply, or that expects a future manifest shape or a new env var, is only partially exercised. That residual gap is bounded by the durable no-retry guard (agent-update-state.json), which prevents a failing version from re-triggering in a loop.

docs.title: New units and removed components
docs.text: The updater is authoritative over kiosk-side bundle state. When a bundle release adds a new always-on service (a unit marked enable in the manifest), the update enables and starts it after the agent health check passes. When a release drops a file or unit, the updater compares the manifest against the device receipt (agent-manifest.json) and, again only after the agent is confirmed healthy, stops + disables the unit and removes the file. Both actions happen only post-health, so an unhealthy update rolls back the changed agent files and reconciles nothing.

docs.title: Interrupted updates self-heal
docs.text: The version file and receipt are written last, only on success. If power is lost mid-update the version is not advanced, so the backend still sees the old version, the update stays pending, and the next poll re-runs the updater; the checksum loop re-syncs any half-written file. Combined with the durable no-retry guard (agent-update-state.json), a kiosk cannot get stuck in a half-updated state.

docs.title: Trust model
docs.text:
Two controls now protect a kiosk update:

  • Manifest signing is implemented (see below). A kiosk with a baked key verifies the signature before trusting the manifest, the file hashes or any downloaded file.
  • The signing key and backups need the admin password. Kiosk signing is host-side, and GET /api/backup/export — which can include the kiosk signing key and stored plugin secrets — answers only an admin session (CLV-9, see Admin authentication). A LAN client without the password can no longer download the key or a backup.

Residuals:

  • Unsigned kiosks still trust the LAN. A kiosk with no key baked keeps integrity-only (sha256) checks, so a LAN attacker who can MITM the backend could serve matching-sha files. Bake the key to close that gap.
  • The server process holds the HMAC key, so code an admin installs (a plugin) can read it. Moving to Ed25519 manifests signed at release time, where the server holds only the public key, is planned (see below).
  • No anti-rollback. The bundle version is a content hash (a change marker, not a monotonic counter), so a server rolled back to an older bundle will be adopted.

docs.title: Manifest signing (closing the LAN-MITM)
docs.text:
The backend signs the bundle manifest with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret generated on first run at <data dir>/kiosk-signing.key (see Data directory; mode 0600; the path is logged the first time it is created). When a kiosk has that secret baked, it verifies the manifest signature before trusting the manifest, the file hashes, or any downloaded file — closing the LAN man-in-the-middle gap that plain sha256 integrity leaves open.

Enable it on a kiosk (out-of-band — never over the LAN):

  1. On the server, read the secret over your existing trusted access. The server creates it at startup and logs the path (Kiosk manifest signing key: …):
  2. Unraid: /mnt/user/appdata/calvin/kiosk-signing.key
  3. Docker: /var/lib/calvin/kiosk-signing.key in the container, which is the data volume (CALVIN_DATA_DIR), so it survives image updates
  4. Source checkout: backend/data/kiosk-signing.key (or $CALVIN_DATA_DIR/kiosk-signing.key)
  5. Pass it to provisioning:
  6. Over SSH: copy the key and install-kiosk.sh from the server, then run sudo bash install-kiosk.sh --backend-url <url> --signing-key-file <path> (exact commands in KIOSK_INSTALL.md). Don't pass the key to the curl … | sudo bash form: that script comes over plain HTTP.
  7. Zero-touch: bake-kiosk-firstrun.sh ... --signing-key-file <path> (or --signing-key <hex>).
  8. Manual: setup-kiosk.sh --backend-url <url> --signing-key <hex>.

The key is written to a dedicated root-only file /etc/default/calvin-kiosk-signing (mode 0600) — never the world-readable /etc/default/calvin-kiosk.

Behavior once a key is baked (fail-closed): the updater aborts and installs nothing if the signature is invalid, missing (an attacker must not be able to strip it to fall back to LAN-trust), or uses an unknown algorithm. A kiosk with no key baked keeps the previous LAN-trust behavior, so signing is opt-in per kiosk — but note the backend always signs, so a keyed kiosk requires a backend running this version or newer.

Key rotation: delete <data dir>/kiosk-signing.key on the server (a new one is generated on the next manifest request) and re-bake / re-run --signing-key on each kiosk. There is no automatic rotation.

Stronger isolation (planned): the shared key means the server process — and therefore any installed plugin — can forge manifests. The plan is Ed25519 manifests signed at release time in CI (private key in a GitHub Actions secret), with kiosks pinning the public key: the server then holds no signing key at all. That supersedes the earlier per-kiosk KDF idea (calvin-580); kiosk-side verification for the current HMAC scheme is unchanged until it lands.

docs.title: Python version floor (min_python)
docs.text:
The bundle manifest carries "min_python": "3.9". The updater checks the kiosk's Python version before downloading anything; if the device Python is below 3.9 the update is aborted with a python-too-old status and the current agent is left in place. The agent reports the updater's status and message on its next config poll, so the backend's agentUpdateStatus is "error" and its agentUpdateMessage is "device python < 3.9; keeping current agent" — the kiosk will need an OS upgrade before the agent can be updated, and the Screens list marks it "update needs a newer OS".

The display-agent itself enforces the same floor at startup and exits immediately if it runs on Python older than 3.9.

docs.title: Initial install
docs.text:
The one-command installer (deploy/kiosk-agent/install-kiosk.sh, served at /api/kiosks/install.sh with the server URL baked in, and baked onto the card by bake-kiosk-firstrun.sh) downloads setup-kiosk.sh + setup-common.sh from /api/kiosks/installer/*. It checks them against the installer hashes in the signed manifest, then runs setup-kiosk.sh. Those hashes are signed but are not part of the bundle version, so editing a setup script never flags kiosks for an agent update.

setup-kiosk.sh calls bootstrap_kiosk (in scripts/setup-common.sh), which fetches update-kiosk.sh from the backend, verifies it against the manifest, and runs it with --bootstrap. --bootstrap installs the whole bundle (agent, units, updater), enables the boot units, and seeds both /var/lib/calvin/agent-version.json and the device receipt /var/lib/calvin/agent-manifest.json. It performs no restart, health check, or rollback — first boot has nothing running and reboots afterward. The updater is now the single install path; there is no separate bundle-install routine.

docs.title: Future option: zipapp
docs.text: If the agent is ever split into multiple Python modules, packaging it as a zipapp .pyz file is a supported path — the bundle endpoint can serve any allowlisted file. PyInstaller and PyCrucible were rejected because they produce architecture-specific artifacts; the current python3 script works on any Debian-family Raspberry Pi OS without recompilation.

docs.title: "Update all" kiosks
docs.text: Bulk-updating all kiosks at once is not yet implemented. Each kiosk must be triggered individually. Bulk update is tracked as calvin-3d1.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Nothing happens on first boot: confirm you flashed a clean image (no Imager customization) and that cmdline.txt on the card contains systemd.run=/boot/firmware/firstrun.sh.
  • Wifi doesn't connect: check --wifi-country was set (regulatory domain) and the PSK is correct.
  • Provisioning failed: the screen shows the last status. SSH in as the admin user (if you baked a key) and read journalctl -u calvin-kiosk-firstboot. If the server was unreachable for the whole 15-minute wait, the unit fails and systemd retries it every minute (Restart=on-failure) until the server answers. Fix, then sudo rm /var/lib/calvin/firstboot.done && sudo systemctl start calvin-kiosk-firstboot.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Calvin installs root-owned helper scripts so the calvin user can restart the compose runtime or reboot the device without receiving broad sudo access.

docs.title: Restart Helper
docs.text:
The backend may run /usr/local/bin/restart-calvin-services.sh with sudo under a narrow sudoers rule:

calvin ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/bin/restart-calvin-services.sh

The helper restarts the compose app, X, and kiosk units:

sudo /usr/local/bin/restart-calvin-services.sh
sudo /usr/local/bin/restart-calvin-services.sh app
sudo /usr/local/bin/restart-calvin-services.sh kiosk
sudo /usr/local/bin/restart-calvin-services.sh x

docs.title: Service Units
docs.text:
The current Raspberry Pi runtime units are:

  • calvin-app.service - runs docker compose -f /etc/calvin/docker-compose.yml up -d
  • calvin-x.service - starts the X session
  • calvin-kiosk.service - starts Chromium at http://localhost:8000

Legacy native units such as calvin-backend.service, calvin-frontend.service, and calvin-frontend-dev.service are removed by setup.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Helpers listed in sudoers must be immutable from the app's perspective:

  • Owner/group: root:root
  • Mode: 0755 or stricter
  • /usr/local/bin should remain root-owned and not writable by calvin

If a helper were owned by calvin, code running as calvin could replace it and gain root the next time sudo executed that path.

Fix existing installs once:

sudo chown root:root /usr/local/bin/restart-calvin-services.sh /usr/local/bin/reboot-calvin.sh
sudo chmod 0755 /usr/local/bin/restart-calvin-services.sh /usr/local/bin/reboot-calvin.sh

docs.title: Reboot
docs.text:
Reboot permission still uses the existing polkit rule:

  • /etc/polkit-1/rules.d/50-calvin-reboot.rules

Setup also installs /usr/local/bin/reboot-calvin.sh with a narrow sudoers rule.

docs.title: Quick Start - Development on Windows (Develop Branch)
docs.text: This guide will help you get started with development on Windows using the develop branch.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3.12+ - Download from https://www.python.org/downloads/
  • Node.js 20+ - Download LTS from https://nodejs.org/
  • Git - Download from https://git-scm.com/download/win
  • UV - Will be installed automatically by the setup script

docs.title: Step 1: Clone the Repository (if not already cloned)
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/osterbergsimon/calvin.git
cd calvin

docs.title: Step 2: Switch to Develop Branch
docs.text:
git checkout develop
git pull origin develop

docs.title: Step 3: Run Setup Script
docs.text:
.\setup-windows.ps1

This will: - Check all prerequisites (Python 3.12+, Node.js 20+, UV) - Warn if you are not on develop (it never switches branches for you) - Install backend dependencies (with dev extras) - Install frontend dependencies

docs.title: Step 4: Start Development Servers
docs.text:
Option A: Use Makefile (Recommended)

.\make.ps1 dev

This runs the Docker Compose dev stack (backend with hot reload and the Vite dev server) and streams its logs. Docker must be running.

Option B: Manual Start

Terminal 1 - Backend: 

cd backend
uv run uvicorn app.main:app --reload --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

Terminal 2 - Frontend: 

cd frontend
npm run dev

docs.title: Verify It Works
docs.text:
1. Backend: http://localhost:8000
  2. Frontend: http://localhost:5173
  3. API Docs: http://localhost:8000/docs
  4. Health Check: http://localhost:8000/api/health

docs.title: Available Commands
docs.text:
Use .\make.ps1 or .\Makefile.ps1 for common tasks:

.\make.ps1 install        # Install all dependencies
.\make.ps1 dev           # Start development servers
.\make.ps1 test          # Run all tests
.\make.ps1 test-backend  # Run backend tests only
.\make.ps1 test-frontend # Run frontend tests only
.\make.ps1 lint          # Run linters
.\make.ps1 format        # Format code
.\make.ps1 type-check    # Run type checkers
.\make.ps1 build         # Build for production
.\make.ps1 clean         # Clean build artifacts

docs.title: Pull Latest Changes
docs.text: git pull origin develop

docs.title: Create a Feature Branch
docs.text: git checkout -b feature/your-feature-name develop

docs.title: Switch Back to Develop
docs.text: git checkout develop

docs.title: Keyboard Support
docs.text:
• Keyboard input is handled by the browser (KeyboardHandler.vue listens for DOM keydown events), so it works the same on Windows, Linux, and the Pi.
  • You don't need WSL: develop on Windows, deploy to Raspberry Pi.
  • There is no backend hardware-keyboard path: the old evdev helper has been removed.

docs.title: Hot Reload
docs.text: Both backend and frontend support hot reload: - Backend: Uses uvicorn --reload (auto-restarts on code changes) - Frontend: Uses Vite dev server (instant updates in browser)

docs.title: "uv: command not found"
docs.text:
• Restart PowerShell after installing UV
  • Or add UV to PATH: C:\Users\<username>\.cargo\bin\

docs.title: "node: command not found"
docs.text:
• Restart PowerShell after installing Node.js
