docs.text: • calvin-5vw — Baked-key manifest signing: close LAN-MITM on the kiosk update channel (the immediate next spec; closes accepted-risk #4).

docs.title: Kiosk Updater Self-Verification — Design
docs.text: Date: 2026-07-15 Status: Approved (brainstorming), pending implementation plan Follows: calvin-lxw (kiosk-agent self-update). Precedes: updater-driven bootstrap (tracked separately).

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
The kiosk updater (deploy/kiosk-agent/update-kiosk.sh) safely updates the agent and systemd units — verify (sha256 + py_compile) → backup → atomic swap of changed files → restart only affected services → auto-rollback if the agent is unhealthy. But the updater is part of its own bundle (update-kiosk.sh and calvin-kiosk-update.service are in BUNDLE_FILES), and it is the one component not protected by that safety net:

  • The health check + rollback only fire when calvin-display-agent.service is among the restarted units. The updater's bundle entries have restart_unit = None, so a change to only the updater triggers no restart, no health check, and no rollback.
  • A syntactically or structurally broken new update-kiosk.sh would be swapped in, this run would finish fine (the agent is untouched), and the breakage would surface only on the next update — with no automatic recovery.

This matters because the updater is the bootstrap for every future kiosk-side change: as long as it can always safely replace itself with a verified-good new updater, any capability it lacks can be delivered later through the updater itself, with no manual Pi intervention. So safe self-replacement is the linchpin of "provision a kiosk once and never touch it again."

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Guarantee the updater never transitions into a broken state: a new update-kiosk.sh is verified before it is trusted, and a bad one aborts the whole update atomically, leaving the known-good updater installed.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Enabling brand-new systemd units on update (a new always-on service starting on boot) — deferred, reachable later via the hardened updater. Tracked separately.
  • Removing files/units dropped from the bundle (decommissioning a component) — deferred, same rationale. Tracked separately.
  • Updater-driven bootstrap (making the updater the single install path, collapsing install_kiosk_bundle) — the immediate next piece, its own spec.
  • Verifying .service unit files with systemd-analyze verify (needs systemd, noisy) — out.

docs.title: 1. --self-check mode (new, in update-kiosk.sh)
docs.text:
update-kiosk.sh --self-check exercises the updater's read/startup plumbing and mutates nothing:

  1. Source the env file; require CALVIN_BACKEND_URL.
  2. curl the manifest from $CALVIN_BACKEND_URL/api/kiosks/agent/manifest.
  3. Parse it with python3 (must yield a version and a files list).
  4. Exit 0 on success, non-zero on any failure.

It must not: swap files, restart services, write the state file, write the version file, create backups, or touch the ready marker. Because it triggers no update, it cannot recurse. It honors the existing overrides (CALVIN_CURL, CALVIN_PYTHON, CALVIN_SYSTEMCTL, CALVIN_AGENT_STATE_DIR, CALVIN_KIOSK_ENV_FILE) so tests mock it and production hits the real backend. Implemented as an early branch at the top of the script (after option parsing, before any mutating work).

docs.title: 2. Verify-phase integration (pre-swap, abort-whole-on-fail)
docs.text:
In the existing pre-swap verify loop (update-kiosk.sh ~L68–82, where the agent is already py_compiled), add per-file checks on the staged copy in $STAGE:

  • any *.sh file → bash -n "$STAGE/<name>" (syntax);
  • the updater specifically (name == "update-kiosk.sh") → additionally bash "$STAGE/update-kiosk.sh" --self-check, run with the current environment.

If either fails: write_state error verify "<reason>" "$version" and exit 1. This runs before any file is swapped, so a bad new updater aborts the entire update atomically — the installed updater stays byte-identical and nothing else changes. This upholds the existing "verify everything before swapping anything" invariant and closes the "no health-check/rollback for an updater-only change" gap: the updater is now verified even though it is never restarted.

The # atomic replace comment on the swap install line is corrected (it describes a new-inode replacement, not an atomic rename).

docs.title: 3. Residual risk (documented, not solved here)
docs.text: bash -n + a fetch/parse dry-run catches dead-on-arrival updaters — syntax errors, broken startup, unbound-variable-under-set -u, config/fetch/parse failures — which is the overwhelmingly common breakage. It does not exercise the swap/restart path of a hypothetical updater that starts cleanly but misbehaves only mid-apply. That residual case is bounded by the existing durable no-retry guard (last_failed_version), which prevents a failing version from looping. Documented in KIOSK_PROVISIONING.md.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Extend scripts/tests/test_update_kiosk.sh (mocked curl/systemctl, temp filesystem):

  • valid new updater — a staged update-kiosk.sh that passes bash -n and --self-check is adopted and installed; the run completes success.
  • broken-syntax new updater — a staged update-kiosk.sh with a syntax error → whole update aborts; the installed updater is byte-identical to before; agent-update-state.json shows error/verify; no other changed file was swapped.
  • self-check-failing new updater — a staged updater that parses (bash -n passes) but whose --self-check exits non-zero (simulated via an unreachable backend / malformed manifest for the self-check subprocess) → same atomic abort + intact installed updater.
  • --self-check mode contract — exits 0 on a good mocked manifest; exits non-zero when the backend is unreachable; and provably mutates nothing (no state file, no version file, no swap, no systemctl restart calls recorded in the mock log).

docs.title: Follow-ups (filed as bd issues)
docs.text:
• Updater-driven bootstrap: update-kiosk.sh --bootstrap (install-only, no restart/health), rewire setup-kiosk.sh to install + run it, delete the duplicate install_kiosk_bundle.
  • Updater: systemctl enable brand-new units declared in the manifest.
  • Updater: remove installed files/units that have been dropped from the bundle.

docs.title: Offline Kiosks — CSP-Enforced Single Attack Surface
docs.text: Status: Design / approved for planning Date: 2026-07-15 Branch: feature/offline-kiosks (based on develop) Related: epic calvin-dd9 (per-device/per-kiosk settings, Mode B), calvin-ks7 (kiosk-safe handoff overlay), calvin-dd9.7 (SSE push channel)

docs.title: Goal
docs.text:
Guarantee that a Calvin kiosk browser only ever connects to its Calvin server ('self') plus an explicitly declared whitelist. This makes the Calvin server the single internet-facing component ("one attack surface toward the internet"), and the guarantee is enforced by the browser via Content-Security-Policy — not by code review or plugin-author discipline.

This is the attack-surface framing, chosen deliberately over the alternative "kiosk survives the server being unreachable" (resilience) framing. Resilience / offline-snapshotting is explicitly out of scope (see Non-goals).

docs.title: Guiding principle: "remote" = "not self"
docs.text:
The browser has no concept of LAN vs. internet. grafana.lab.example.com and api.met.no are both simply "an origin that is not Calvin." Split-horizon DNS, VPNs, and reverse-proxied intranet domains make host-based "internal vs. external" classification unenforceable at the browser layer.

Therefore Calvin does not classify remoteness by network topology. It trusts exactly one origin — the Calvin server ('self') — and treats everything else as external by definition, intranet services included. The only ways a resource reaches the kiosk browser are: (a) served by Calvin (so it is self), or (b) its origin is on an explicit, admin-visible whitelist. CSP's 'self' is the only line that is actually browser-enforceable, which is what makes "one attack surface" a provable property rather than a hopeful one.

docs.title: Current state (audit, on develop)
docs.text:
Almost all external fetching is already backend-side — the server calls the external API and the kiosk hits /api/*. The remaining kiosk→internet leaks are narrow:

# Source Status Notes 1 frontend/src/stores/images.js (~L161–167) returns raw remote CDN URL (image.url/raw_url) to <img src> for picsum/unsplash/nasa-apod/immich Live leak The server proxy GET /api/images/{id} already exists and caches via remote_image_cache. The frontend just bypasses it for remote images. 2 frontend/index.html <link rel="dns-prefetch" href="https://openweathermap.org"> Live (minor) Deprecated OpenWeatherMap legacy. Delete. 3 frontend/src/components/WeatherWidget.vue (L14, L62) OpenWeatherMap icon CDN Dead code Imported nowhere. Deprecated legacy. Delete.

docs.title: Already clean
docs.text:
• All plugin data fetching is backend-side (yr_weather→met.no, sl_departures→SL, mealie→instance, calendars, image scans). The kiosk never calls these.
  • yr_weather renders weather icons as local emoji glyphs (_glyph), no CDN.
  • Fonts are self-hosted in frontend/src/assets/fonts/ (OFL), no Google Fonts.
  • Web-component plugin bundles (chromecast, test-plugin) contain no external refs.

docs.title: Cross-origin browser consumers that exist today (need whitelisting)
docs.text:
• Built-in web-service embeds. Calvin ships a built-in iframe service (WEB_EMBED_PLUGIN_ID = "iframe" in stores/webServices.js), rendered by WebServiceViewer.vue / components/service/IframeViewer.vue. Users add a web service by URL; it renders in an iframe pointing at that (cross-origin) URL. This is a first-class feature and the primary cross-origin consumer.
  • Service-plugin handoff / iframe links. CardGrid/ItemList open a plugin click_url via HandoffOverlay; the IframeRenderer renders a plugin url. These are frame-src consumers governed by the same whitelist.
  • chromecast. Browser-native Cast: loads its SDK from gstatic and discovers devices via mDNS browser↔device. Cannot be proxied. The one genuinely hard plugin.

docs.title: Per-plugin matrix ("which plugin needs what")
docs.text: Plugin(s) Browser-side external need Handled by picsum, unsplash, nasa-apod, immich, image-processor image bytes existing /api/images/{id} proxy — route through it yr_weather, sl_departures, system-monitor, imap, calendars none (local glyphs / text) already self built-in web-service iframe user-configured service origin frame-src auto-derived from service config service-plugin handoff/iframe links link origin (often the plugin's own service) same frame-src whitelist chromecast Cast SDK origin + browser-native discovery declares browser_origins; off in sealed mode

docs.title: 1. Strict CSP served by FastAPI (the enforcement backstop)
docs.text:
FastAPI serves a Content-Security-Policy header (and/or <meta> equivalent) on the SPA response:

default-src 'self';
img-src 'self' data:;
connect-src 'self';
font-src 'self';
frame-src 'self' <derived + whitelisted origins>;
style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline';   # see implementation risk below
script-src 'self';
  • The policy is generated dynamically from current configuration, because frame-src depends on the currently-configured web-service instances and enabled plugins. It cannot be a static string. Regenerate on the response that serves index.html (and refresh when config changes).
  • Effective policy = 'self'
  • Σ(enabled plugins' declared browser_origins)
  • system allowlist (admin manual entries)
  • auto-derived origins from configured web-service instance URLs.

frame-src coverage. Web-service embeds, HandoffOverlay links, and IframeRenderer all read from frame-src: - Handoff/iframe to the plugin's own configured service origin → auto-derived from the service instance config → works with no extra setup. - Handoff/iframe to an off-whitelist origin → blocked by CSP; must degrade to the kiosk-safe handoff error overlay (calvin-ks7), not a broken frame. In sealed mode this is the intended behavior.

docs.title: 2. Whitelist model — two sources, split by who knows the origin
docs.text:
• Plugin manifest — browser_origins: [] (new, optional, default empty). Origins intrinsic to the plugin, known by the author, identical for every user (e.g. chromecast's Cast SDK origins). Ships with the plugin. Validated at load. Default empty = the plugin promises the kiosk only talks to Calvin.
  • System settings — admin allowlist. Site-specific origins only the operator knows (their self-hosted services). Two sub-sources:
  • Auto-derived from configured web-service instance URLs (no double entry — if you added the service, its origin is trusted for framing).
  • Manual admin entries for anything not captured automatically.

Whitelist granularity (browser-enforceable only): - ✅ exact host: https://grafana.lab:3000 - ✅ subdomain wildcard: https://*.lab.example.com - ✅ explicit IP host: http://192.0.2.50:3000 - ❌ CIDR / IP ranges (192.0.2.0/24) — not expressible in CSP; not supported. For a whole subnet, use a wildcard DNS domain. Calvin will not accept CIDR entries, to avoid a gap between what is configured and what is enforced.

docs.title: 3. Sealed mode
docs.text: An opt-in lockdown flag (global, and/or per-kiosk to fit epic calvin-dd9's per-kiosk config model): - Ignores the system allowlist and refuses to enable any plugin with a non-empty browser_origins → the effective CSP collapses to self-only. - Honest trade: a sealed kiosk cannot show external web-service embeds or cast — it is calendars / photos / local-data plugins only. This is a deliberate lockdown, not the default.

docs.title: 4. Plugin contract change
docs.text:
• Add optional manifest field browser_origins (list of CSP host-sources; default []). Documented in PLUGIN_PACKAGE_FORMAT.md.
  • Loader validates entries are well-formed CSP host-sources (no CIDR).
  • Backend-side network access requires no declaration — it is invisible to the kiosk.

docs.title: Enforcement layers (defense in depth)
docs.text:
1. Runtime CSP (browser blocks any undeclared origin) — the hard backstop.
  2. Consistent server-side image proxying — images always served via /api/images/{id}; a plugin cannot leak an image even by accident.
  3. Manifest validation at load — browser_origins must be explicit and well-formed; malformed → rejected.
  4. CI contract test in calvin-plugins (extends test_validate_plugins.py) — a plugin's built bundle + sample payload must reference no origin outside its declaration.

docs.title: Phasing
docs.text:
Phase 1 — Close today's leaks + baseline CSP (ships standalone; the real value). - stores/images.js: always route remote images through /api/images/{id}; never return a raw remote URL to the browser. - Delete dead WeatherWidget.vue; remove the index.html OpenWeatherMap dns-prefetch. - Serve the strict CSP with frame-src auto-derived from configured web-service instances so existing embeds keep working with zero admin action. - Outcome: every non-web-service, non-cast plugin is sealed-clean; the kiosk talks only to Calvin + the operator's own configured service origins.

Phase 2 — Whitelist model + plugin contract. - System-settings admin allowlist (domains, *. wildcards, explicit IP hosts; no CIDR), merged with auto-derived service origins into the CSP. - browser_origins manifest field + loader validation. chromecast declares its Cast origins.

Phase 3 — Sealed mode + guardrail. - Sealed-mode flag (global and/or per-kiosk via calvin-dd9). - CI contract test in calvin-plugins.

docs.title: Non-goals (YAGNI)
docs.text:
• Generic interactive reverse-proxy for cross-origin services (WebSocket tunneling, auth/cookie rewriting, subpath rewriting, the same-origin-iframe privilege-inversion problem). Cross-origin services are handled by whitelisting, which also keeps iframes cross-origin-sandboxed. No shipping plugin needs a reverse-proxy; revisit only if a concrete need appears.
  • CIDR / IP-range enforcement — not expressible in CSP.
  • "Kiosk survives server-down" offline snapshotting — a resilience feature, not an attack-surface feature. Separate future brainstorm if wanted.

docs.title: Implementation risks / open questions
docs.text:
• CSP vs. Vue/Vite inline styles. Vue/Vite typically inject inline <style>; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' is likely required (or nonces). Tune the policy against the real built app so the dashboard is not broken by the policy. Verify script-src 'self' is sufficient for the production build (no inline scripts).
  • Dynamic CSP generation must reflect config changes (web-service add/remove, plugin enable/disable) without a rebuild — regenerate per index.html response.
  • HandoffOverlay degradation on CSP-blocked frames must be graceful (ties into calvin-ks7).
  • Service-plugin payload images (ImageWithCaption / any image_url renderer): no shipping plugin uses these today, but if one does, its image_url must route through a server image proxy or CSP will block it. Treat as a guard, not a Phase-1 fix.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
• CSP header present and correct on the SPA response; frame-src reflects configured web-services and enabled-plugin browser_origins.
  • Remote images resolve to /api/images/{id} and load under img-src 'self'.
  • A web-service embed to a configured origin renders; an off-whitelist frame is blocked and degrades to the handoff error overlay.
  • Sealed mode: system allowlist ignored, browser_origins plugins refused, effective CSP is self-only.
  • calvin-plugins contract test fails a plugin that references an undeclared origin.

docs.title: Kiosk Manifest Signing (HMAC) — Design
docs.text: Date: 2026-07-16 Status: Approved (brainstorming), pending implementation plan Closes: calvin-5vw. Follows: calvin-l83 / the authoritative-updater work (5ti+ixk+0ug, PR #103). Forward-composes with: calvin-580 (KDF-derived per-kiosk keys — no kiosk-side rework).

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
The kiosk update channel has integrity (sha256) but no authenticity: the manifest and its files come from the same plain-HTTP backend over the LAN, and the updater runs as root. A LAN attacker who can MITM the backend can serve a malicious manifest plus matching-sha malicious files and obtain root on every kiosk. The authoritative-updater spec documented this as an accepted risk explicitly to be closed here.

The fix must respect two hard constraints from the existing design:

  • The kiosk is dependency-free. The updater and agent are pure-stdlib python3 — no pip packages on a bare Pi. So verification must use only the standard library.
  • No trust-on-first-use window. The provisioning bake step runs on the operator's workstation, which reaches the server over a trusted path; it is the out-of-band channel used to plant trust before the kiosk ever talks to the backend over the LAN.

docs.title: Decision: HMAC-SHA256 with a shared, baked secret
docs.text:
Python's stdlib provides hmac + hashlib on both sides; it does not provide Ed25519 (that needs a native cryptography/PyNaCl wheel, which would break the dependency-free kiosk). HMAC-SHA256 closes the LAN-MITM threat with zero new dependencies on backend or kiosk.

Key scope: one shared deployment key (this spec). The manifest is a global artifact (build_manifest() is identical for every kiosk), so a single key signs the single manifest and every kiosk verifies with the same baked secret. Residual risk: the secret lives on every kiosk, so a kiosk that is already root-compromised holds a secret usable to forge to another kiosk the attacker can also MITM — narrow lateral movement after an already-total local compromise. KDF-derived per-kiosk keys (calvin-580) remove that residual risk later; because the kiosk-side verification here is deliberately key-source-agnostic (bake a key, verify the manifest HMAC with it), that upgrade needs no kiosk rework.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Asymmetric signatures / public-key distribution — rejected: needs a native crypto lib on the kiosk. (HMAC symmetric is sufficient for the LAN-MITM threat.)
  • Confidentiality / encryption of the update channel — out of scope; this is about authenticity only. The bundle is not secret.
  • Serving the secret over the network — explicitly forbidden (see §3). The secret travels out-of-band only.
  • Per-kiosk keys, key rotation tooling, revocation — deferred (calvin-580 for per-kiosk; rotation is a documented manual re-bake).
  • Transferring a per-kiosk key over the wire after a shared-key handshake — rejected during brainstorming: it reintroduces a TOFU/MITM window and needs encryption for confidentiality; the KDF derivation (calvin-580) achieves per-kiosk isolation without any wire transfer.

docs.title: 1. Backend key management — backend/app/services/kiosk_signing.py (new)
docs.text:
A small, single-responsibility module: load-or-create the key, sign, verify.

  • New setting kiosk_signing_key_path: Path (default ./data/kiosk-signing.key), added to backend/app/config.py Settings.
  • load_or_create_key(path) -> bytes: if the file exists, read the hex and return the decoded bytes. Otherwise generate secrets.token_hex(32) (256-bit), write it with os.open(path, O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_WRONLY, 0o600) then os.write; if a concurrent creator won the race (FileExistsError), read the existing file. Return the decoded key bytes.
  • On first creation the module logs the key path via loguru (logger.info) — the value is never logged. The path is a fixed setting with a documented default (KIOSK_PROVISIONING.md), so operators can find it later without a per-startup log. (No main.py/lifespan change.)
  • canonical(manifest: dict) -> bytes: json.dumps(manifest, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")).encode(). Manifest values are only str/int/bool/list/dict (no floats), so this round-trips identically on both sides.
  • sign(manifest, key) -> str: hmac.new(key, canonical(manifest), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest().
  • verify(manifest_without_sig, signature_hex, key) -> bool: recompute and hmac.compare_digest.

docs.title: 2. Signing the manifest — kiosk_bundle.py + the manifest route
docs.text:
• build_manifest() is unchanged (produces the unsigned dict).
  • New build_signed_manifest(root=None) -> dict: m = build_manifest(root); sig = kiosk_signing.sign(m, key); return {**m, "signature": sig, "sig_alg": "hmac-sha256"}. The signature fields are siblings of the signed content, never part of the canonical bytes.
  • GET /api/kiosks/agent/manifest returns build_signed_manifest(). The backend always signs (key auto-created) — no toggle. Old kiosks ignore the two extra keys (they already ignore unknown fields), so the wire change is backward-compatible.
  • The manifest version hash is unchanged — _version_from still hashes name:sha256 only; signing does not perturb it.

docs.title: 3. Obtaining the secret for baking (out-of-band)
docs.text:
There is no public key to publish — with HMAC the secret is the verifier, so it must never be served over the LAN (that would leak it to the very attacker we defend against, or reintroduce TOFU). The operator reads it from the server out-of-band, over their existing trusted server access:

cat <kiosk_signing_key_path>       # e.g. cat ./data/kiosk-signing.key on the server

and passes the hex to provisioning. Because the key is a secret, it is stored in a dedicated 0600 root-owned file — /etc/default/calvin-kiosk-signing — not the world-readable (0644) /etc/default/calvin-kiosk that also holds non-secret config (backend URL, kiosk id) read by the unprivileged agent. Only root-side code (the updater and the bootstrap shim) needs the key; the calvin-user agent never does. This isolation also sidesteps the truncate-and-rewrite in install_kiosk_config (the key lives in a separate file it doesn't touch).

  • scripts/bake-kiosk-firstrun.sh gains --signing-key <hex> (and --signing-key-file <path> reading a local copy) → the generated first-boot script writes CALVIN_KIOSK_SIGNING_KEY=<hex> into /etc/default/calvin-kiosk-signing, mode 0600.
  • scripts/setup-kiosk.sh gains --signing-key <hex> → writes the same 0600 file for manual installs. If a key is neither passed nor already present, the file is not created.
  • Omitting it everywhere → no signing file → CALVIN_KIOSK_SIGNING_KEY absent → current LAN-trust behavior (opt-in per kiosk).

docs.title: 4. Kiosk verification — fail-closed when a key is present
docs.text:
The updater sources the dedicated signing-key file (SIGNING_ENV_FILE="${CALVIN_KIOSK_SIGNING_ENV_FILE:-/etc/default/calvin-kiosk-signing}", sourced after the main env file) to pick up CALVIN_KIOSK_SIGNING_KEY (hex, or absent). Verification is pure stdlib (hmac + hashlib, compare_digest): parse the fetched manifest JSON, remove the signature and sig_alg keys, recompute canonical() over the remainder, HMAC with the decoded key, and compare_digest against the provided signature. The CALVIN_KIOSK_SIGNING_ENV_FILE override lets tests point the signing file at a temp path.

Applied wherever the manifest is fetched-and-trusted:

  • deploy/kiosk-agent/update-kiosk.sh — verify immediately after fetching the manifest, before the min_python check, file parsing, or any download. Covers the default update path and --bootstrap (both fetch the manifest through this code). --self-check also verifies (catches a misconfigured/rotated key early, read-only).
  • bootstrap_kiosk() in scripts/setup-common.sh — the critical first fetch: it selects and runs the root updater by sha from the manifest. It must verify the manifest signature with the baked key before trusting that sha and running the updater. A small verify snippet is duplicated here (justified: it is the trust bootstrap; the updater it is about to run cannot be trusted to verify itself).

Rules when CALVIN_KIOSK_SIGNING_KEY is set (non-empty):

  • Valid signature → proceed.
  • Invalid signature → abort: write_state error verify "manifest signature invalid" "$version", install nothing. (bootstrap_kiosk error_exits without running the updater.)
  • Missing signature (signature/sig_alg absent) → also abort. This is the downgrade defense: an attacker must not be able to strip the signature to fall back to LAN-trust. Message: manifest signature required but missing.
  • Unknown sig_alg (present but not hmac-sha256) → abort (fail closed). The kiosk implements only HMAC-SHA256; it must not silently accept a signature it cannot check, nor treat an unknown algorithm as "unsigned". Message: unsupported manifest sig_alg.

When CALVIN_KIOSK_SIGNING_KEY is unset/empty: no verification — unchanged behavior (backward compatible with existing kiosks and existing tests).

This closes the MITM: without the secret an attacker can neither forge a valid tag nor strip the signature to downgrade.

docs.title: 5. Rollout / compatibility
docs.text:
• The backend must be on this version before baking keys onto kiosks (it always signs after this change). A keyed kiosk pointed at an older, unsigned backend fails closed — correct for a security control; documented.
  • The signature covers the manifest; individual files are chained via the manifest's per-file sha256 (the updater already verifies each downloaded file against its manifest sha). So signing the manifest authenticates the whole bundle.
  • Key rotation = regenerate kiosk-signing.key on the server and re-bake / re-run --signing-key on the affected kiosks. No rotation tooling (YAGNI). Documented.

docs.title: Backend — backend/tests/unit/test_kiosk_signing.py + test_kiosk_bundle.py
docs.text:
• load_or_create_key: creates a 64-hex-char file at 0600 when absent; returns the same key on a second call (idempotent); does not overwrite an existing key.
  • build_signed_manifest: carries sig_alg == "hmac-sha256" and a signature that kiosk_signing.verify accepts for the canonical manifest; the version hash equals the unsigned manifest's (signing doesn't perturb _version_from).
  • Tamper detection: flipping any file sha256, bumping version, or editing the signature each makes verify return False.
  • canonical is stable/sorted and excludes the signature siblings.

docs.title: Updater — scripts/tests/test_update_kiosk.sh (extend; mocked curl/systemctl)
docs.text:
• key set + valid signature → update proceeds and installs as today.
  • key set + tampered manifest (sha/version changed after signing) → abort with error/verify, nothing installed.
  • key set + tampered/garbage signature → same abort.
  • key set + missing signature (manifest without signature) → abort (downgrade defense), nothing installed.
  • no key set → all pre-existing blocks pass unchanged (backward compatibility).
  • The mock manifest gains a correctly-computed HMAC (a tiny helper signs the mock manifest with the test key using the same canonicalization).

docs.title: Setup — scripts/tests/test_setup_kiosk_bundle.sh (extend) + env-write coverage
docs.text:
• setup-kiosk.sh --signing-key <hex> writes CALVIN_KIOSK_SIGNING_KEY=<hex> into the dedicated signing file (path overridable via CALVIN_KIOSK_SIGNING_ENV_FILE) at mode 0600, and leaves the main /etc/default/calvin-kiosk free of the secret.
  • bootstrap_kiosk <url> <key> with a valid manifest signature → verifies, then runs --bootstrap.
  • bootstrap_kiosk <url> <key> with a bad/missing manifest signature → aborts; the updater is never executed (marker not written).

docs.title: Files touched

docs.title: Sealed Mode — Design
docs.text: Status: Design / approved for planning Date: 2026-07-16 Branch: feature/sealed-mode (off develop, which includes offline-kiosks Phase 1 #99 + Phase 2 #102) Tracks: the sealed-mode half of calvin-bns (Phase 3 of the offline-kiosks CSP design, docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-15-offline-kiosks-csp-design.md). The Phase-3 CI contract test is explicitly deferred (see Non-goals).

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Give the operator an opt-in lockdown switch that collapses the kiosk Content-Security-Policy to self-only — no web-service embeds, no admin allowlist, no plugin browser_origins. A sealed kiosk talks to nothing but its Calvin server. This is a deliberate, honest trade: a sealed kiosk shows only calendars / photos / local-data plugins, and cannot show external web-service embeds or any plugin that declares browser_origins.

docs.title: Guiding principle
docs.text:
Sealed mode is enforced in two layers, in priority order:

  1. Browser-enforced (the backstop): the CSP served to the kiosk collapses to the baseline self-only policy. This is the property that actually holds regardless of plugin-author discipline or UI state.
  2. Honest UX (defense against foot-guns): the operator cannot enable a plugin that declares browser_origins while sealed, so they don't end up with a silently browser-blocked widget.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
In scope: a global sealed_mode config flag; middleware CSP suppression when sealed; a GET/PUT /api/security/sealed-mode API; an enable-time guard that refuses to enable a browser_origins plugin while sealed; a sealed-mode toggle in the existing Security settings category.

Out of scope (Non-goals): - Per-kiosk sealed mode. The SecurityHeadersMiddleware has no per-request kiosk context today (CSP is stamped on every response with no kiosk_id). Per-kiosk lockdown needs ?kiosk=<id> → KioskDB.overrides plumbing that does not exist yet — deferred to epic calvin-dd9. This phase is global-only. - Force-disabling already-enabled plugins when sealed mode is switched on. Their external content is already neutered by the CSP backstop; we do not flip their enabled state. (The Security UI notes they exist — see Frontend.) - The CI contract test ("a plugin's built bundle + sample payload references no origin outside its declared browser_origins"). Deferred: dist.js is minified (URL scanning is false-positive-prone against vendored code and comments), no plugin ships a sample payload, and no shipping plugin declares browser_origins yet — so there is nothing to catch today. The existing AST validator already enforces that declared browser_origins are well-formed host-sources. Filed as a scoped follow-up.

docs.title: Background (current state, post-#102)
docs.text:
• SecurityHeadersMiddleware (backend/app/middleware/security_headers.py) stamps a CSP on every non-exempt response, built by build_csp(frame_origins, allowed_origins) in backend/app/services/csp.py.
  • The middleware currently unions three origin sources inside a never-500 try/except (falling back to [], [], [] on any error): get_web_service_origins() (auto-derived iframe embeds) → frame_origins; get_allowed_origins() (admin allowlist) + get_plugin_browser_origins() (enabled plugins' declared origins) → allowed.
  • build_csp([], []) is exactly the baseline self-only policy (Phase 1 output).
  • ConfigService (backend/app/services/config_service.py) is the global key-value store: get_value(key, default) / set_value(key, value, value_type), with value_type auto-detected ("bool" for booleans).
  • Plugin enable/disable flows through plugins/management.py (the plugin-type update path that sets enabled); a plugin's declared origins are on its class metadata.browser_origins (reachable via the plugin loader/manager).

docs.title: 1. The flag
docs.text:
• Config key sealed_mode, boolean, default False.
  • Read: await config_service.get_value("sealed_mode", False).
  • Write: await config_service.set_value("sealed_mode", value, value_type="bool").
  • Helper get_sealed_mode() -> bool (in csp.py, next to get_allowed_origins): reads the config value and coerces to a plain bool (a stored non-bool → treat truthiness defensively; but persisted values are always bool via the API).

docs.title: 2. CSP suppression (middleware)
docs.text:
async def dispatch(self, request, call_next):
    response = await call_next(request)
    if _is_csp_exempt(request.url.path):
        return response
    try:
        if await get_sealed_mode():
            # Sealed: collapse to baseline self-only — no embeds, allowlist, or
            # plugin origins reach the kiosk browser.
            frame_origins, allowed, plugin_origins = [], [], []
        else:
            frame_origins = await get_web_service_origins()
            allowed = await get_allowed_origins()
            plugin_origins = await get_plugin_browser_origins()
    except Exception:
        # Never 500. Note the fallback is already the sealed/self-only shape, so
        # a config/DB hiccup fails toward locked-down, not open.
        logger.warning("CSP origins lookup failed; falling back to baseline self-only policy")
        frame_origins, allowed, plugin_origins = [], [], []
    response.headers["Content-Security-Policy"] = build_csp(
        frame_origins, [*allowed, *plugin_origins]
    )
    return response
  • When sealed, build_csp([], []) emits the baseline self-only policy — byte-identical to the unsealed empty-config output.
  • The exception fallback is unchanged in shape ([], [], []), so it now doubles as the fail-safe: any error → self-only, the safe direction.

docs.title: 3. Block-enable guard (plugin management)
docs.text:
• In the plugin enable path (backend/app/api/routes/plugins/management.py), before a request sets a plugin enabled = True:
  • If await get_sealed_mode() is True and the target plugin's metadata.browser_origins is non-empty → raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Cannot enable a plugin that declares browser_origins while sealed mode is on. Disable sealed mode first (Settings → Security).") and change nothing.
  • Only the enable→True transition is guarded. Disabling, or updating an already-enabled plugin's config without changing enabled, is unaffected.
  • The plugin's declared origins are read from its class metadata via the loader (plugin_loader.get_plugin_class(type_id).metadata.browser_origins) — the same source get_plugin_browser_origins reads. A plugin with no metadata or empty browser_origins is never blocked.

docs.title: 4. API (backend/app/api/routes/security.py)
docs.text:
Add to the existing security router:

  • GET /api/security/sealed-mode → { "sealed_mode": <bool> }
  • PUT /api/security/sealed-mode — body { "sealed_mode": <bool> }; persists via set_value("sealed_mode", value, value_type="bool"); returns the stored value.
  • SealedModeBody(BaseModel) with a single sealed_mode: bool field. Follows the existing AllowedOriginsBody conventions.

docs.title: 5. Frontend (SecuritySettings.vue + stores/security.js)
docs.text:
• Store: add fetchSealedMode() -> Promise<bool> (GET, returns response.data?.sealed_mode ?? false) and saveSealedMode(value) (PUT { sealed_mode }).
  • Component: a sealed-mode toggle at the top of the Security category (it is the master switch), with data-test="sealed-mode-toggle":
  • Loads via fetchSealedMode on mount alongside the allowlist.
  • Explainer: "Sealed mode locks the kiosk to your Calvin server only — no external embeds, allowed origins, or plugins that reach outside. Calendars, photos, and local-data plugins keep working."
  • When on, the allowlist editor below is visibly marked inactive (dimmed + "Ignored while sealed mode is on") — the allowlist is preserved (not cleared), just not applied. Toggling sealed off restores it.
  • No change to the plugin-enable UI is required beyond surfacing the API error: the 403 from §3 is rendered by the existing plugin-action error handling. (Verify during implementation; if the existing handler swallows the detail, surface it.)

docs.title: Data flow
docs.text: Operator flips the sealed toggle → PUT /api/security/sealed-mode → sealed_mode in ConfigDB → on the next response SecurityHeadersMiddleware reads it and emits the self-only CSP → the kiosk is locked down on its next page load. Independently, while sealed, an attempt to enable a browser_origins plugin is refused at the API.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
• PUT with a non-bool body → FastAPI/Pydantic 422 (typed bool field).
  • Config-read failure in the middleware → caught by the existing never-500 guard → self-only policy (which is also the sealed output) — fail-safe.
  • Enable guard: 403 with an actionable message; nothing persisted.
  • get_sealed_mode treats a missing/corrupt config value as False only via the default; a stored bool is authoritative.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
Backend unit (test_csp.py): - get_sealed_mode() returns the stored bool; missing key → False.

Backend integration (test_security_headers.py): - With sealed_mode config True, the CSP on /api/health is baseline self-only (frame-src 'self' with no origins) even when an enabled iframe web-service, an admin allowlist entry, and a plugin browser_origins are all present. - With sealed_mode False/absent, those origins appear (regression guard — proves sealed mode is what suppressed them).

Backend integration (sealed-mode API + enable guard): - GET defaults to {"sealed_mode": false}; PUT true persists and GET returns it; PUT false restores. - With sealed on, enabling a plugin whose metadata declares browser_origins → 403, nothing changed; enabling a plugin with empty browser_origins → allowed; with sealed off, the browser_origins plugin enables normally.

Frontend (SecuritySettings.spec.js): - Toggle renders current state from GET, saves via PUT on change. - When sealed on, the allowlist editor is marked inactive.

docs.title: CLV-9 — Admin auth for state-changing routes: design
docs.text: Status: approved by the owner 2026-10-29 (all section 10 calls as written). Audit sources: CLV-4 report §2.1 S2, S8.

docs.title: 1. Why
docs.text:
Today anyone who can reach Calvin can change it, and so can any web page a LAN user opens:

  • A multipart POST /api/plugins/install (sent cross-site by browsers with no preflight) extracts the zip, pip-installs its dependencies.packages, then imports plugin.py in the server process, and only then validates it. A rejected upload has already run its code. (Checked on current develop: management.py install → plugin_loader.load_installed_plugins() → _validate_just_installed_plugin; same in both GitHub/local install routes in github.py.)
  • GET /api/backup/export?include_signing_key=true hands the kiosk signing key and every stored plugin secret to any LAN client. With the key, an attacker signs manifests that kiosks apply as root.
  • No Host check, so DNS rebinding lets a public web page read the family's calendar and photos.

CLV-8 (merged) fixed path traversal and secret masking; none of the above.

docs.title: 2. Goals / non-goals
docs.text:
Goals - An admin secret is required for every state-changing route and every route that leaks secrets. - Kiosks keep working with no setup at all: viewing, and the touch interactions people use on the dashboard (next photo, switch screen, calendar view, theme), stay open. - First run stays one step: the first person to open Settings picks a password. - Cross-site requests and DNS rebinding are rejected. - A rejected plugin upload never runs code in the server process. - A plan (not a build) for an asymmetric kiosk signing key whose private half isn't in the server. - KIOSK_PROVISIONING's trust-model section brought up to date.

Non-goals - User accounts, roles, multiple admins, OAuth/SSO. - TLS (still a reverse-proxy job). - Sandboxing installed plugins: an admin-installed plugin still runs in the server, as today.

Anti-goals (would be a failure even if it "works") - A kiosk Pi that needs a password typed on it to show the dashboard. - An upgrade that silently locks people out with no way back in. - Docker/Unraid/reverse-proxy users getting a blank 400 page with no hint how to fix it.

docs.title: 3. The model: three tiers of route
docs.text:
Tier Who Examples Public read anyone on an allowed Host dashboard data: config, events, images, plugin data, kiosk config/manifest/installer Public "viewer" writes anyone, same-origin only images/next, images/previous, calendar/refresh, plugins/{id}/fetch, system/display/power/on|off, POST /api/config restricted to display keys Admin logged-in admin session everything else that writes, plus secret-leaking reads

Enforcement is default-deny for writes: one global FastAPI dependency looks at the matched route template and method. Every POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE needs admin unless the route template is on a short public allowlist. So a new route is protected without anyone remembering to.

Admin-only reads (explicit list, because GETs default to public): - /api/backup/* (export carries secrets and optionally the signing key) - /api/config/git/branches (outbound fetch) - /api/plugins/{id}/scan, /api/plugins/local/suggest (outbound probes / filesystem listing) - /api/system/update/stream (update log)

POST /api/config is one endpoint for both harmless and dangerous keys. Without admin, it accepts a request only if every key is on a display allowlist (the keys the dashboard itself writes: dashboardScreens, regionsLocked, showUI, themeMode, selectedTheme, darkModeStart, darkModeEnd, lastSideViewMode, … — the builder confirms the list by tracing the non-Settings callers of configStore.updateConfig). Anything else (gitRepoUrl, gitBranch, rotation, update settings, …) → 401.

Accepted residual: someone on the LAN can still rearrange the dashboard or flip the theme. That's the "trusted LAN for display state, never for code or secrets" line.

GET /api/kiosks/{id}/config keeps registering kiosks on first poll (it's a GET; unchanged).

docs.title: 4. The admin secret and sessions
docs.text:
• One admin password, any characters, minimum 8. Stored as an scrypt hash (stdlib hashlib.scrypt, random salt) in a file, admin-auth.json (mode 0600), next to the signing key: $CALVIN_DATA_DIR/admin-auth.json in Docker, ./data/admin-auth.json from source; override with ADMIN_AUTH_PATH. A file, not the DB, so it is never in a backup or a GET /api/config, and so recovery is "delete one file".
  • Session = cookie calvin_admin, HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, Path=/, Max-Age 400 days (browser cap). Value is stateless: issued_at.generation.HMAC(server_secret, …). server_secret and generation live in the same file. A cookie (not a bearer header) because EventSource, file downloads (/api/backup/export) and plain fetch calls can't add headers.
  • Changing the password bumps generation → every other session is signed out. "Sign out" just clears the cookie.
  • Login rate limit: per client IP, 5 failures per minute, then 429 with a doubling cooldown (in memory; resets on restart).
  • Endpoints (all public, all same-origin-checked):
  • GET /api/auth/status → {configured: bool, authenticated: bool}
  • POST /api/auth/setup {password} → only while not configured; sets the password, logs you in
  • POST /api/auth/login {password} / POST /api/auth/logout
  • POST /api/auth/password {current, new} (admin) → change + sign out others

docs.title: First run and upgrade
docs.text:
• Not configured (fresh install or upgrade from today): admin routes answer 401 {"code": "setup_required"}. Opening Settings shows a single card: "Choose an admin password — anyone on your network who knows it can change Calvin." Two fields, one button, and you're in. Kiosks never see it (they don't open Settings).
  • Whoever reaches Settings first claims it. Cross-site pages and rebinding can't (§5), but another LAN device could, in that window. For people who care: CALVIN_ADMIN_PASSWORD (env var, Docker / Unraid template field) pre-sets it on first start, so there's no open window at all.
  • Forgot it: delete admin-auth.json (or set CALVIN_ADMIN_PASSWORD, which always wins on startup) and restart; Settings asks for a new one. Documented in the Settings card and the docs.

docs.title: Frontend
docs.text:
• An auth Pinia store (status, login, logout, setup).
  • /settings renders a lock screen (setup or login) until authenticated; everything else in Settings is unchanged.
  • A global axios response interceptor (the default instance and services/api.js): on 401 admin_required it opens the login dialog in place; after login the user retries the action. Covers the dashboard ⋯ menu (reboot, update, hide-controls if it ever needs admin).
  • On a touch kiosk the lock screen also shows the existing "set up from your phone" URL + QR (CLV-11's serverUrl.js), since typing on a kiosk is hard anyway (audit F2).
  • Settings gets a "Sign out" and a "Change password" control (Security tab).

docs.title: 5. Host and Origin checks
docs.text:
Host (DNS rebinding) — a middleware on every request (not only /api, since rebinding can read the page too). Allowed without config: - IP literals (v4/v6), localhost, *.localhost - single-label names (calvin, raspberrypi) - .local, .lan, .home, .home.arpa, .internal, .localdomain - the host of PUBLIC_URL - anything in CALVIN_ALLOWED_HOSTS (comma list; * turns the check off)

Anything else → 400 with a plain-text body naming the env var to set. This blocks rebinding, which always arrives with the attacker's public domain as Host, while every normal LAN way of reaching Calvin (IP, mDNS, router names) keeps working. Reverse-proxy users with a real domain set PUBLIC_URL (they already should) or CALVIN_ALLOWED_HOSTS.

Origin (cross-site writes) — for every unsafe method under /api: - Origin present → its host:port must equal the request's Host (scheme ignored, so a TLS proxy in front still matches), or be in the existing CORS_ORIGINS setting (keeps the Vite dev server on :5173 working). Otherwise 403. - Origin absent → reject only if Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site. Non-browser clients (curl, the kiosk agent) send neither, and they still need the cookie for admin routes. - CORS_ALLOW_ALL (dev only) skips the Origin check.

SameSite=Strict on the cookie already stops cross-site requests from carrying the session; the Origin check additionally protects the public writes and the setup endpoint.

docs.title: 6. Plugin import in a subprocess
docs.text:
New install order for zip upload, GitHub install and local install:

  1. Extract to plugins/{id}/ (unchanged, already traversal-safe).
  2. pip install declared packages (already a subprocess; unchanged).
  3. New: run python -I -m app.plugins.check_plugin <plugin_dir> (the server's own interpreter, cwd = backend dir, minimal env, 60 s timeout). The child imports plugin.py, runs the same register_module discovery + metadata validation, and prints {"errors": [...], "type_ids": [...]}.
  4. Errors, non-zero exit, timeout or garbage output → roll back (remove dir, undo pip) → 400 with the errors. The server process never imports it.
  5. Only a clean result → plugin_loader.load_installed_plugins() in-process, as today.

POST /api/plugins/inspect stays manifest-only (it never imported code).

Honest limits, written into the docs: the child runs as the same user, so it is a "don't load rejected code into the server" guard, not a sandbox. The real gate is §3: only the admin can upload.

docs.title: 7. Asymmetric kiosk signing — plan only (extends calvin-580)
docs.text:
Today: HMAC with a shared secret in kiosk-signing.key, readable by the server process (and by any code an admin installs). Plan:

  • Ed25519. Kiosks pin the public key (/etc/default/calvin-kiosk-signing holds it instead of the secret). The alg field in the manifest already exists; add ed25519, keep hmac-sha256 accepted during a transition.
  • Where the private key lives: the kiosk bundle is shipped with the server (image / checkout), so its manifest is static per release. Sign it at release time in CI (private key in a GitHub Actions secret) and ship kiosk-manifest.sig inside the image. The server only serves the signature; it holds no signing key at all, so a compromised server or plugin can't forge an update. For source/Pi installs that build their own bundle: an offline calvin-sign-bundle CLI run by the owner, with the key off the box.
  • This makes calvin-580's per-kiosk HMAC KDF unnecessary (a stolen public key forges nothing); close 580 in favour of a new "Ed25519 release-signed kiosk manifests" bead.
  • Checked: kiosk_bundle.build_manifest() is content-only (version + per-file sha256, no server URL), so it is identical for every server running the same release and can be signed at release time.
  • Kiosk side: update-kiosk.sh verifies with python3 -c + cryptography or openssl pkeyutl (Bookworm's openssl 3 supports Ed25519 raw verify); pick at build time.

docs.title: 8. Docs
docs.text:
• KIOSK_PROVISIONING "Trust model": rewrite — signing is implemented (not "future work calvin-5vw"); state what admin auth now protects (the key is no longer downloadable without the admin password); remaining residuals (unsigned kiosks trust the LAN; the server process holds the HMAC key until §7 lands).
  • New docs/configuration/ADMIN_AUTH.md: first run, CALVIN_ADMIN_PASSWORD, forgotten password, CALVIN_ALLOWED_HOSTS, what's public vs admin.
  • Docker/Unraid template: add CALVIN_ADMIN_PASSWORD and CALVIN_ALLOWED_HOSTS (optional fields).

docs.title: 9. Tests (definition of done)
docs.text:
Backend (pytest, TestClient): - Every non-allowlisted unsafe route → 401 without a session (parametrised over app.routes, so a future route without protection fails the test). Same for the admin-only GETs. - Allowlisted viewer writes work without a session; POST /api/config with a display key works, with gitBranch → 401. - Cross-origin Origin → 403 on a viewer write and on login; same-origin → OK; Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site without Origin → 403. - Foreign Host (evil.example) → 400; IP / calvin.local / single-label / CALVIN_ALLOWED_HOSTS → OK. - First run: status configured=false → setup → logged in → admin route OK; second setup → 409; CALVIN_ADMIN_PASSWORD pre-sets; password change invalidates old cookie; rate limit → 429. - Kiosk path: GET /api/kiosks/{id}/config, manifest, install.sh, agent files all work with no session. - A plugin zip whose plugin.py writes a marker file at import and fails validation → 400, and the server process's sys.modules never contains it (and a "good" zip still installs). - Existing tests: a conftest fixture logs the test client in by default, so the 1000+ existing tests keep their meaning; auth tests opt out.

Frontend (vitest): auth store; lock screen renders setup vs login; 401 interceptor opens login.

docs.title: 10. Calls I made (please check)
docs.text:
1. Password, not a generated token — easier to type on a phone, and survives "I lost the token".
  2. Unconfigured = admin routes closed (not open-with-a-nag). Upgrading users hit the setup card once.
  3. First visitor to Settings claims it; CALVIN_ADMIN_PASSWORD for those who want zero window.
  4. Dashboard interactions stay public (§3), so no kiosk pairing is needed in this task.
  5. Host allowlist by name shape (+ PUBLIC_URL, + env) rather than a strict configured list.
  6. Kiosk-screen login: no on-screen keyboard here; the lock screen points to the phone URL/QR.
  7. Asymmetric signing: plan only, release-time CI signing; recommend replacing calvin-580.

docs.title: 11. Reviewer questions, settled
docs.text:
A fresh reviewer read this as a builder. Their points, and how they're settled:

  • Non-browser writers? None that matter. The kiosk agent (calvin_display_agent.py) and the installer and updater scripts only GET. PUT /kiosks/{id}/overrides and POST /kiosks/{id}/update are called only from the Settings › Kiosks tab, so they become admin. The dev script scripts/seed_test_calendar.py writes calendar sources and will need a login (my call: it reads CALVIN_ADMIN_PASSWORD and logs in first).
  • Plugin-defined routes? Plugins can't add routes: the host's route set is fixed, and plugin data comes from GET /plugins/{id}/data. So the allowlist is keyed on the host route template. Answered.
  • Mixed POST /api/config. Settings always runs logged in, so its whole-config saves are fine. The dashboard callers only send display keys. A mixed request without admin is rejected as a whole. My call.
  • Kiosk ⋯ menu (reboot/update). These need admin. On a 401 they open the same login dialog, and that dialog shows the phone URL and a QR code. My call.
  • Proxies. Host and Origin are compared against the Host header as received. Reverse proxies normally preserve it; if one doesn't, set CALVIN_ALLOWED_HOSTS or PUBLIC_URL. X-Forwarded-* is not trusted. The rate limit is keyed on the peer IP. Behind a proxy everyone shares one bucket, and the cooldown stays short (doubling from 60 s, capped at 15 min). My call.
  • Subprocess context. The child imports app.plugins.* and app.config settings, but no DB init. Built-in plugins import the same way at load. A failed check rolls back pip through the existing _uninstall_pip_requirements. My call.
  • Unraid template. It lives in this repo (deploy/unraid/calvin.xml). The two optional env fields go there.
  • Forgot password. Deleting admin-auth.json also rotates server_secret, so every old cookie dies. Answered.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: Calvin keeps its whole setup in one SQLite DB plus a few files in the data dir. Every fresh install (new dev env, rebuilt container, new Pi/Unraid deploy) means re-entering calendars, photo sources, web services, layout, screens, keyboard map, kiosks and plugin credentials by hand. A backup must bring a fresh install back to a configured, working state in one step: from the Settings UI, from the API, or headlessly on first start.

docs.title: Goals / non-goals
docs.text:
• Goal: one portable file that captures the configuration and restores it on any deploy mode (dev, Docker/Unraid, all-in-one Pi), with a preview before anything is written.
  • Goal: headless seeding: a dev setup or fresh deploy configures itself on first start from a file.
  • Non-goal: backing up photos, image caches, weather/calendar caches, logs, or the Python venv. Photos are user content managed elsewhere; caches rebuild themselves.
  • Anti-goal: a restore that half-applies and leaves Calvin broken with no way back, or that silently drops plugin instances the layout points at.

docs.title: What is in a backup
docs.text:
Part Source Included App settings, layout, screens, regions, display schedule, theme choice, clock bar, security allowlist / sealed mode, git branch, plugin type configs (plugin_<id>_config) config table (every row, raw value + value_type) always Keyboard map keyboard_mappings always Plugin types (enabled flag, display_order, theme rows) plugin_types always Plugin instances = calendar sources, image sources, web services, backend plugins (id, type, name, enabled, config, display order) plugins always Kiosks and per-kiosk overrides (id, hostname, overrides) kiosks always; last_seen, agent version/status and last_applied_version are runtime state and left out Installed plugin packages PLUGIN_DIR/<id>/ (no __pycache__) default on (include_packages) Installed theme packages theme dir /<id>/ default on, same switch Secrets inside plugin configs see below default on (include_secrets) Kiosk manifest signing key KIOSK_SIGNING_KEY_PATH default off (include_signing_key) Photos, caches, logs, venv — never

Instance ids are kept exactly: screens/regions reference instances by id (serviceId), so a restore that re-derived ids would orphan the layout.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
A secret is a config key the host already treats as sensitive (SENSITIVE_FIELDS in api/routes/plugins/config.py: password, api_key, token, secret, …) or a field the plugin's instance_config_schema declares with type: "password". Applies to instance configs and to plugin_<id>_config rows.

  • Included by default. The whole point is a one-step restore, and the DB they come from already holds them in plain text. The UI shows a warning next to the toggle and on the download: the file contains passwords and API keys in plain text; store it like a password. Backup files written to disk by Calvin are created 0600.
  • Excluded on request. Secret values are replaced by "" and the backup records which instance/field was stripped. On restore, an instance whose secret is missing cannot pass its plugin's validation, so it is restored disabled with its other settings intact, and the result lists it as "needs credentials". In merge mode a stripped secret never overwrites an existing value on the target.
  • Passphrase encryption of the file is a follow-up (needs a crypto dependency and a passphrase flow), not in this change.

docs.title: Kiosk signing key
docs.text: Kiosks verify agent bundle manifests against the server's HMAC key. A fresh install generates a new key, so existing kiosks would reject updates until re-provisioned. Including the key is opt-in with a warning (anyone with the file can sign kiosk updates). When a backup carries it, restore writes it (0600) only if the caller also asks for it (restore_signing_key), so a dev box restoring a prod backup does not silently take over prod's key.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
A zip file, calvin-backup-<host>-<UTC timestamp>.zip:

backup.json                 # the manifest + all DB data (below)
packages/plugins/<id>/...   # installed plugin package files
packages/themes/<id>/...    # installed theme package files
signing-key                 # only if include_signing_key

backup.json:

{
  "format": "calvin-backup",
  "format_version": 1,
  "created_at": "2026-10-29T10:00:00Z",
  "calvin_version": "0.1.0",
  "schema_revision": "4ca1bddc0e65",
  "source": {"hostname": "pi-kitchen", "deploy": "docker|pi|dev"},
  "options": {"include_packages": true, "include_secrets": true, "include_signing_key": false},
  "stripped_secrets": [{"scope": "instance", "id": "mealie-1a2b", "field": "api_token"}],
  "packages": {"plugins": [{"id": "mealie", "version": "1.2.0"}], "themes": []},
  "data": {
    "config": [{"key": "...", "value": "...", "value_type": "json"}],
    "keyboard_mappings": [{"key_code": "KEY_1", "action": "generic_prev"}],
    "plugin_types": [{"type_id": "ical", "plugin_type": "calendar", "enabled": true, "common_config_schema": {}}],
    "plugin_instances": [{"id": "ical-1a2b", "type_id": "ical", "plugin_type": "calendar", "name": "Family", "enabled": true, "config": {}, "display_order": 0}],
    "kiosks": [{"id": "hallway-3f9a2c", "hostname": "pi-hallway", "overrides": {}}]
  }
}

Restore also accepts a bare backup.json (no packages), so a hand-written or scripted seed file works.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
• format_version is the backup file's own schema, independent of the DB migration chain. Restore looks it up in a migration table (MIGRATIONS[n] upgrades a vn document to vn+1) and applies steps up to the current version. v1 is the first version, so the table starts empty; the machinery is in place and tested.
  • A format_version newer than this Calvin supports is rejected before anything is written ("made by a newer Calvin, upgrade first"). Missing format/format_version, or a wrong format, is rejected as "not a Calvin backup".
  • calvin_version and schema_revision are informational (shown in the preview). DB rows are re-created through the current models, so DB schema drift is absorbed: unknown columns in the backup are ignored, missing ones take model defaults.
  • Paths are never stored absolute: packages are relative inside the zip and land in the target's own PLUGIN_DIR / theme dir. Instance configs are restored verbatim (e.g. a local-images image_dir); this is the only deploy-specific content and is called out in the docs.

docs.title: Restore semantics
docs.text:
Two modes:

  • replace (default): the target ends up matching the backup. Config rows, keyboard mappings and plugin instances not in the backup are removed (kiosks are always merged, see below). Installed plugin packages not in the backup are not uninstalled (harmless, and uninstalling runs pip); their instances are removed.
  • merge: the backup wins for everything it contains; everything else on the target is kept.

Steps, in order:

  1. Validate (nothing written): zip safety (no absolute paths / .., size cap), backup.json parses, format/version check + migrations, structure validated with pydantic models, every package has a manifest.
  2. Plan / preview (dry_run): counts per section; packages to install vs already installed (with version differences); instances to create, update, remove; instances whose type is neither installed nor in the backup (will be skipped); stripped secrets; kiosks; whether a signing key is present; config keys added/changed/removed. This is what the dry run and the UI preview return.
  3. Safety backup: before applying, the current setup is exported to <backup dir>/pre-restore-<timestamp>.zip, so a bad restore can be undone by restoring that file.
  4. Apply:
  5. Install missing plugin/theme packages from the backup through plugin_installer.install_plugin / theme_installer.install_theme (pip deps, rollback on failure), then plugin_loader.load_installed_plugins() and load_plugin_types_for_single() / _register_theme_in_db(), the same steps as the install endpoint. An installed plugin is never downgraded or overwritten; a version difference is a warning.
  6. Config rows (replace: delete rows not in the backup), keyboard map, plugin type rows (enabled + display_order), kiosks. All DB writes go through retry_on_db_locked.
  7. Instances (plugin type rows are written after them, because updating a running instance through the instance manager also sets its type's enabled flag): in replace mode, existing instances not in the backup are stopped, unregistered and deleted (as the delete endpoint does). Each backup instance goes through the instance manager: apply_plugin_config_update(type_id, {**config, "_instance_id": id, "_instance_name": name, "_instance_enabled": enabled}, None, db_type), which creates or updates and starts it. Its display_order is then set on the row. If the type is not loadable, the instance is kept as a disabled row and reported. Secrets stripped from the backup are filled from the target's current values; an instance still missing one is restored disabled and listed as needing credentials. If the plugin's validation rejects the config (usually a stripped secret), the row is written disabled with the same id, so the layout keeps pointing at it and the user only fills in the missing field.
  8. Signing key, if present and restore_signing_key.
  9. Result: the plan plus what actually happened per item, with warnings. The UI then reloads so stores pick up the new config.

Restore is not one DB transaction (it spans file installs, pip and live plugin objects); the safety backup is the undo.

docs.title: API (/api/backup/*)
docs.text:
• GET /backup/export?include_packages=&include_secrets=&include_signing_key= → zip download.
  • POST /backup/preview (multipart file, mode) → plan.
  • POST /backup/restore (multipart file, mode, restore_signing_key) → result.
  • GET /backup/files → stored backups in the backup dir (name, size, time, kind).
  • POST /backup/files → write a backup to the backup dir now.
  • GET /backup/files/{name} → download one; POST /backup/files/{name}/restore → restore one (with mode, dry_run).
  • GET/PUT /backup/schedule → {enabled, interval_hours, retention}.

docs.title: Settings UI
docs.text:
Maintenance → new Backup & restore section:

  • Download backup: toggles for "Include plugin packages" (on), "Include passwords and API keys" (on, warning text), "Include kiosk signing key" (off, warning text), and a Download button.
  • Restore: file picker → preview (summary counts, packages to install, instances skipped / needing credentials, version info, warnings) → mode (Replace / Merge) and, if the file has a key, "Also restore kiosk signing key" → confirm → result → reload UI.
  • Automatic backups: enable toggle, interval, keep N; list of stored backups with download.

docs.title: Headless
docs.text:
• CLI: uv run python -m app.services.backup export [--out FILE] [--no-packages] [--no-secrets] [--include-signing-key] and uv run python -m app.services.backup restore FILE [--mode replace|merge] [--dry-run] [--restore-signing-key]. The CLI opens the DB and loads plugins the way the server does. Export is safe while the server runs; restore should run with the server stopped (otherwise use the API).
  • Restore on first start: at startup, after plugins load and before defaults are seeded, Calvin restores from CALVIN_RESTORE_FROM (a file path), or else from <backup dir>/restore-on-start.zip|.json if present. Mode from CALVIN_RESTORE_MODE (default replace). It runs once per file content: the file's SHA-256 is recorded in config key backup_seed_applied_sha256 and a file with the same hash is skipped, so the env var can stay set across restarts and the file can live on a read-only mount. A failed seed is logged and startup continues.
  • Backup dir: BACKUP_DIR env, else $CALVIN_DATA_DIR/backups, else <db dir>/../backups (backend/data/backups in dev, /var/lib/calvin/backups in Docker).

docs.title: Scheduled backups
docs.text: Off by default. When on, a periodic job (APScheduler, like the existing schedulers) writes auto-<timestamp>.zip to the backup dir every interval_hours (default 24) with packages and secrets, no signing key, and deletes the oldest auto-* files beyond retention (default 7). Pre-restore and manual files are never pruned.

docs.title: Decisions made during review (builder's calls, flagged for the reader)
docs.text:
• Validation failure detection. apply_plugin_config_update returns a result without instance_id when the plugin's validate_config rejects the config; that is the signal to write the disabled row directly (PluginDB, via retry_on_db_locked). Restore never calls test_connection. Creating an instance runs the plugin's normal initialize(); a failure there is reported per instance and does not stop the restore.
  • Kiosks are always merged, even in replace mode. Kiosks re-register themselves on their next poll, and deleting a live device's row would drop its overrides for no gain.
  • Install-local config keys. Keys starting with backup_ (seed marker, automatic-backup schedule) belong to the install, not the setup: they are not exported and survive a replace. Everything else in config, including the security allowlist, sealed mode and git branch, is the user's setup and is restored.
  • Dangling layout references. An instance that cannot be restored (type neither installed nor in the backup) is a warning in preview and result, not a failure; the layout is left as it is so installing the plugin later brings the region back.
  • Trust. Calvin has no auth layer; /api/plugins/install already accepts arbitrary plugin zips that run code in-process, so restore does not widen that. The doc says so.
  • One restore at a time. An in-process lock guards restore and the automatic backup job; a second restore gets 409.
  • Seed and defaults. Seed restore runs right after _initialize_plugins (which may create the default local-images instance) and before keyboard and config defaults, so defaults only fill what the backup does not set.
  • Secret matching uses the same name rule as mask_sensitive_config (substring match, recursing into nested dicts) plus schema password fields, on instance configs and plugin_<id>_config rows.
  • KIOSK_SIGNING_KEY_PATH is the existing kiosk_signing_key_path setting; CALVIN_DATA_DIR is set by the Docker image; BACKUP_DIR is new.

docs.title: Calls left to the builder
docs.text: Module layout (app/services/backup/), pydantic model details, the exact size cap, UI copy and layout within the existing settings shell components.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
• conftest.py - Pytest configuration and shared fixtures
  • unit/ - Unit tests for individual components
  • integration/ - Integration tests for API endpoints

cd backend
uv run pytest

docs.title: Test Markers
docs.text:
Tests are marked with markers for easy filtering:

  • @pytest.mark.unit - Unit tests
  • @pytest.mark.integration - Integration tests
  • @pytest.mark.e2e - End-to-end tests
  • @pytest.mark.slow - Slow running tests

Run tests by marker: 

uv run pytest -m unit
uv run pytest -m integration

docs.title: Fixtures
docs.text:
Common fixtures available in conftest.py:

  • test_db - Async database session for testing
  • test_client - FastAPI test client
  • temp_db_path - Temporary database file path
  • temp_image_dir - Temporary directory for test images
  • mock_env_vars - Mocked environment variables

docs.title: Test Repository Setup for E2E Tests
docs.text: This document explains how to set up a test GitHub repository for end-to-end testing of the plugin installation system.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The E2E tests (test_github_plugin_e2e.py) use a real GitHub repository to validate the full plugin installation flow. This provides confidence that the system works with real-world GitHub repositories.

docs.title: Option 1: Use an Existing Test Repository
docs.text:
If a test repository already exists, set the environment variable:

export TEST_GITHUB_REPO="https://github.com/your-org/test-plugins"
export TEST_GITHUB_BRANCH="main"  # Optional, defaults to "main"

docs.title: Option 2: Create Your Own Test Repository
docs.text:
1. Create a new GitHub repository (public or private with appropriate access)

  2. Repository structure: 

    test-plugins/
├── plugins.json          # Optional: manifest file
├── plugin1/
│   ├── plugin.json
│   └── plugin.py
├── plugin2/
│   ├── plugin.json
│   ├── plugin.py
│   └── frontend/
│       └── dist.js
└── README.md

  3. Example plugin.json: 

    {
  "api_version": 1,
  "id": "test_e2e_plugin",
  "name": "Test E2E Plugin",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "type": "service",
  "description": "A test plugin for E2E testing",
  "author": "Test Author",
  "license": "MIT"
}

  4. Example plugin.py: 

    """Test plugin for E2E testing."""
from app.plugins.definitions import PluginMetadata
from app.plugins.protocols import ServicePlugin


class TestE2EPlugin(ServicePlugin):
    metadata = PluginMetadata(
        type_id="test_e2e_plugin",
        name="Test E2E Plugin",
        description="A test plugin for E2E testing",
    )

    async def fetch(self, start_date=None, end_date=None):
        return {"status": "ok"}

  5. Optional: plugins.json manifest: 

    {
  "plugins": [
    {
      "id": "test_e2e_plugin",
      "name": "Test E2E Plugin",
      "path": "plugin1",
      "version": "1.0.0",
      "type": "service",
      "description": "A test plugin for E2E testing"
    }
  ]
}

  6. Push to GitHub: 

    git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial commit: Test plugins for E2E testing"
git remote add origin https://github.com/your-org/test-plugins.git
git push -u origin main

docs.title: Run all E2E tests:
docs.text:
cd backend
uv run pytest tests/e2e/test_github_plugin_e2e.py -m e2e -v

docs.title: Run with custom repository:
docs.text:
TEST_GITHUB_REPO="https://github.com/your-org/test-plugins" \
uv run pytest tests/e2e/test_github_plugin_e2e.py -m e2e -v

docs.title: Skip E2E tests (default in CI):
docs.text:
# E2E tests are marked with @pytest.mark.e2e and @pytest.mark.slow
# They won't run unless explicitly requested
uv run pytest  # Skips E2E tests

docs.title: Test Behavior
docs.text:
• Network check: Tests skip if network is unavailable
  • Repository check: Tests skip if repository doesn't exist or is inaccessible
  • Graceful degradation: Tests provide helpful skip messages
  • Cleanup: Tests clean up installed plugins after running

docs.title: CI/CD Integration
docs.text:
E2E tests are marked with @pytest.mark.e2e and @pytest.mark.slow, so they:

  • Skip by default in CI/CD pipelines (fast, reliable builds)
  • Can be run manually for validation
  • Can be run in scheduled jobs (e.g., nightly builds)

docs.title: Example CI configuration:
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/test.yml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Run unit and integration tests
        run: uv run pytest -m "not e2e"  # Skip E2E tests

  test-e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    if: github.event_name == 'schedule'  # Run on schedule only
    steps:
      - name: Run E2E tests
        run: |
          export TEST_GITHUB_REPO="https://github.com/calvin-dashboard/test-plugins"
          uv run pytest tests/e2e/ -m e2e -v

docs.title: Benefits of E2E Tests
docs.text:
1. Real-world validation: Tests actual GitHub API integration
  2. Catch integration issues: Network problems, rate limits, API changes
  3. Validate branch fallback: Real main/master branch behavior
  4. Test actual plugin structure: Real plugin.json and plugin.py files

docs.title: Mocked Tests (Default)
docs.text:
• ✅ Fast (no network calls)
  • ✅ Reliable (no external dependencies)
  • ✅ Test error cases easily
  • ✅ Run in CI/CD without network

docs.title: E2E Tests (Optional)
docs.text:
• ✅ Real-world validation
  • ✅ Catch integration issues
  • ❌ Slower (network calls)
  • ❌ Can be flaky (network issues)
  • ❌ Require internet connection

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text:
• Use mocked tests for regular CI/CD (fast, reliable)
  • Use E2E tests for:
  • Manual validation before releases
  • Scheduled nightly builds
  • Local development validation
  • Debugging integration issues

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This document outlines the test coverage for the new plugin installation and system management features.

docs.title: Test Strategy
docs.text:
We use a hybrid approach for testing GitHub plugin installation:

  1. Mocked Tests (default, fast, reliable)
  2. Unit and integration tests with mocked GitHub API
  3. Fast execution, no network dependencies
  4. Run in all CI/CD pipelines

  5. Test error cases and edge cases easily

  6. E2E Tests (optional, real GitHub repository)

  7. End-to-end tests using a real GitHub repository
  8. Validate actual GitHub API integration
  9. Marked as @pytest.mark.e2e and @pytest.mark.slow
  10. Skip gracefully if network/repo unavailable
  11. Can be run manually or in scheduled jobs

docs.title: 1. backend/tests/unit/test_plugin_installer_github.py
docs.text:
Purpose: Unit tests for GitHub plugin installation functionality

Test Classes: - TestPluginEnumeration: Tests plugin enumeration from repositories - Auto-discovery of plugins - Enumeration using plugins.json manifest - Skipping invalid plugins - Skipping common non-plugin directories

  • TestPluginInstallFromRepo: Tests installing plugins from repositories
  • Basic installation from repo
  • Installation with frontend static assets for web components
  • Path traversal protection
  • Error handling for non-existent plugins

  • Error handling for already installed plugins

  • TestVersionChecking: Tests version checking during installation

  • Installing newer versions
  • Rejecting older versions
  • Disabling version checking

Coverage: - ✅ Plugin enumeration (auto-discovery and manifest-based) - ✅ Repository installation - ✅ Frontend static asset installation from repos - ✅ Version checking - ✅ Security (path traversal protection)

docs.title: 2. backend/tests/integration/test_api_plugins_github.py
docs.text:
Purpose: Integration tests for GitHub plugin API endpoints

Test Classes: - TestGitHubPluginEnumeration: Tests /api/plugins/github/enumerate endpoint - Successful enumeration - Branch fallback (main → master) - Error handling (not found, invalid URL)

  • TestGitHubPluginInstallation: Tests /api/plugins/github/install endpoint
  • Successful installation
  • Branch fallback during installation
  • Missing parameters validation

  • Path traversal protection

  • TestPluginUninstallAPI: Tests /api/plugins/installed/{id} DELETE endpoint

  • Successful uninstall
  • Uninstall with frontend static assets
  • Error handling for non-existent plugins

Coverage: - ✅ GitHub enumeration API - ✅ GitHub installation API - ✅ Branch fallback logic - ✅ Uninstall API - ✅ Frontend static asset cleanup on uninstall

docs.title: 3. backend/tests/integration/test_api_system.py
docs.text:
Purpose: Integration tests for system management API endpoints

Test Classes: - TestSystemRestartEndpoints: Tests restart endpoints - Restart backend (/api/system/restart-backend) - Restart frontend (/api/system/restart-frontend) - Fallback to dbus if systemctl fails - Error handling when all methods fail - Reload UI endpoint

  • TestSystemUpdateEndpoints: Tests update endpoints
  • Get update status
  • Trigger update

Coverage: - ✅ Backend restart API - ✅ Frontend restart API - ✅ Systemctl and dbus fallback - ✅ Error handling - ✅ Update status API

docs.title: 4. backend/tests/e2e/test_github_plugin_e2e.py
docs.text:
Purpose: End-to-end tests using a real GitHub repository

Test Classes: - TestGitHubPluginE2E: Tests with real GitHub repository - Enumerate plugins from real repo - Install plugin from real repo - Branch fallback with real repo - Install plugin with frontend from real repo

Coverage: - ✅ Real GitHub API integration - ✅ Actual repository structure - ✅ Network error handling - ✅ Graceful skipping when unavailable

Note: These tests are marked @pytest.mark.e2e and @pytest.mark.slow and skip by default. See E2E Test Repository Setup for setup instructions.

docs.title: Mocked Tests (Default)
docs.text:
GitHub API: - Uses unittest.mock.patch to mock httpx.AsyncClient.get - Returns mock zip file content - Tests branch fallback by returning 404 then 200 - Fast, reliable, no network dependencies

System Commands: - Uses unittest.mock.patch to mock subprocess.run - Tests both success and failure scenarios - Tests fallback from systemctl to dbus

docs.title: E2E Tests (Optional)
docs.text: Real GitHub Repository: - Uses actual httpx.AsyncClient to call GitHub API - Tests with real repository structure - Validates actual branch fallback behavior - Gracefully skips if network/repo unavailable - Can be configured via TEST_GITHUB_REPO environment variable

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• All tests use temporary directories for isolation
  • Tests clean up after themselves
  • Integration tests use mocked external services
  • Unit tests focus on business logic
  • Integration tests focus on API contracts
